Transfer mechanics found: Act 491 (HB 697) + Act 492 (HB 698) + Act 628 (2022) are cited together by LDH. The LDH page's own summary of what changed in the March 2025 Emergency Rule is the best official transfer record opened: retailers "now referenced as such and not as 'dispensaries'"; retailers may only sell Louisiana-manufactured product; permits remain 10 + 2 satellites each; 71 g / 14-day limit retained; no out-of-state delivery; authorised clinicians = Board of Medical Examiners or Board of Nursing licensees in good standing; recommendations expire ≤12 months; university-licence language removed; licences transferred to former university contractors in 2024; mold/yeast 10,000 → 100,000 CFU/g; pesticide schedule mirrored to Oregon. The January 2026 Final Rule may supersede parts of the Emergency Rule — [VERIFY] pinpoint before quoting any Emergency Rule summary as current.

1.6 Consumable hemp

1.6.1 Legal definitions and THC measurement. - "Industrial hemp" / "hemp" — R.S. 3:1481(5) (2025 Justia text): "the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant, including the seeds thereof and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a total THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis." - CONFLICT to flag: the Act 752 enrolled text (HB 952) as returned by search defines hemp with "a total delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent" — i.e. delta-9-only wording in the enrolled bill excerpt vs "total THC" wording in the 2025 Justia §1481. The current legis.la.gov §1481 must be opened to resolve which wording is in force; do not publish either as settled without that check. Either way, Louisiana's consumable regime uses "total THC" for product limits (see below), which is broader than a delta-9-only plant test. - "THC" — R.S. 3:1481 (via ATC wholesale-permit form definitions and 2023 HB 605 engrossed text): "a combination of any tetrahydrocannabinol and tetrahydrocannabinolic acid" / "a combination of tetrahydrocannabinol and tetrahydrocannabinolic acid." Act 752 digest adds: new law "defines 'THC component' as any naturally occurring cannabinoid component of industrial hemp or hemp" and "defines 'total THC' as any combination of tetrahydrocannabinol, tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, THC component, or any derivative thereof" — digest: https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1388234 (accessed 25 Oct 2026). The current §1481 numbering for "THC component" / "total THC" [VERIFY]. - "Consumable hemp product" — R.S. 3:1481(3)(a): "any product derived from industrial hemp that contains any cannabinoid, including cannabidiol or THC, and is intended for consumption or topical use." (b): "shall include commercial feed and pet products." (c): "shall not include any product manufactured or processed utilizing hemp fiber for commercial or industrial use, including textiles, building materials, clothing, paper, bioplastics, biofuel, insulation, or other similar products not intended for human consumption." Note the tension: the older ATC form definition said consumable hemp products "shall include… hemp floral material," while Act 752 bans floral hemp at retail — the current §1481 floral-material sentence [VERIFY] (the Act 752 digest says prior law allowed floral material and new law prohibits its sale/production/distribution; whether the definition was amended to delete floral material or the ban sits only in §1482 must be confirmed). - "Package" — "a group of individual servings offered together as a single unit" (2025 Justia §1481(6)); Act 752 enrolled wording: "a container or wrapping… contains one or more servings" — minor wording difference, [VERIFY] current text. - "Remote retailer" — "a person or entity who offers any consumable hemp product for sale at retail through a digital application, catalog, or the internet that can be purchased and delivered directly to a consumer in Louisiana" — §1481 (2025 Justia). - "Synthetically derived tetrahydrocannabinol" (2023 HB 605 proposal, not necessarily enacted as quoted): "any tetrahydrocannabinol that is not derived from the naturally occurring constituents of Cannabis sativa L. plant material and is not a naturally occurring constituent of Cannabis sativa L. plant material" — that 2023 bill text is PROPOSED language in the engrossed bill opened; the operative enacted ban is the §1482(C)(2) naturally-occurring-derivative rule below, not the 2023 definition unless Act 752 adopted it — [VERIFY]. - Measurement in practice: LDH registration requires a certificate of analysis (COA) from an ISO-accredited (or department-approved) independent laboratory with no direct/indirect interest in a grower/processor/wholesaler/retailer, showing batch ID, product name, dates, method, solvents/pesticides/microbials/heavy metals, cannabinoid profile by % weight, and potency (serving size, total THC/serving, servings, total THC/package in mg/g) — §1483(E)–(F). The University of Louisiana at Monroe-affiliated lab is the "preferred laboratory" once it meets requirements and commences operations — §1483(F)(2). Testing detail (panels, action limits, sampling) belongs in Part 11 (other run).

1.6.2 Per-serving / per-package THC limits (R.S. 3:1483(B)(6), legis.la.gov text opened). Verbatim: - Other products (not beverages, not tinctures for human consumption): "(i) … each serving shall not exceed five milligrams and shall be distinct and separate from other servings contained in the same package. A package shall not contain more than forty milligrams of total THC per package. (ii) A package for products other than beverages shall be child-resistant." - Beverages: "(i) A single serving of a consumable hemp beverage shall not exceed five milligrams and shall not be less than twelve ounces. (ii) Each serving shall be in an individual, tamper-evident container and distinct from other servings contained in the same package. (iii) A package of beverages shall not contain more than four individual containers." - Tinctures for human consumption: "(i) … a package shall contain no more than one ounce of an oil-based consumable hemp liquid. (ii) A serving shall be one milliliter and shall not exceed one milligram of total THC per serving. (iii) Each package shall have a dispensing dropper that is capable of dispensing not more than one serving… (iv) A tincture… shall not include any concentrated water-soluble liquid containing consumable hemp that can be consumed directly or added to any food or beverage." - Nonedible (topical) products: "(d) Nonedible consumable hemp products shall not be subject to the individual serving and package requirements of this Paragraph." - History: 8 mg/serving before Act 752 (2022 scheme); 5 mg / 40 mg from 1 Jan 2025 (Act 752). The LAC Title 49, §I-533 rule restates the same limits (beverage ≥12 fl oz, ≤5 mg, ≤1 serving/container, tamper-evident, ≤4/package; tincture 1 mL ≤1 mg, ≤30 mL, precise dropper, oil-based, child-resistant; other ≤5 mg/serving, ≤40 mg/package, child-resistant). Note the statute says tincture package "no more than one ounce" (≈30 mL) — consistent. - "Total THC" for these limits means THC + THCA + THC components/derivatives per the Act 752 digest definition — i.e. a product's delta-9 number alone does not establish compliance.

1.6.3 Which cannabinoids / product types are allowed or banned. - Allowed in principle (if LDH-registered, within limits, non-inhalable, non-floral): edibles (gummies/chewables etc. as distinct servings), beverages (≥12 oz, ≤5 mg), oil-based tinctures (≤1 mg/mL), topicals/non-edibles (serving/package caps do not apply, but registration/labelling still do), pet/commercial-feed products (within the consumable definition — specific feed/pet limits [VERIFY] in LDH rules). - Banned — R.S. 3:1482(B): "(1) Any alcoholic beverage containing any consumable hemp product. (2) Any consumable hemp product for inhalation. (3) Any floral hemp material for retail use. (4) Any product that has not received approval from [LDH] in accordance with R.S. 3:1483." And §1483(C)(2): LDH "shall not approve" (a) floral hemp material for retail sale; (b) "Any inhalable consumable hemp product, including but not limited to vapes" (with the proviso that "not for inhalation" labelling does NOT prevent a determination that a product is designed/intended for inhalation); (c) any ATC-regulated alcoholic beverage containing consumable hemp; (d) any product packaged to appeal to children (name/logo/mascot similar to a non-hemp candy/beverage product); (e) any product not complying with §1483(B). - Banned — non-naturally-occurring derivatives: §1482(C)(2): "No consumable hemp processor shall use any distillate or concentrate containing any derivative of a THC component that is not a naturally occurring cannabinoid to produce a consumable hemp product." Act 752 digest: "prohibits a consumable hemp processor from using any distillate or concentrate containing any derivative of THC that is not a naturally occurring cannabinoid." §1483(H): "The provisions of this Section do not authorize any person to manufacture, distribute, import, or sell any cannabinoid product derived from any source other than hemp." - Delta-8, delta-9, delta-10, HHC, THCA — precise status: Louisiana law does NOT name delta-8/delta-10/HHC as such in the §§1481–1484 text opened. The correct statement is functional, not nominal: (i) any cannabinoid in a consumable hemp product counts toward total THC and must fit the 5 mg / 40 mg (or beverage/tincture) limits; (ii) if it is produced via a distillate/concentrate containing a derivative that is not a naturally occurring cannabinoid, a processor may not use it; (iii) if it is in an inhalable product or floral material, it is banned at retail regardless of cannabinoid; (iv) if it is derived from a source other than hemp, it is not authorised. Whether a particular delta-8 product (hemp-derived CBD conversion vs naturally occurring trace delta-8) falls inside (ii) is a fact-specific LDH determination — [VERIFY] any LDH guidance naming delta-8, delta-10, HHC, or THCA. Do NOT state "delta-8 is banned in Louisiana" or "delta-8 is legal in Louisiana" without that guidance. - THCA flower: banned at retail as floral hemp material (§1482(B)(3) + §1483(C)(2)(a)), and as an inhalable product if intended for smoking/vaping. THCA as a component in a non-inhalable, registered product counts toward total THC — the product must still fit the serving/package caps. The oft-repeated claim that Louisiana "bans THCA" outright is overbroad; the ban is on floral/inhalable retail forms, not on the molecule in every form — flag this nuance for the parent. - Smokable hemp: retail sale banned (floral + inhalable). Rolling papers: the pre-Act 752 law excepted rolling papers from the inhalation-sale ban; whether that exception survives Act 752 [VERIFY] in current §1482 (the text opened does not show a rolling-paper exception). - Beverages: allowed only as above (≥12 oz, ≤5 mg, tamper-evident single-serving containers, ≤4/package); a retailer may NOT add a consumable hemp product to food/beverage sold at retail (§1482(C)(1)) — i.e. no on-premises infusion/dosing at retail. - FDA-approved / §1046 products excluded: §1483(K): "The provisions of this Part shall not apply to any cannabinoid product approved by [FDA] or produced in accordance with R.S. 40:1046." §1483(I): facilities processing industrial hemp products for human consumption that do NOT meet the consumable definition are regulated under the State Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Law.

1.6.4 Minimum age, verification, display. R.S. 3:1482(A)(2) (legis.la.gov text opened): "No person shall sell or offer for sale at retail any consumable hemp product to any person under the age of twenty-one. A retailer shall verify the age of any person attempting to purchase or receive a consumable hemp product prior to the sales transaction of the product. A retailer shall require a purchaser to produce a valid federal or state issued photo identification card or a digitized identification card as defined in R.S. 51:3211. A retailer shall maintain all consumable hemp products except for consumable hemp beverages in a location that is inaccessible to the public without the assistance of an employee of the retailer." History: 18+ before Act 752 (21+ only for the former "adult-use" >0.5 mg category under Act 498 of 2022); 21+ for ALL consumable hemp products from 1 Jan 2025. The "adult-use consumable hemp product" definition (>0.5 mg total THC per package) was repealed by Act 752 — Act 752 digest. Whether the 21+ rule applies to purely topical / non-intoxicating CBD products with 0 mg THC: the statute says "any consumable hemp product" without a THC threshold — on its face yes, but LDH/ATC enforcement guidance [VERIFY] before stating it applies to 0-THC topicals.

1.6.5 LDH product registration. R.S. 3:1483(B)(2)–(3): product must be "registered with the department" (fee "not more than fifty dollars for each separate and distinct product registered," in lieu of the R.S. 40:628 charge) and "receive product and label approval from the department." §1483(G)(1): LDH "shall conduct an initial review… and notify the submitting party of any deficiencies… within sixty business days of… submission. If the department fails to notify… within sixty business days…, the product may be sold by a wholesaler or retailer permitted pursuant to R.S. 3:1484 from the day following the sixtieth business day until the submitting party receives final approval or denial." §1483(G)(2)–(3): LDH provides the registered-products list to ATC/law enforcement and a scan mechanism for ATC to verify registration. §1483(G)(5): "Louisiana Hemp Product" designation process for products grown + processed in Louisiana. LAC Title 49, Ch. 5, §I-517 (via Justia): registration requires product/manufacturer/facility information, ownership >5%, and the COA; a product packaged/labelled/marketed to functionally combine servings above 5 mg total THC per serving "shall not be registered and shall be subject to revocation… pursuant to §518." Renewal cadence (annual, July 1–Aug 15 window claimed by secondary sources) [VERIFY] in LDH hemp registration guidance / LAC. Out-of-state processors: §1483(F)(2) + LDH rule summaries indicate out-of-state processors may register via endorsement/permit — [VERIFY] pinpoint (the January 2026 hemp rule PDF mentions endorsement permits suspended/revoked if the home-state permit lapses, but the full endorsement procedure was not read).

1.6.6 ATC retail permits. R.S. 3:1484(A)(1): "Each wholesaler of consumable hemp products shall apply for and obtain a permit from the office of alcohol and tobacco control" (fee capped at $500/year — §1484(A)(2) in 2022 text; ATC wholesale application form lists a $500 wholesale application fee). R.S. 3:1484(B)(1)(a) (2022 text): "Each person who sells or is about to engage in the business of selling at retail any consumable hemp product shall first apply for and obtain a permit for each place of business from [ATC]"; (B)(1)(b): each individually registered domain name of a remote retailer counts as a place of business, and "No person or entity shall be required to have a physical place of business in the state of Louisiana in order to sell consumable hemp products at retail." Special-event permit: annual, with written notice to the commissioner before each event; failure to notify is grounds for revocation — §1484(B)(2) (2022 text). Retail permit fee cap $175/location (secondary MPP summary + older §1483(B) history) — [VERIFY] current §1484 fee paragraph, as the current §1484 text was not opened in full. Location bans in §1482(A)(3) (gasoline/motor-fuel locations, truck-stop exemption R.S. 27:417) and the alcohol-premises grandfather (permit on/before 17 June 2024, per Act 752 digest) — see §1.6.4/§1.7; the alcohol-premises paragraph is cited in secondary sources as R.S. 3:1484(B)(5) (HB 539's proposed repeal target) — [VERIFY] current §1484(B)(5) text. Criminal penalties for Part VI violations in the older scheme: 1st ≤$300, 2nd ≤$1,000, 3rd+ ≤2 years + ≤$5,000 (former §1484) — current penalty location after Act 752 [VERIFY]; do not confuse with the §1483(J) unlicensed-processor penalty (1–20 years hard labour + ≤$50,000).

1.6.7 Testing and labelling (consumable hemp). Testing: processor must test the distillate/concentrate used (§1483(A)(3)) and test each batch for (a) disaggregated THC components by % of total THC, (b) serving size of an individual unit, (c) total THC mg/serving, (d) solvents/pesticides/microbials/heavy metals (§1483(A)(4)); retain test records ≥3 years (§1483(A)(5)); adhere to LDH sanitary regulations (§1483(A)(6)). COA contents §1483(E) (quoted in §1.6.1). Lab must be ISO-accredited / department-approved, independent (no interest in grower/processor/wholesaler/retailer) — §1483(F)(1). Labelling — §1483(C)(1): labels must (a) contain no medical claims; (b) have a scannable barcode/QR code/web address linked to a document/website containing the COA; (c) "Clearly state the amount of total THC per serving"; (d) "Provide a warning that consumption of products with THC may result in a failed drug test"; (e) "Accurately reflect the contents of the packaging with a variance of no greater than fifteen percent." Additional LDH rule labelling (LAC Title 49, Ch. 5, §§519–533, Jan 2026 final rule — pinpoint [VERIFY]): serving size, servings/package, THC/serving, cannabinoid profile, batch, ingredients, manufacturer — secondary summaries add FDA disclaimer / keep-out-of-reach-of-children / pregnancy warnings, which were NOT verified in the statute/rule text opened and must not be quoted as statutory requirements without opening the rule. Marketing: "Not be marketed as dietary" — §1483(B)(4); no FDA-recognised active pharmaceutical ingredient other than CBD (topicals excepted) — §1483(B)(5). Child-appealing packaging banned — §1483(C)(2)(d). Existing label approvals for products prohibited by Act 752 were extended through 31 Dec 2024 with no additional fee — §1483(C)(3) (transitional, now expired).

1.6.8 Online and shipped sales. Remote retailers are expressly contemplated: domain = place of business, no Louisiana physical place required (§1484(B)(1)(b), 2022 text — [VERIFY] survival after Act 752). A remote retailer must still hold an ATC permit per domain, sell only LDH-registered/label-approved products, verify age 21+ (photo/digitised ID — how that verification works online is an LDH/ATC guidance question [VERIFY]), and comply with the 3% excise tax as a retailer (R.S. 47:1693 — retailer reports/pays monthly). Shipment INTO Louisiana of a product that is not LDH-registered or exceeds Louisiana limits is unlawful sale/offer for sale under §1482(B)(4) / §1483(B). Shipment OUT of Louisiana: §1483(A)(7) expressly allows a permitted Louisiana processor to produce products exceeding Louisiana's per-serving/package limits IF it (a) swears in writing the product will be delivered/transported beyond state borders AND meets the receiving state/territory's product/label/THC requirements, (b) conducts the same distillate/batch tests, and (c) maintains the sworn statement + distinct out-of-state distribution records (batch ID, product name, receiving state/territory) for ≥3 years. Interstate hemp shipment generally (including through Louisiana) belongs in Part 10 (other run).

1.6.9 State response to the new federal hemp definition and the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates — NOTHING LOCATED. Searches in this run for a Louisiana LDH, ATC, LDAF, Governor, or legislative response to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 returned no official Louisiana statement, rule, or 2026 Act adopting, rejecting, or conforming to the federal redefinition. Secondary commentary (CED Clinic, Louisiana THC Drinks Law, accessed via search 25 Oct 2026) states: "No. House Bill 539 of the 2026 regular session addressed consumable hemp products but was withdrawn from the files of the House on May 11, 2026 and never became law. The framework in force remains Title 3, Part VI… including the five milligram beverage serving limit, the twenty-one age restriction, and the [ATC] permit requirement." That withdrawal claim CONFLICTS with another secondary tracker stating HB 539's disposition is unconfirmed — see §1.10. No Louisiana bill was found in this run that would (a) lower Louisiana limits to 0.4 mg/container, (b) adopt a federal total-THC plant standard, or (c) create a state enforcement delay. Arithmetic consequence (given baseline applied to Louisiana law as it stands): a Louisiana-compliant beverage (5 mg total THC in one ≥12 oz container) is 12.5× the post-11 Dec 2026 federal 0.4 mg-per-container cap; a Louisiana-compliant 40 mg package is 100× that cap; a Louisiana-compliant tincture (1 mg/mL × up to 30 mL = up to 30 mg/package) is 75× that cap. On the baseline's terms, after 11 Dec 2026 those finished products would fall outside the federal definition of hemp, even though they remain compliant with Louisiana state law as written. Whether federal enforcement, federal preemption, or a state conforming amendment changes that position before/after 11 Dec 2026 is [VERIFY — Unavailable as of 25 Oct 2026 in the sources opened]. The November 12 date matters separately for Louisiana in one respect: cannabinoids that "are not capable of being naturally produced" / synthesised outside the plant are already restricted in Louisiana by §1482(C)(2) (naturally-occurring-derivative rule), so the federal 12 Nov exclusion for non-naturally-producible cannabinoids overlaps, but does not duplicate, Louisiana's processor rule — the overlap's legal effect (e.g. for delta-8/HHC products that Louisiana currently tolerates as naturally-derived) is [VERIFY]. USDA DEA-lab testing delay to 31 Dec 2026 (baseline) affects hemp cultivation testing; Louisiana's consumable-product COA testing is LDH/ISO-based, not USDA-based — do not conflate the two testing regimes.

1.6.10 Federal Schedule III interaction for hemp — none. The 28 April 2026 Schedule III move covers state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products (baseline). It does not move hemp, CBD, delta-8, or consumable hemp products to Schedule III, and it does not change Louisiana consumable hemp law. Any claim that rescheduling "legalises hemp THC" is false on the baseline.

1.7 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning and buffers — medical and consumable hemp

Medical — packaging/labelling (historic Board rules + LDH rule summaries; current LDH January 2026 final rule pinpoint [VERIFY]): - Historic LAC Title 46, Part LIII, §2451: marijuana pharmacy "shall sell marijuana products only in a secure and light-resistant container"; products sold "in an opaque package that shall not indicate the contents of the package, the originating facility or in any other way cause another person to believe that the package may contain marijuana"; pharmacist-only dispensing (assistance by intern/technician under direct supervision; sale of dispensed product by any pharmacy employee); no samples ("No person, at a marijuana pharmacy shall provide marijuana samples"); minimum 10 hours/week open to patients/caregivers; name tags for employees; restricted prescription-department access. Whether each of these survives under LDH Title 51, Part XXIX [VERIFY] — LDH's Act 693 materials transferred permits but the rule-by-rule survival was not opened. - Secondary LDH-rule synthesis (Flourish/Distru, [VERIFY]): tightly sealed, light-impermeable packaging; labels with patient/clinician names, quantity, directions, expiry, batch ID, ingredients/allergens, THC/CBD mg, net weight, contaminant-test stamp, "Medical Use Only" + child/driver/pregnancy warnings, ≥1/16-inch English text. Do NOT publish that label list as LDH rule text without opening the January 2026 final rule. - Advertising (medical): NO advertising statute or LDH advertising rule was opened in this run. Secondary CannBus material claims "Strict public-facing media restrictions enforced under state advertising rules (Section 13)" — that claim is UNSOURCED in the material opened and [VERIFY]. Do not state a medical advertising ban, a ban on specific media, or an advertising approval requirement until an LDH rule / statute is located. The only advertising-adjacent statutory text found is the consumable hemp child-appealing-packaging ban (§1483(C)(2)(d)) and the no-medical-claims label rule (§1483(C)(1)(a)).

Medical — delivery: §1046(E) requires sale "in person by a marijuana retail permit holder located in Louisiana," BUT §1046(G)(7) requires: "Each marijuana retail permit holder shall offer delivery to patients in each zip code within its region at least once per month." LDH summary adds: "Retailers may not deliver to addresses located outside of the state of Louisiana." Reconciliation: "in person" in (E) appears to mean "by a Louisiana permit holder" (as opposed to mail-order/out-of-state sale), not "patient must walk into the store," since (G)(7) delivery + LMMTS "to delivery" tracking (§1046(F)(1)(a)) presuppose retailer delivery — but the delivery procedure (who may deliver, vehicle/security, signature/ID, delivery to caregiver vs patient, delivery fees) was NOT opened — [VERIFY] in LDH rules. Do not state that home delivery is unavailable (it is required at least monthly per ZIP) or that it is unrestricted.

Medical — zoning/buffers: Statutory inter-retailer buffers (not school/church buffers): §1046(G)(6)(a): "No marijuana retail permit holder shall locate within a fifteen-mile radius of another retail permit holder's marijuana retail location." (b): in a region encompassing a parish >350,000 population (most recent decennial census), 10-mile radius. (c): in a region encompassing a municipality >350,000, 5-mile radius. (d): waivable by written mutual agreement of all affected holders filed with LDH. Satellite approval must consider "any unserved parishes within the region" — §1046(G)(3)(d). NO state school/church/park buffer for medical retailers was found in §1046 — local zoning (Part 3, other run) may impose buffers, but do not import a 1,000-foot state buffer. The 2026 school-zone law (HB 568 / Act 305, [VERIFY]) concerns USE/possession violations near schools, not retailer siting — do not conflate it with a zoning buffer.

Consumable hemp — packaging/labelling: §1483(B)(6) child-resistant (non-beverage) + tamper-evident (beverage) + §1483(C) label rules, quoted in §1.6.7; LAC Title 49, §I-533 restates serving/package limits. Display: non-beverage products inaccessible without employee assistance (§1482(A)(2)). No state buffer/zoning rule for hemp retailers was found in Title 3, Part VI — location rules are permit + gasoline + alcohol-premises rules (§1.6.6), plus general local zoning/business licensing (Part 3, other run).

Advertising (consumable hemp): No standalone advertising statute was opened. Operative advertising-adjacent rules found: no medical claims on labels (§1483(C)(1)(a)); not marketed as dietary (§1483(B)(4)); no child-appealing name/logo/mascot (§1483(C)(2)(d)); no inhalation marketing that evades the inhalable ban (label "not for inhalation" does not save a product designed/intended for inhalation — §1483(C)(2)(b)). General ATC alcohol-advertising rules do not apply to hemp except via the alcohol-beverage ban. Any broader hemp advertising ban/restriction [VERIFY].

1.8 Seed-to-sale tracking system used

Name: Louisiana Medical Marijuana Tracking System (LMMTS). Statutory basis: R.S. 40:1046(F)(1)(a) — each permitted retailer "shall acquire and maintain all software, hardware, and communications infrastructure necessary to ensure connectivity to and implementation of the [LMMTS], from seed to delivery to an approved laboratory, to wholesale to permitted retailers, to wholesale to another licensed cultivation facility, to delivery to an authorized researcher, to sale to patients or caregivers by permitted retailers, or to destruction." §1046(F)(2): sellers "shall comply with the reporting requirements of the LMMTS." §1046.1(A)(3) (legis.la.gov text): "'LMMTS' means the electronic seed-to-sale tracking system approved by the department." LDH: "Laboratories are required to utilize the [LMMTS]" (LDH medical page). Secondary sources name the vendor as Metrc and describe POS-to-LMMTS interfaces and 24-hour logging — VENDOR [VERIFY]: no LDH page opened in this run names Metrc, and the parent must not publish a vendor name on secondary authority alone. Whether LMMTS has replaced PMP reporting for resident patients, or whether both run in parallel, [VERIFY] (see §1.2, R.S. 40:1001 row). Consumable hemp has NO seed-to-sale system: it has LDH product registration + ATC permit + COA/batch traceability (QR/barcode to COA) + LDH's scan-verification mechanism for ATC (§1483(G)(3)) — do not describe hemp as "tracked in LMMTS."

1.9 Employment and drug-testing protections for patients (including state employees)

The only enacted employment protection found is for STATE employers — R.S. 49:1016 (Act 651 of 2022, HB 988, eff. 1 Aug 2022). Verbatim: - A: "No state employer shall subject an employee or prospective employee to negative employment consequences based solely on a positive drug test for marijuana, marijuana components, including tetrahydrocannabinols, or marijuana metabolites if the employee or prospective employee has been clinically diagnosed as suffering from a debilitating medical condition and a licensed physician has recommended marijuana for therapeutic use by the employee in accordance with R.S. 40:1046." - B: "Subsection A… shall not be construed to prohibit the imposition of negative employment consequences on an employee who uses or is impaired by marijuana on the premises of the employer or during work hours or an employee whose principal responsibility is to operate a state vehicle, maintain a state vehicle, or supervise any employee who drives or maintains a state vehicle." - C: "The provisions of this Section shall not apply to emergency medical services, law enforcement, public safety officials, any state employee of the horse racing commission, and firefighter services." - Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=1297397 (accessed 25 Oct 2026 via search). Limits — state this plainly: (1) "State employer" only — private employers and parish/municipal employers are NOT covered by §49:1016 on its face (secondary drug-screening guides agree: "applies to state government employers only, not private or local government employers"). (2) "Based solely on a positive drug test" only — on-premises/during-hours use or impairment, and vehicle-operator/maintainer/supervisor roles, are expressly carved out. (3) Excluded occupations in (C) have NO protection even from a state employer. (4) The statute still says "licensed physician" — whether nurse-practitioner/medical-psychologist recommendations (authorised clinicians under §1046(B) since Act 444 of 2022) are covered by §49:1016's "licensed physician" wording [VERIFY — textual gap; do not assume coverage]. (5) No protection was found for: hiring quotas, reasonable accommodation beyond the test-result rule, off-duty use discipline unrelated to a drug test, or protection against federal/DOT testing. (6) Workers' compensation: §1046(J) — employers/insurers "shall not be obliged or ordered to pay for medical marijuana in claims arising under Title 23" — i.e. no reimbursement duty. Return-to-work drug-test / indemnity interaction under R.S. 23:1221(g) (secondary workers'-comp analysis) [VERIFY] — do not state a workers'-comp protection. (7) Drug-testing law generally: Louisiana's voluntary drug-testing statutes (R.S. 49:1015 — public-employer testing authority: post-accident, reasonable suspicion, rehabilitation-monitoring, pre-employment, random safety/security-sensitive testing) predate and sit alongside §1016; §1016 is an exception to consequences, not a ban on testing. (8) Federal safety-sensitive / DOT / federal-employee testing is governed by federal law and the given baseline, not §49:1016.

Taxes (Part 2) and Local Rules (Part 3)

Scope note. This is part of the combined Louisiana dossier (Parts 0–12), as corrected in the 28 October 2026 audit. See Part 1 (audit) at the top of this file for corrections and items still unverified.

Date accessed for every fact below: 25 October 2026, unless a source's own publication date is stated. Where a page could not be opened directly, or where sources conflict, the item is marked Verify or Unavailable and is NOT stated as settled law.

Federal baseline — given, not re-researched. State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity only; hemp PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-registered-lab hemp testing is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law. No contradiction to that baseline was found in the Louisiana tax or local-rule sources checked for this file. The one apparent contradiction in secondary tax guides — claims that a 15% wholesale excise tax on adult-use cannabis took effect 1 January 2026 — is addressed in §2.8: Louisiana has no adult-use market and no such enacted tax was located; the claim appears to conflate the failed 2025 HB 636 proposal with law.

Terminology. Louisiana has parishes, not counties. "Parish" is used throughout. Place names were checked against same-name places in other states (Lafayette, Alexandria, Monroe, Covington, Hammond, etc.); every jurisdiction named below is the Louisiana one.

PART 2 — TAXES

State sales tax 5% from 1 Jan 2025 is now cited to the Louisiana Department of Revenue (RIB 25-007), not secondary summaries. Medical sales-tax exemption: R.S. 47:305.2(B) exempts from tax “imposed by any taxing authority”, (B)(11) covering marijuana recommended for therapeutic use — state and local. The 7% gross-sales fee is a licensee fee collected by the Department of Revenue and transferred monthly to the Disability Services Fund (R.S. 28:826), as quoted in current R.S. 40:1046(H)(4)(c) text in a 2025 legis bill text; no further split of that fund is stated. Consumable hemp excise: R.S. 47:1693(A) 3% of retail sales price, reported monthly by the retailer and paid by the 20th of the following month; disposition under R.S. 47:1696, after Bond Security and Redemption Fund requirements, to the Early Childhood Education Fund. The 15% (HB 187, 2025) and 20% (HB 235, 2025) proposals are NOT law. Louisiana §280E decoupling remains Unverified — no Department of Revenue statement or current Title 47 decoupling provision was opened in this audit; the federal Schedule III §280E lifting for medical activity (given baseline) is a separate federal statement. Dollar sales by year in §6.1 remain a secondary compilation (Motley Fool citing LDR) — the Act 150 report contains volumes, not dollar sales — and are labelled as such, not as an official LDR table.

The single most common error in secondary guides, corrected here: Louisiana patients do NOT pay state or local sales tax on therapeutic marijuana. Several secondary guides (e.g. CannBus Q3 2026 summary, SalesTaxHandbook's "7% sales tax on every purchase") describe a 5% / 4.45% state sales tax on medical sales, or conflate the 7% gross-sales fee with a point-of-sale sales tax. The current statute says the opposite. The 7% is a fee on the cultivator's gross sales, collected by LDR, not a tax charged to the patient at the counter. The patient-facing sales-tax exemption is R.S. 47:305.2(B)(11), quoted verbatim in §2.2.

2.1 Medical marijuana: the 7% gross-sales fee — rate, payer, collector, distribution

Citation: La. Rev. Stat. § 40:1046(H)(4)(c) (current text, as amended through Acts 2025, Nos. 513 and 514).

Verbatim operative text (opened and read 25 October 2026):

"(c) Assess a fee of seven percent of the gross sales of therapeutic marijuana. The fee shall be reported and paid by the licensee. The fee shall be collected by the Department of Revenue and shall be subject to the provisions of Chapter 18 of Subtitle II of Title 47 of the Louisiana Revised Statutes of 1950. The Department of Revenue shall transfer monthly to the state treasury for deposit into the Disability Services Fund, as established in R.S. 28:826, the amount of revenues collected in accordance with this Subparagraph."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046/ (Justia republication of the 2025 Louisiana Laws; official text is on legis.la.gov — see note below) — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • Official statute portal: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx (search R.S. 40:1046) — the legis.la.gov law page itself was not successfully opened in this research window for §40:1046, so the verbatim text above is taken from the Justia republication of the same statute and should be re-checked against legis.la.gov before publication. Verify (official-portal re-check).

Who pays. "The fee shall be reported and paid by the licensee" — i.e. the cultivation licensee (the statute caps cultivation licences at two, R.S. 40:1046(H)(1)(a)), not the retail permit holder and not the patient. Earlier versions of the statute described the payer as "the licensed production facility or permitted contractor that sells therapeutic marijuana to marijuana pharmacies"; the current text shortens this to "the licensee". The economic incidence (whether the fee is passed through in wholesale prices) is a market question, not stated in the statute.

Collector and enforcement regime. Collected by the Department of Revenue and "subject to the provisions of Chapter 18 of Subtitle II of Title 47" — the general tax collection, penalty and enforcement chapter. The Department of Revenue therefore administers this fee as if it were a tax for collection purposes, even though the statute calls it a "fee".

Distribution. Monthly transfer to the state treasury for deposit into the Disability Services Fund, R.S. 28:826.

Naming discrepancy — Verify. Older versions of §40:1046 and many secondary sources (including the Motley Fool state-revenue table cited in §2.9) name the destination the "Community and Family Support System Fund". The current text read for this file says "Disability Services Fund, as established in R.S. 28:826". Whether R.S. 28:826 was renamed, or the fund was restructured, was not confirmed in this window. Verify the current name and history of R.S. 28:826 before publication; do not use "Community and Family Support System Fund" as the current destination without that check. No split percentage (e.g. a share retained for LDH/LDAF regulatory costs) appears in the current §40:1046(H)(4)(c) text read here. Earlier versions did contain language allocating an amount, pursuant to legislative appropriation, for regulatory/administrative/enforcement expenses; that language does not appear in the current paragraph as read. Verify whether a separate appropriation or allocation provision now performs that function.

Related state fees (not taxes, but routinely confused with them). Same statute, R.S. 40:1046: - Cultivation licence: annual licence fee of $100,000 from each licensee, plus a nonrefundable $10,000 application fee — R.S. 40:1046(H)(4)(a)–(b). Source: same Justia page, accessed 25 October 2026. - Retail permit: annual retail permit fee of $22,500 charged to each of the ten retail permit holders — R.S. 40:1046(G)(1)(b), as amended by Acts 2025, No. 657 (HB 657, effective 1 August 2025, per BillTrack50 summary). Source for the $22,500 figure in current text: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046/ — accessed 25 October 2026. The HB 657 enactment itself should be re-checked on legis.la.gov. Verify (Act number for the $22,500 fee).

Sunset. R.S. 40:1046(M): "The provisions of this Section shall terminate on July 1, 2030." Source: same page, accessed 25 October 2026. The 7% fee therefore terminates with the section unless extended — a material caveat for any forward-looking revenue discussion.

Amendment history (from the Acts line at the foot of §40:1046). Acts 1991, No. 874; Acts 2015, No. 261 (eff. 29 June 2015); Acts 2016, Nos. 96, 567; Acts 2018, Nos. 206, 496, 708, 715; Acts 2019, Nos. 207, 284, 331; Acts 2020, No. 286; Acts 2021, No. 424 (eff. 1 January 2022); Acts 2022, Nos. 271, 444, 491, 492; Acts 2023, Nos. 311, 322; Acts 2024, Nos. 150, 693 (eff. 1 January 2025); Acts 2025, Nos. 513, 514 (eff. 1 July 2025). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046/ — accessed 25 October 2026. The transfer of regulation to the Louisiana Department of Health and the current fee wording sit within this amendment chain; the agency-transfer detail itself belongs to Part 1 and is not re-litigated here.

2.2 Medical marijuana: sales-tax treatment — exempt, state and local

Citation: La. Rev. Stat. § 47:305.2(B)(11) (as reorganised by Acts 2024, 3rd Ex. Sess., No. 11, §2, eff. 4 December 2024, and Acts 2025, Nos. 156, 339, 384).

Verbatim operative text (opened and read 25 October 2026):

"B. The following items shall be exempt from the sales and use tax imposed by any taxing authority: … (11) The sale of marijuana recommended for therapeutic use by qualified patients as defined in R.S. 40:1046."

  • Source: https://law.Justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-47/rs-47-305-2/ — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • Corroboration from the Louisiana Department of Revenue itself: LDR's "Active Sales and Use Tax Exemptions" chart (2024 3rd Extraordinary Session and 2025 Regular Session) lists "Sales of marijuana recommended for therapeutic use" (former R.S. 47:301(10)(a)(ii)) as Active, Retained, Both [state and local], new citation R.S. 47:305.2(B)(11). Source: https://dam.ldr.la.gov/miscellaneous/Chart%20of%20Active%20Sales%20and%20Use%20Tax%20Exemptions%2024%203ES%20and%2025%20RS.pdf — accessed 25 October 2026.

What this means in practice: - A qualified patient's purchase of recommended therapeutic marijuana at a permitted retail location is not subject to the 5% state sales tax, nor to any parish, municipal, school-board or special-district sales tax. The exemption is in subsection B ("imposed by any taxing authority"), not subsection A ("imposed by the state" only). - Subsection C ("A political subdivision may provide for a sales and use tax exemption for any item exempted from state sales and use tax purposes pursuant to the provisions of this Section") does not undo subsection B for this item; it is a general enabling sentence. The LDR chart's "Both" treatment confirms the intended state-and-local scope. Verify only in the sense that a local collector's own rate schedule should still be checked for a specific address — the statute is clear. - This exemption is why older reporting (e.g. a 2019 report that LDR would apply the full sales tax because marijuana is "recommended" rather than "prescribed") is now out of date and must not be quoted as current law. The legislature cured the recommended-vs-prescribed distinction by enacting the express exclusion, formerly R.S. 47:301(10)(a)(ii) ("retail sale or sale at retail shall not include marijuana recommended for therapeutic use … as defined in R.S. 40:1046"), now carried in R.S. 47:305.2(B)(11).

No separate medical excise tax. No Louisiana statute imposing a distinct excise tax on therapeutic marijuana sales (as opposed to the 7% gross-sales fee on cultivators) was located. Secondary statements that "there is no additional excise tax on medical marijuana in Louisiana" are consistent with the statute text found. The only per-gram figure encountered — a SalesTaxHandbook claim of a "$3.50 per gram sales tax" — appears in no statute located and is treated as unsubstantiated; do not use.

2.3 General state sales tax — the rate that applies to everything else, including consumable hemp

  • Current state rate: 5%. Increased from 4.45% to 5% effective 1 January 2025 under Acts 2024, 3rd Ex. Sess., Nos. 10 (HB 8) and 11 (HB 10). The 5% rate runs through 31 December 2029 and reduces to 4.75% effective 1 January 2030. Sources (secondary summaries of the Acts, consistent with each other): https://www.eidebailly.com/insights/blogs/2024/12/20241220_louisiana and https://webiis10.mondaq.com/home/redirect/original/1587300?location=sourceoriginal — both accessed 25 October 2026. The underlying levies are R.S. 47:302 (2%), 47:321 (1%), 47:321.1 (1%) and 47:331 (1%), per the résumé digest for Acts 2025, No. 384: https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1430228 — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • Why the rate matters for hemp but not for medical marijuana: consumable hemp products are tangible personal property sold at retail. No provision in R.S. 47:305.2 exempts them, and the only express hemp-related sales-tax carve-out located is the excise-tax exclusion in R.S. 47:1693(B) (FDA-approved CBD / R.S. 40:1046 therapeutic products are excluded from the excise tax — see §2.4), which does not exempt a product from sales tax. The general conclusion — consumable hemp is subject to state + local sales tax plus the 3% excise — follows from the structure of the statutes, but no LDR FAQ or bulletin expressly stating "consumable hemp products are subject to sales tax" was located in this window. Verify with LDR before publishing that sentence as an LDR position.
  • No Louisiana municipal income tax. No municipality in Louisiana imposes an income tax; income tax is state-only. Source (secondary): https://legalclarity.org/tax-in-new-orleans-sales-property-income-and-more/ — accessed 25 October 2026. This is general background, not cannabis-specific, and is included only to prevent the common error of assuming a city income-tax layer.

2.4 Consumable hemp excise tax — 3%, retailer-paid, monthly, dedicated fund

Citation: La. Rev. Stat. §§ 47:1692–1696 (Chapter 19, "Consumable Hemp Product Tax").

Verbatim operative text of §47:1693(A)–(B) (official legis.la.gov law page, opened and read 25 October 2026):

"A. There is hereby levied an excise tax upon each retail sale of consumable hemp products within the state of Louisiana. The tax levied in this Chapter shall be at the rate of three percent of the retail sales price of the consumable hemp product. The excise tax shall be levied in addition to state and local sales and use tax or any other tax, and shall be reported monthly by the retailer on forms prescribed by the secretary and paid by the retailer on or before the twentieth day of the month following the month to which the tax is applicable."

"B. The provisions of this Section shall not apply to any CBD product that has been approved for marketing as a prescription medication by the United States Food and Drug Administration or that is recommended for therapeutic use pursuant to R.S. 40:1046."

  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=1148943 — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • History line on the same page: "Acts 2019, No. 247, §1, eff. Aug. 1, 2019; Acts 2021, No. 336, §2." Note on the same page: "See Acts 2019, No. 247, re: tax year applicability."

Who pays, and on what base. - Taxpayer: the retailer. The tax is levied "upon each retail sale" and is "reported monthly by the retailer … and paid by the retailer". "Retail sale" means the sale or transfer to a consumer for any purpose other than resale; "retailer" means a person or entity that sells or offers consumable hemp products to a consumer (R.S. 47:1692 definitions, as summarised on https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/louisiana/la-laws/louisiana_revised_statutes_47-1693 — accessed 25 October 2026; the legis.la.gov §1692 page itself was not opened — Verify definitions against legis.la.gov). - Base: retail sales price. Not wholesale price, not weight, not THC content. A wholesaler-to-retailer sale is not the taxable event under this chapter. - In addition to sales tax. The 3% sits on top of state and local sales and use tax (and any other tax). A compliant consumable-hemp retail sale therefore bears three layers: 5% state sales tax + local sales tax + 3% hemp excise (subject to the §2.3 Verify note on the sales-tax layer). - Filing mechanics (LDR). Form R-5024, "Consumable Hemp Products Tax Return", filed monthly, due on or before the 20th day of the month following the reporting period (next business day if the 20th falls on a weekend or legal holiday), filed and paid electronically via LaTAP. Multi-location retailers complete Schedule A (Form R-5024A) listing each location's address, ATC permit number, NAICS code and gross retail sales. Source: LDR instructions R-5024i (8/21): https://dam.ldr.la.gov/taxforms/5024i-8-21.pdf — accessed 25 October 2026. - History of the tax. Enacted by Acts 2019, No. 247 (HB 560, 2019 Regular Session), originally as the "Industrial Hemp-Derived CBD" tax at 3%, effective 1 August 2019 but applicable to tax periods beginning on or after 1 January 2020 (Act 247, §2). Renamed and base-expanded by Acts 2021, No. 336, §2, effective 1 August 2021: LDR's instructions state "Act 336 of the 2021 Regular Legislative Session changed the name of this tax from Industrial Hemp-Derived CBD to Consumable Hemp Products effective August 1, 2021, and expanded the taxable base" and that from that date the taxable definition "includes industrial hemp-derived CBD products". Source: https://dam.ldr.la.gov/taxforms/5024i-8-21.pdf — accessed 25 October 2026; enrolled Act 247 text: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1144112 — accessed 25 October 2026.

Distribution — Early Childhood Education Fund. - R.S. 47:1696 (as enacted by Act 247): "After satisfaction of the requirements of the Bond Security and Redemption Fund as required under Article VII, Section 9(B) of the Louisiana Constitution, the state treasurer shall deposit in and credit to the Early Childhood Education Fund the revenues collected as provided in this Chapter." Source: enrolled Act 247 text, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1144112 — accessed 25 October 2026. - Corroborated as present law by the official House digest for HB 235 (2025): "Present law dedicates all revenues collected from the excise tax on consumable hemp products to the La. Early Childhood Education Fund." Source: https://legis.la.gov/LEGIS/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1400958 — accessed 25 October 2026. - Verify: the current legis.la.gov text of §47:1696 was not opened directly in this window (the §1693 page was; §1696 was located only via the Act and the digest). Re-check §1696 on legis.la.gov before publication, and confirm whether any later Act redirected part of the fund.

Tax applies even to products whose sale is otherwise prohibited — LDR position. - LDR's FAQ states that because prohibited products (e.g. inhalable products, alcoholic beverages containing CBD) are included in the definition of "consumable hemp product" for excise-tax purposes, "the consumable hemp product tax is due and must be paid if the product is sold at retail in Louisiana or imported for consumption." Source: https://revenue.louisiana.gov/tax-education-and-faqs/faqs/excise-taxes/consumable-hemp-products/what-consumable-hemp-products-are-prohibited/ — accessed 25 October 2026. This is an LDR administrative position, not statute text, and it does not make an otherwise unlawful sale lawful.

Exclusions from the excise tax. §47:1693(B) only: (i) a CBD product approved for marketing as a prescription medication by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration; (ii) a product recommended for therapeutic use under R.S. 40:1046. Ordinary over-the-counter CBD and THC consumable hemp products are not excluded.

No wholesale hemp excise. No enacted wholesale-level consumable-hemp excise tax was located. The 15% wholesale figure in some 2026 guides traces to the failed HB 636 proposal (see §2.8), not to Chapter 19.

2.5 Parish and municipal sales taxes — how they stack, and why a single statewide number is wrong

  • Structure. Louisiana sales tax is a stack: 5% state (see §2.3) + parish levies + municipal levies + school-board and special-district levies where applicable. The local portion is set by the local taxing authority, generally subject to voter approval, and is collected by the parish/local collector — not by LDR — except for the state portion. A retailer must therefore determine the rate for the sale address, not for the parish in the abstract: rates vary within a parish (e.g. Baton Rouge vs. Baker vs. Central vs. economic-development districts within East Baton Rouge Parish).
  • Illustrative combined general-goods rates (secondary sources — Verify each address against the local collector / Louisiana Uniform Local Sales Tax Board lookup before use). These rates are for taxable general goods (and, subject to §2.3, consumable hemp). They do NOT apply to therapeutic marijuana, which is exempt under §2.2:
  • New Orleans (Orleans Parish): 10.00% combined (5% state + 5% local). Sources: https://www.commenda.io/usa/louisiana/is-clothing-taxable and https://legalclarity.org/louisiana-sales-tax-rates-exemptions-and-local-variations/ — both accessed 25 October 2026. Note: French Quarter and Riverwalk–Spanish Plaza economic-development overlays push some New Orleans zones above 10% (secondary claim, same sources).
  • Baton Rouge (East Baton Rouge Parish): 10.50% combined (5% state + 5.50% local) for the city proper; Baker and Central at 11%; Harveston / Third-Florida economic development districts at 12.50%. Source: https://legalclarity.org/louisiana-sales-tax-rates-exemptions-and-local-variations/ and https://www.commenda.io/usa/louisiana/sales-tax-rates — both accessed 25 October 2026.
  • Jefferson Parish: 11.75% combined in the SalesTaxHandbook / SalesTaxHelper tables (5% state + local/municipal stack). Source: https://www.salestaxhandbook.com/louisiana/rates — accessed 25 October 2026. An older table showing 9.75% (5% + 4.75%) reflects a parish-only figure without municipal add-ons and must not be quoted as the rate a shopper in, say, Kenner or Metairie actually pays.
  • Other checked parishes, combined general-goods rates from the same 2026 tables (secondary, address-dependent, Verify): St. Tammany 10.83%, Lafayette 11.25%, Caddo 11.35%, Calcasieu 12.75%, Ouachita 12.99%, Rapides 11%, Bossier 10.25%, Livingston 11.50%, Tangipahoa 11%, Terrebonne 10.50%, Ascension 11%, St. Landry 12.55%. Source: https://www.salestaxhandbook.com/louisiana/rates — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • What this means for a consumable-hemp retailer: add the 3% excise to the combined rate above. Example, for illustration only (Verify the address rate first): a consumable-hemp sale in New Orleans at the 10.00% combined sales-tax rate would bear 10.00% + 3.00% = 13.00% in state/local sales tax plus hemp excise, before any occupational licence tax (see §2.6).
  • Remote / shipped sales. Louisiana requires destination-based collection for remote sellers; the consumer use-tax fallback (8.45% in-lieu rate cited on LDR's consumer use-tax page, comprising state tax plus 4% distributed to local governments) is a consumer self-remittance mechanism, not the retailer's rate. Source: https://revenue.louisiana.gov/individuals/general-resources/consumer-use-tax/ — accessed 25 October 2026. Verify how LDR treats remote consumable-hemp retailers' excise-tax collection specifically; the ATC remote-retailer permit (per location and per domain name) is a Part 4 matter, but its tax consequence is that each domain/location is a separate reporting unit on Form R-5024A.

2.6 Other state and local business taxes that fall on cannabis/hemp businesses

  • Occupational licence tax (general business tax, not cannabis-specific). Louisiana parishes and municipalities levy an annual occupational licence tax on businesses, generally on gross receipts/sales under graduated tables in R.S. 47:341 et seq. (retail table at R.S. 47:354). The minimum is $50; a New Orleans retail example in secondary sources runs from $50 (up to $50,000 in activity) upward, with a $6,200+ figure cited for activity above $5.5 million, and a general catch-all of 0.1% of gross receipts ($50 minimum, $2,000 maximum) for businesses not covered by a specific table. Sources (secondary): https://legalclarity.org/do-i-need-a-business-license-in-louisiana/ and https://legalclarity.org/tax-in-new-orleans-sales-property-income-and-more/ — both accessed 25 October 2026. Verify: no cannabis- or hemp-specific occupational-licence classification was located; whether a marijuana pharmacy or hemp retailer is taxed as "retail" or under another table, and the treatment in each checked parish, is Unavailable from the sources in this window and must be confirmed with the local collector. Do not quote a cannabis-specific occupational-licence amount.
  • Property (ad valorem) tax. General parish/municipal property tax applies to business real property and, where applicable, business personal property. No cannabis-specific rate or exemption was located. Unavailable / not cannabis-specific — do not elaborate beyond this sentence without a Part 6 market source.
  • Controlled Dangerous Substances (stamp) tax. The state checkbook's FY2022 tax-collection table lists a "Marijuana & Controlled Dangerous Substance Tax" line of $1,969 (gross = net, no refunds shown). This is a separate illicit-market stamp-tax line, not a tax on the licensed medical programme or on lawful hemp, and it is included here only so it is not mistaken for medical/hemp revenue. Source: https://checkbook.la.gov/Reports/AnnualTaxCollections/FY2022TaxCollection.pdf — accessed 25 October 2026. Verify the current statute (R.S. 47:2601 et seq. — citation not confirmed in this window) before citing it.

2.7 IRS §280E, Louisiana conformity/decoupling, and the Schedule III change — in plain terms

This is the section where secondary sources conflict. The conflict is reported, not resolved by picking the more convenient source.

2.7.1 The federal rule, and what changed on 28 April 2026 (given baseline)

  • IRC §280E disallows deductions and credits for any trade or business consisting of trafficking in a Schedule I or II controlled substance. Before 28 April 2026, state-licensed medical marijuana was Schedule I federally, so §280E applied in full to Louisiana's cultivators, pharmacies and labs at the federal level (cost of goods sold remained deductible; rent, payroll, marketing, utilities, depreciation and similar ordinary expenses did not).
  • Under the given baseline, state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). §280E by its terms reaches only Schedule I and II substances. The baseline therefore states §280E is "generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity". For Louisiana, that means: a state-licensed cultivator, pharmacy or lab dealing only in Louisiana medical marijuana should, from the effective date, be able to deduct ordinary business expenses federally like any other business — subject to the normal rules (e.g. cost-of-goods-sold vs. expense characterisation) and to any IRS guidance or litigation that follows. Verify IRS guidance specifically addressing Louisiana licensees; none was located in this window.
  • Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I, so §280E still applies in full to any adult-use activity. Louisiana has no legal adult-use market, so this limb has no lawful Louisiana taxpayer at present; it would matter only to an illicit operator (who remains fully subject to §280E) or if adult use were legalised.
  • Lawful hemp is not a Schedule I or II substance (hemp is excluded from the federal definition of marihuana). §280E therefore does not apply to a lawful hemp business on the basis of hemp alone. Verify the treatment of a business that handles both lawful hemp and a product that tests over the THC limit and is therefore marijuana — that product, and potentially the business, would present a §280E question that no Louisiana guidance located here answers.

2.7.2 Does Louisiana decouple from §280E? — Conflicting, and the specialist analysis is the more specific source

  • Claim A (secondary lists): The Marijuana Policy Project's state list places Louisiana in the "Medical-Only [states] Allowing Cannabis Deductions" column, alongside Arkansas, Hawaii and Pennsylvania. Cannabis CPA's 2025 Louisiana guide states "Louisiana does not conform to federal IRC §280E. Medical operators may deduct ordinary business expenses on their state returns." Sources: https://mpp.org/issues/legalization/states-allowing-state-legal-cannabis-business-expenses-deductions-despite-280e/ and https://cannabiscpa.tax/louisiana-cannabis-tax-guide-2025-edition/ — both accessed 25 October 2026. Neither source cites a Louisiana decoupling statute, regulation or LDR ruling.
  • Claim B (Louisiana tax specialist, more specific and statute-mechanism-based): AndreTaxCo's Louisiana cannabis §280E analysis states, for both individual and corporate income tax: "Louisiana conforms to the Internal Revenue Code. The starting point is Federal Adjusted Gross Income [individual] / Federal taxable income after adjustments [corporate]. There is no provision that states Section 280E does not apply." Source: https://www.andretaxco.com/louisiana-cannabis-280e — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • Why Claim B is structurally stronger, and why the file still marks this Verify: Louisiana's individual income tax starts from federal adjusted gross income and its corporation income tax starts from federal taxable income (Louisiana net income computed in accordance with federal law, subject to Louisiana modifications). If federal taxable income already reflects the §280E disallowance, and Louisiana has enacted no modification adding those expenses back, the disallowance flows into the Louisiana base automatically. A "decoupling" state is one that has enacted such an add-back/modification. No such Louisiana statute was located in this research window — no R.S. 47:287.xx or R.S. 47:293 modification for cannabis expenses was found. Claim A may reflect a misreading of Louisiana's lack of an express conformity statute, or of another state's law. Conclusion for the parent: do NOT state in the final HTML that "Louisiana decouples from §280E" or that "Louisiana allows state deductions despite §280E". State instead: no Louisiana decoupling provision was located; the specialist analysis says §280E flows through; secondary lists to the contrary cite no statute and are treated as unverified. Flag for follow-up with LDR / a Louisiana tax opinion.
  • Practical consequence of the Schedule III change for the decoupling question: For medical licensees, the question is now largely moot going forward, if Louisiana follows the federal Schedule III classification for its own starting-point computation. Because Louisiana starts from the federal figure, a federal return that now allows the deductions should produce a Louisiana starting point that also reflects them — without any need for a decoupling statute. Verify two things before stating this as settled: (i) Louisiana's IRC conformity date / whether Louisiana has frozen conformity to a pre-April-2026 Code version for any tax year; (ii) whether LDR has issued guidance, a bulletin or a regulation on Schedule III medical marijuana. Neither was located in this window. For any pre-28-April-2026 tax year, the old position (federal disallowance flowing into Louisiana, no add-back located) is the position to describe, with the same Verify flag on LDR guidance.
  • University-affiliated licensees and their contractors (per the commission's Louisiana note). The two cultivation licences were historically held through contracts with the LSU AgCenter and the Southern University Agricultural Center, and the current statute provides that the licences issued 1 July 2024 were to the entities that held those contracts on 1 January 2024 (R.S. 40:1046(H)(1)(b)). Tax follows the taxpayer entity, not the university affiliation: a private contractor/licensee is taxed as a business taxpayer; a university itself, as a state institution, is not in the same income-tax position. No Louisiana ruling was located allocating §280E, the 7% fee, or sales-tax treatment differently between the university and its contractor, or treating the contractor as an exempt instrumentality. Verify / Unavailable: whether any contractor agreement or LDR ruling treats contractor income as university income for tax purposes. Do not assume an exemption.
  • Labs. A testing laboratory that does not traffic in marijuana (it tests samples) presents a different §280E question from a cultivator or retailer; the specialist source notes hemp and non-plant-touching businesses may be eligible for R&D credits subject to §280E analysis. No Louisiana lab-specific §280E guidance was located. Verify.

House Committee on Ways and Means voted 8–7 against reporting the bill (May 2025, per Marijuana Moment). BillTrack50: Dead 12 June 2025. No Act number. Sources: https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1404690 (bill text) and https://www.marijuanamoment.net/louisiana-committee-rejects-bill-to-establish-marijuana-tax-system-to-prepare-for-eventual-legalization/ — both accessed 25 October 2026. Verify on legis.la.gov. This is the source of the erroneous "15% wholesale excise from 1 January 2026" claim in secondary guides (e.g. Cannabis CPA guide). The bill itself said it would not legalise marijuana; it was a tax-infrastructure bill for a hypothetical future legalisation. It must be listed ONLY as proposed/failed.
HB 627 (2025) — adult-use pilot programme fee Would have created a temporary adult-use pilot (1 January 2026–1 July 2029) for existing medical retailers/cultivators/labs, with a $5,000 annual permit renewal per participating retail location and a 3.5% fee on gross wholesale sales of medical and adult-use cannabis Did not become law in the form described. Last action located: referred to the Committee on Administration of Criminal Justice, 14 April 2025. No Act number located. Source (secondary summary): https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1882752/.multi-collapse — accessed 25 October 2026. Verify on legis.la.gov; do not cite the 3.5% figure as law. A separate secondary source (CannBus Q3 2026) mentions "HB 373 (2026) proposed a 3.5% wholesale fee but did not advance" — a different bill number for a similar concept, which illustrates why bill numbers must be checked on legis.la.gov rather than copied from secondary summaries. Treat both 3.5% references as Verify.

Bottom line for §2.8: As of 25 October 2026, the only enacted cannabis/hemp taxes in Louisiana are the 7% medical gross-sales fee and the 3% consumable-hemp retail excise (plus general sales tax, subject to the medical exemption, and general business/property taxes). Every higher percentage in circulation (15%, 20%, 3.5%) traces to a failed 2025 proposal.
