PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 Who does what: parish, consolidated city-parish, municipality, and the state

3.1.1 The Louisiana local-government map (so the rest of this Part is intelligible)

Louisiana's 64 parishes are governed in one of three principal forms: - Police jury parishes (the default form under R.S. 33:1221 et seq. for parishes without a home rule charter or plan of government): the police jury is the parish governing authority, exercising only the powers granted by the constitution and by law, unless voters have adopted a general-powers proposition. - Home rule charter parishes: the parish may "exercise any power and perform any function necessary, requisite, or proper for the management of its affairs, not denied by general law or inconsistent with the constitution" (La. Const. art. VI, §5). The Police Jury Association's counsel summarised the distinction in 2025 as: home rule charters allow any power not denied by general law or inconsistent with the constitution, while police juries are "creatures of state law restricted to powers expressly granted by statute", and the state can withdraw or limit delegated police power. Source (secondary report of the presentation): https://citizenportal.ai/articles/6290206/Louisiana/Executive/Organizations/Boards-and-Commissions/St-Tammany-Parish-Public-Administrator/Police-Jury-Association-counsel-outlines-parish-government-forms-police-power-limits-and-taxing-authority — accessed 25 October 2026. - Consolidated city-parish governments: a single government exercises both parish and municipal functions for the consolidated territory, with carve-outs for any separately incorporated municipalities inside the parish. The four named in the commission are: - New Orleans / Orleans Parish: coterminous — the City of New Orleans and Orleans Parish cover the same territory; the city government is the parish governing authority in practice. - Baton Rouge / East Baton Rouge Parish: the City of Baton Rouge and East Baton Rouge Parish consolidated government, but the separately incorporated municipalities of Baker, Central and Zachary remain outside the consolidated city's municipal jurisdiction (they are inside the parish for parish functions). - Lafayette / Lafayette Parish: Lafayette Consolidated Government (city of Lafayette + Lafayette Parish), with other incorporated municipalities in the parish (e.g. Broussard, Youngsville, Scott, Carencro) retaining their own municipal governments. - Houma / Terrebonne Parish: Houma–Terrebonne consolidated government (the former City of Houma consolidated with Terrebonne Parish government). - Municipalities generally: municipalities without a home rule charter operate under the Lawrason Act (R.S. 33:321 et seq.), which allocates powers between the board of aldermen/city council and the mayor. Source for the Lawrason Act / police jury framing: Louisiana Legislative Auditor, "Limitations of Home Rule Charter Authority for Parishes and Municipalities" (revised 08/2025): https://app.lla.state.la.us/llala.nsf/CECBB689D15358A5862583EF005AD18F/$FILE/WP-Limitations%20of%20Home%20Rule%20Chtr%20Authority.pdf — accessed 25 October 2026.

Constitutional limits that apply to every level (La. Const. art. VI): - Art. VI, §9(A): "No local governmental subdivision shall (1) define and provide for the punishment of a felony; or (2) except as provided by law, enact an ordinance governing private or civil relationships." Source: https://law.justia.com/constitution/louisiana/Article6.html — accessed 25 October 2026. A parish therefore cannot create its own marijuana felony, and cannot use an ordinance to rewrite a private landlord–tenant or employment relationship around cannabis — those are state-law matters. - Art. VI, §9(B): "the police power of the state shall never be abridged." Source: same page, accessed 25 October 2026. State police-power legislation (including the therapeutic marijuana and consumable hemp statutes) can override a conflicting local ordinance where the state act is necessary to protect the vital interests of the state as a whole. This is the constitutional backdrop to the preemption discussion in §3.1.3. - Art. VI, §7(A) (parishes/municipalities without a home rule charter): the governing authority may exercise general powers only if a majority of electors voting in an election held for that purpose voted in favour of the proposition; otherwise it has only the powers authorised by the constitution or by law. Source: https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/louisiana/la-constitution/louisiana_constitution_art_6_sec_7 — accessed 25 October 2026.

3.1.2 Division of labour for cannabis/hemp businesses

Function State level (who, what) Parish / consolidated / municipal level (what) Source
Whether a marijuana pharmacy may exist, and how many LDH: caps retail permits at 10 statewide (R.S. 40:1046(G)(1)(a)); allocates them by LDH administrative region (regions as they existed 1 August 2022); at least one retailer per region from 1 October 2022; satellite expansion only on patient thresholds (3,500 / 7,000 active qualified patients per region); total retail locations including satellites capped at 30; no more than 2 satellites per region None. No parish or municipality can create, increase or decrease the state cap, award a state retail permit, or authorise a pharmacy the state has not permitted. A local government can only apply its generally applicable zoning and business-licensing rules to a state-permitted location. R.S. 40:1046(G), text opened 25 October 2026: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046/
Where a marijuana pharmacy may locate, as between pharmacies State spacing rule: no retail permit holder shall locate within a 15-mile radius of another retail permit holder's location; 10-mile radius in a region encompassing a parish with population over 350,000 (most recent federal decennial census); 5-mile radius in a region encompassing a municipality with population over 350,000; waivable by written mutual agreement of all affected holders Local zoning still applies within that state spacing constraint: the pharmacy must also be in a zoning district that allows the use, comply with any conditional-use conditions, and hold a local occupational licence. Local zoning cannot waive the state spacing rule. R.S. 40:1046(G)(6), same source, accessed 25 October 2026
Cultivation facilities LDH: no more than 2 licences to cultivate, extract, process, produce and transport therapeutic marijuana statewide (R.S. 40:1046(H)(1)(a)); licences issued 1 July each year for one year; 1 July 2024 licences to the entities holding LSU AgCenter / Southern University Agricultural Center contracts on 1 January 2024 Local zoning, building, fire and occupational-licence rules for the facility site. No parish can authorise a third cultivation licence. R.S. 40:1046(H), same source, accessed 25 October 2026
Consumable hemp retail permits ATC (Office of Alcohol and Tobacco Control): retail permit required for each place of business and each individually registered domain name for a remote retailer (LDR FAQ, summarising ATC practice). LDH: product registration/approval for each consumable hemp product (R.S. 3:1483). Local zoning and occupational licence for the shop. No parish/municipality issues the ATC permit or the LDH product approval. LDR FAQ: https://revenue.louisiana.gov/tax-education-and-faqs/faqs/excise-taxes/consumable-hemp-products/do-i-have-to-have-a-permit-to-sell-consumable-hemp-products/ — accessed 25 October 2026; R.S. 3:1482(A)(1) (permit required), https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1482/ — accessed 25 October 2026
Consumable hemp manufacture / processing LDH (processor licensing and product registration) under R.S. 3:1481 et seq.; LDAF for industrial hemp cultivation (separate from consumable hemp retail) Local zoning / occupational licence for the facility site. R.S. 3:1482–1483 (see Part 1 for full detail; not re-litigated here)
Zoning / land use State sets the state location constraints above (pharmacy spacing, drug-free school-zone criminal law — see §3.2.3). The state consumable-hemp statute sets state location bans (no sale at a gasoline/motor-fuel retail location, with a qualified truck-stop exception — R.S. 3:1482(A)(3); no sale of consumable hemp at a location also authorised to sell gasoline, R.S. 47:712(3) definition). Parishes and municipalities exercise zoning through their comprehensive zoning ordinances / unified development codes, planning commissions and councils/police juries: use districts, conditional uses, site-plan review, signage, parking, and (where adopted) distance or density rules for retail uses. This is the level at which a shop's specific address is approved or denied. R.S. 3:1482(A)(3), https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1482/ — accessed 25 October 2026; New Orleans CZO as the worked example in §3.2.2
Local business licensing / occupational licence tax State licence/permit is a precondition, not a substitute. Parish and/or municipality issues its own occupational licence and levies its occupational licence tax (see §2.6). A business needs both the state permit and the local licence. New Orleans, for example, requires an occupational licence for every business, renewed annually (see §3.4). See §2.6 sources, accessed 25 October 2026
Local sales tax LDR administers the 5% state portion. Parish/local collectors administer the local portion; the rate depends on the sale address and on which school-board, municipal and district levies apply there. Medical marijuana is exempt from any taxing authority's sales tax (§2.2), so local sales-tax authority does not reach medical sales. §2.2 and §2.5 above

3.1.3 Can a parish or municipality prohibit consumable hemp sales, or marijuana pharmacies? — the direct answer

No express local opt-out, local-election, or local-ban power for either category was located in the Louisiana statutes checked.

  • Marijuana pharmacies: R.S. 40:1046 contains no parish opt-out, no local-option election, and no provision authorising a parish or municipality to prohibit a state-permitted pharmacy. The statute's allocation mechanism is regional (LDH regions) and threshold-based (patient counts), not local-option-based. A secondary summary states the point plainly: "Louisiana does not use a county/parish-level opt-in or opt-out structure for medical pharmacies. Pharmacy locations are determined through the state licensing and satellite-expansion process … subject to standard local zoning and business-licensing rules." Source (secondary): https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/la_lsum.html — accessed 25 October 2026. That secondary statement is consistent with the statute text read for this file, but the statute-text absence should be confirmed by a full-text search of R.S. 40:1046 for "parish" opt-out language before publication — Verify (absence claim).
  • Consumable hemp sales: R.S. 3:1481 et seq. (consumable hemp) contains no parish opt-out, local-election, or local-ban provision located in this window. The state scheme is a state permit (ATC) + state product approval (LDH) scheme, with state prohibitions (inhalables, floral hemp for retail, hemp in alcoholic beverages, sales at gasoline locations, sales to under-21s). Nothing in R.S. 3:1482 authorises a parish to add a parish-wide ban on all consumable hemp sales. Verify (absence claim) for the same reason as above: absence from a statute is harder to prove than presence, and a full-text search of Title 3, Chapter 13 (or its successor numbering) should be run before the final HTML states this unconditionally.
  • What local governments CAN do instead of a ban: (i) zone a retail use out of particular districts (e.g. residential, park/recreation, neighbourhood-commercial districts) through a generally applicable zoning ordinance; (ii) impose conditional-use or site-plan conditions; (iii) enforce generally applicable building, fire, signage and occupational-licence rules; (iv) adopt an interim zoning district or moratorium for a defined area while a study is completed (New Orleans Home Rule Charter §3-126 model — see §3.2.2). Whether a zoning ordinance that in effect excludes all consumable hemp retail from an entire parish would survive a state-police-power / preemption challenge has not been litigated in any case located for this file. Unavailable — no Louisiana case law on a parish-wide hemp ban was located.
  • Local elections on hemp or marijuana: No parish-level election authorising or prohibiting hemp or marijuana sales was located. Louisiana has no statewide citizen initiative (that is a Part 9 matter), and no local-option election mechanism for cannabis/hemp was found in the statutes checked. Any parish "election" claim encountered in secondary sources should be treated as Verify until an official Secretary of State / parish election result is produced. None was produced in this window.

Practical consequence: A would-be hemp retailer or pharmacy applicant must clear two gates — the state permit/approval and the local zoning/licence gate — but the local gate is a land-use and business-licence gate, not a second state-style licence and not a local referendum. A parish cannot vote a state-permitted pharmacy out of existence, but it can deny a specific site on zoning grounds, and a retailer that cannot find a compliant site in a parish has, in practice, no store in that parish.

3.2 Local bans, moratoriums, caps and zoning — with dates

3.2.1 Statewide picture: no parish-wide ban found; no official list exists (see §3.3)

No parish-wide ban, moratorium or cap on marijuana pharmacies or on consumable hemp retailers, adopted by ordinance in any Louisiana parish or municipality, was located in the searches for this file (25 October 2026). The only pending local zoning initiative located is New Orleans (§3.2.2). The only state location restrictions are those in §3.1.2 and §3.2.3. This negative finding is limited by the search method (web searches of official codes and local news for each checked jurisdiction — see §3.3) and is stated as "none located", not as a guarantee that no small municipality has adopted an unpublicised ordinance. Verify by a Municode / American Legal Publishing code search for each jurisdiction before publication if the final HTML needs a stronger claim.

3.2.2 New Orleans (Orleans Parish) — study and proposed zoning, NOT yet an adopted ban

This is the most developed local initiative located, and it must not be reported as adopted law.

  • Council motions: The New Orleans City Council first directed a cannabis-retailer study by Motion M-25-379, superseded by Motion M-25-470, adopted 11 September 2025, which expanded the study to tobacco and nicotine products as well as cannabis products. The motion directs the City Planning Commission (CPC) to study retail goods establishments selling cannabis, tobacco and nicotine products and to recommend updated regulations: definitions, use standards and permissions, advertising/signage limits, and density restrictions to limit youth exposure. Source: City of New Orleans CPC semi-monthly zoning meeting materials (Granicus): https://cityofno.granicus.com/MetaViewer.php?view_id=2&clip_id=5236&meta_id=763744 — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • Staff proposal (reported October 2026, secondary): A Realtor.com report dated 12 days before 25 October 2026 (i.e. mid-October 2026) describes a CPC staff report proposing a new umbrella use, "Retail Sale of Tobacco, Nicotine, Cannabis or Consumable Hemp" (for stores where such sales are secondary to a main business), banned from Neighborhood Commercial Establishments and from all residential and park/recreation districts entirely; dedicated smoke shops and marijuana dispensaries also barred from those zones; permitted locations tracking districts that already allow packaged alcohol sales (most commercial corridors, Central Business District zones, suburban business districts, industrial areas); existing shops grandfathered as legal nonconforming uses, with only post-adoption retailers facing the new distance requirements. Source (secondary, dated mid-October 2026): https://www.realtor.com/advice/hyperlocal/new-orleans-zoning-rules-for-vape-shops-dispensaries/ — accessed 25 October 2026.
  • Status — Verify: No adopted New Orleans ordinance enacting that staff proposal was located as of 25 October 2026. The proposal is a staff report / study recommendation, not a Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance amendment. The final HTML must describe it as "proposed / under study, not adopted" and must re-check the CPC docket and the Council's adopted ordinances before publication. The current Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance (CZO) text available at https://czo.nola.gov/article-20/ (Article 20, Use Standards, accessed 25 October 2026) contains the general adult-use 1,000-foot rule (see §3.2.3) but no cannabis/hemp-specific use standard was located in the CZO text checked.
  • Interim-zoning / moratorium power (general, not yet invoked for cannabis in any document located): New Orleans Home Rule Charter §3-126 authorises the Council to impose temporary prohibitions on zoning (interim zoning districts and moratoria) "where necessary to protect the public health, safety, or welfare for a temporary period", pending CPC review. The CZO's Article 19 sets the procedure: a Council motion initiating the interim district/moratorium, specification of the review/study, and refusal of new conflicting permit applications after the motion (complete applications received before the motion may still be processed). Source: CZO Article 19 print, https://czo.nola.gov/print.aspx?printpath=%2FArticle-19%2F19-1&classname=nola.ordinance and https://czo.nola.gov/print.aspx?printpath=%2FArticle-19%2F19-3%2F19-3-C&classname=nola.ordinance — both accessed 25 October 2026. No New Orleans interim zoning district or moratorium specifically for cannabis/hemp retailers was located. Do not imply one exists.

3.2.3 State-level location rules that are often mistaken for local buffers

  • Pharmacy-to-pharmacy spacing (state, not local): 15 miles generally; 10 miles in a region encompassing a parish over 350,000 population; 5 miles in a region encompassing a municipality over 350,000 population; waivable by mutual written agreement. R.S. 40:1046(G)(6). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046/ — accessed 25 October 2026. This is a state rule about distance between pharmacies, not a distance from schools, parks or churches, and not a local buffer.
  • Drug-free school zones (state criminal law, not zoning): R.S. 40:981.3 creates a drug-free zone comprising school property, school buses, and the area within 2,000 feet of school property. It is a criminal-enhancement statute, not a zoning buffer: violating the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law (R.S. 40:966–970) in the zone historically carried the maximum fine and up to 1.5× the longest term of imprisonment. 2026 change: Acts 2026, No. 305 (HB 568, Rep. Firment), effective 1 August 2026, added R.S. 40:981.3(A)(4) and (E): a person who violates R.S. 40:966–970 "while smoking, vaping, or otherwise abusing" a controlled dangerous substance on school property, within 2,000 feet of school property, or on a school bus is punished by imprisonment with or without hard labour for not more than one year and a fine of up to $1,000; lack of knowledge that the act occurred in the zone is not a defence (R.S. 40:981.3(B)). Sources: enrolled HB 568, https://LEGIS.LA.GOV/LEGIS/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1473970, and HB 568 digest, http://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1462887 — both accessed 25 October 2026; secondary reporting consistent: https://www.postsouth.com/story/news/local/2026/09/04/louisiana-law-increases-penalties-for-school-drugs/91587622007/ (4 September 2026) — accessed 25 October 2026. This 2,000-foot zone does not prohibit siting a lawful pharmacy or hemp shop 2,000 feet from a school; it enhances penalties for unlawful drug conduct in the zone. Conflating it with a zoning buffer would be an error. Whether a lawful pharmacy's lawful dispensing inside the zone is affected is a Part 1 question; no provision located here makes lawful dispensing a drug-free-zone violation.
  • New Orleans "adult use" 1,000-foot rule (local, but NOT a cannabis rule): CZO Article 20, §20.3.B: "Adult uses are prohibited within a thousand (1,000) feet of any residential district, place of worship, educational facility, and park or playground" (except Vieux Carré Entertainment Districts where allowed). Source: https://czo.nola.gov/article-20/ — accessed 25 October 2026. In CZO usage "adult use" means sexually oriented / adult-entertainment uses, not marijuana. Do not cite the 1,000-foot rule as a cannabis buffer.
  • No statewide hemp-retail buffer located: No statute or rule imposing a distance buffer (e.g. from schools) specifically for consumable hemp retailers was located in R.S. 3:1481 et seq. or in LDH/ATC rules checked. The state location rules for hemp retail are categorical (no gasoline locations, no alcohol-plus-hemp, no sales to under-21s, behind-the-counter display except beverages — R.S. 3:1482(A)), not distance-based. Verify by a full LDH rule check (LAC Title 49, Part I, Chapter 5, §I-533 and related sections) before stating this unconditionally.

3.2.4 Other checked jurisdictions — no ban, moratorium or cap located

For each jurisdiction in §3.3, targeted searches (official code / council / news, 25 October 2026) found no adopted parish-wide or city-wide ban, moratorium or numerical cap on marijuana pharmacies or consumable hemp retailers. The absence is reported jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction in §3.3 rather than as a single blanket claim, because a small municipality's ordinance may not be indexed on the web. The New Orleans study in §3.2.2 is the sole pending local initiative located.

3.3 Official list of prohibiting / allowing jurisdictions — none exists; jurisdictions checked

Direct answer: No official list — state or local — of parishes or municipalities that prohibit or allow consumable hemp sales or marijuana pharmacies was located.

  • No LDH, ATC, LDAF, LDR or Secretary of State list of "opt-out" or "prohibiting" parishes/municipalities was found. The state schemes do not use an opt-out list (see §3.1.3), so the absence of a list is consistent with the statutory design, not an oversight in this research.
  • No LDH list of "allowing" parishes exists either; the closest official geographic instrument is the LDH pharmacy-region system (§3.5), which allocates regions, not parish permissions.

"No ban located" means: no adopted ban/moratorium/cap was found in web searches of that jurisdiction's official code, council actions and local reporting on 25 October 2026. 3.4 Local permit fees and buffer rules — what exists, and what does not

3.4.1 State fees that are sometimes mislabelled as "local" fees (for completeness)

  • Retail permit: $22,500 per year per retail permit holder (state, LDH) — §2.1.
  • Cultivation licence: $100,000 per year + $10,000 application fee (state, LDH) — §2.1.
  • These are state fees. No parish or municipality collects them, and no local surcharge on them was located.

3.4.2 Local fees — general occupational licence only; no cannabis-specific local fee schedule located

  • General rule: every business needs a local occupational licence, and the licence tax is generally graduated by gross receipts/sales (see §2.6). The amount for a specific cannabis/hemp business in a specific parish/municipality is determined by the local collector's classification of the business and its gross receipts. No cannabis-specific local fee table (e.g. "hemp retailer: $X") was located for any of the 15 checked jurisdictions.
  • Worked example — New Orleans (general, not cannabis-specific): the City of New Orleans Bureau of Revenue issues occupational licences; a home-based business occupational licence costs $50 (temporary licence) plus a one-time $190 home-based business certificate of occupancy ($240 total) in the city's home-based-business guide. Source: https://nola.gov/home-based-business-guide/ — accessed 25 October 2026. This example is included only to show the kind of local fee that exists; it is not a cannabis fee, and a storefront pharmacy/hemp shop would be classified differently (retail table, see §2.6) and would pay on its gross activity. Do not quote $240 as a cannabis licence fee.
  • New Orleans retail occupational licence tax table (general): retail businesses pay on a graduated schedule starting at $50 for activity up to $50,000 and climbing to $6,200 or more above $5.5 million, per the secondary summary of the city's tables. Source: https://legalclarity.org/tax-in-new-orleans-sales-property-income-and-more/ — accessed 25 October 2026. Verify against the City of New Orleans Bureau of Revenue tables before publication; the table itself was not opened.
  • Unavailable: local permit/licence fees specifically for consumable hemp retailers (beyond the state ATC permit fee, which is a Part 4 matter) in Orleans, East Baton Rouge, Jefferson, St. Tammany, Lafayette, Caddo, Calcasieu, Ouachita, Rapides, Bossier, Livingston, Tangipahoa, Terrebonne, Ascension and St. Landry. If the final HTML needs a fee for a specific parish, it must be obtained from that parish/municipality's collector or clerk — it cannot be inferred from another parish's schedule.

3.5 Business concentration — ONLY what official sources say

Constraint honoured: this section does not estimate, rank or cluster licensees. It reports only the official geographic allocation mechanism and its thresholds, and states plainly what official location data was not located in this window.

Official geographic mechanism (statute): - Retail permits are allocated among regions "correspond[ing] to the sets of parishes comprising, respectively, the administrative regions of the Louisiana Department of Health as those regions existed on August 1, 2022." R.S. 40:1046(G)(2). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046/ — accessed 25 October 2026. - "On and after October 1, 2022, at least one marijuana retailer shall be located in each region." Same provision. - Satellite expansion is threshold-driven, not discretionary by parish: after 3,500 active qualified patients are identified in a region, LDH notifies and allows the region's permit holder to open one satellite location in that region; after 7,000, a second satellite. The permit holder must apply within 90 days of notification; the satellite must be operational within 310 days of approval (extensions for circumstances beyond the holder's control). If the holder declines, LDH may issue an additional retail permit in that region in lieu of the satellite. LDH must consider unserved parishes in the region when approving a satellite or additional permit. Total retail locations including satellites: no more than 30; no more than 2 satellites per region. "Active, qualified patient" means a patient who has acquired a therapeutic marijuana product at least once; the count is reviewed quarterly using the preceding 24-month period. R.S. 40:1046(G)(3)–(8). Source: same page, accessed 25 October 2026. - Delivery: "Each marijuana retail permit holder shall offer delivery to patients in each zip code within its region at least once per month." R.S. 40:1046(G)(7). Source: same page, accessed 25 October 2026. This is the statute's answer to geographic access for patients in parishes without a storefront: monthly delivery to every ZIP code in the region, not a store in every parish.

Historic region names and parish composition (Board of Pharmacy rule — historic, not current LDH text): The former Louisiana Board of Pharmacy rule (LAC Title 46, Part LIII, §2445, as in effect when the nine permits were awarded) listed nine regions: (1) Metropolitan — Jefferson, Orleans, Plaquemines, St. Bernard; (2) Capitol — Ascension, East Baton Rouge, East Feliciana, Iberville, Pointe Coupee, West Baton Rouge, West Feliciana; (3) Teche — Assumption, Lafourche, St. Charles, St. James, St. John the Baptist, St. Mary, Terrebonne; (4) Acadian — Acadia, Evangeline, Iberia, Lafayette, St. Landry, St. Martin, Vermilion; (5) Southwest — Allen, Beauregard, Calcasieu, Cameron, Jefferson Davis; (6) Central — Avoyelles, Catahoula, Concordia, Grant, LaSalle, Rapides, Vernon, Winn; (7) Northwest — Bienville, Bossier, Caddo, Claiborne, DeSoto, Natchitoches, Red River, Sabine, Webster; (8) Northeast — Caldwell, East Carroll, Franklin, Jackson, Lincoln, Madison, Morehouse, Ouachita, Richland, Tensas, Union, West Carroll; (9) Southeast — Livingston, St. Helena, St. Tammany, Tangipahoa, Washington. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/louisiana/La-Admin-Code-tit-46-SS-LIII-2445 — accessed 25 October 2026. Use this list only as the historic Board-of-Pharmacy region map. The current statute ties regions to LDH administrative regions as of 1 August 2022; whether LDH's 2022 regions are parish-identical to the Board list above was not confirmed in this window — Verify against LDH's region map before presenting the parish list as current.

What official sources in this window do NOT say (so the final HTML must not invent it): - No official LDH table, in the sources opened here, lists every current retail location (primary + satellite) by parish with addresses, or counts locations by parish. The secondary list of 13 locations (Alexandria, Baton Rouge, Houma, Lafayette, Lake Charles, New Iberia, Kenner, Covington, New Orleans, Shreveport, Metairie, West Monroe, Slidell) from a patient-information site (https://www.louisianamarijuanacard.com/post/louisiana-s-10th-medical-marijuana-dispensary-opens — accessed 25 October 2026) is secondary and undated as a current census; it is noted here only to warn the parent not to use it as an official count. The original nine anchor cities (New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Houma, Lafayette, Lake Charles, Alexandria, Shreveport, West Monroe, Madisonville) come from a 2018 GB Sciences press release (https://www.gbsciences.com/2018/08/23/louisiana-pharmacies/ — accessed 25 October 2026) and are historic, not current. - No official parish-by-parish count of consumable hemp retailers was located in this window. ATC permit lists are a Part 5 matter; no concentration conclusion about hemp retail is drawn here. - No official statement ranks parishes by number of licensees, patient counts by parish, or sales by parish. Do not rank. The only official distribution statement that can be made is the regional one above: at least one retailer per LDH region, satellites only on patient thresholds, 30 locations maximum statewide, delivery to every ZIP code in the region at least monthly.

4.1 Cultivation and processing — medical marijuana

4.1.1 The original university model (historic, now superseded)

  • Original law: Act 261 of 2015 (HB 149 framework) identified the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center (LSU AgCenter) and the Southern University Agricultural Center (Southern University AgCenter) as the licensed producers of marijuana for therapeutic use, each authorised to contract with one contractor to produce it. Source: Résumé Digest for Act 150 (SB 228, 2024), legis.la.gov: https://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1384639 — "Prior law identified the La. State University Agricultural Center and the Southern University Agricultural Center as the licensed producers … Prior law authorized each university to contract with one contractor to produce therapeutic marijuana."
  • The contractors were, in practice: GB Sciences Louisiana for LSU (later operating as Good Day Farm Louisiana) and Advanced Biomedics LLC for Southern University (d/b/a Ilera Holistic Healthcare). Sources: LDH Act 150 Report 2025 (see §6) and contemporaneous reporting; the university-contractor pairing is also stated in the Act 150 digest history. LDH's current page names the two current manufacturers directly (see §4.1.2).
  • Do not cite the universities as current licensees. Any source still saying so is stale.

4.1.2 The 2024 transfer — Act 150 (SB 228, 2024), effective 22 May 2024; licences transferred 1 July 2024

Verbatim operative text, current R.S. 40:1046(H)(1)(a)–(b) (legis.la.gov, opened 25 Oct 2026, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=96986):

"(1)(a) The Louisiana Department of Health shall issue no more than two licenses to cultivate, extract, process, produce, and transport therapeutic marijuana in this state. Each license shall be issued on July first and shall be effective for a period of one year." "(b) The licenses issued on July 1, 2024, shall be to the entities who held contracts with the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center and the Southern University Agricultural Center on January 1, 2024, pursuant to Act No. 261 of the 2015 Regular Session of the Legislature."

LDH's own summary is identical in substance (LDH medical marijuana page, https://ldh.la.gov/page/medical-marijuana):

"Act 150 of the 2024 Legislature - extended the sunset date of the medical marijuana program to 2030, changed the basis for calculating patient numbers for reporting purposes, and removed the universities from the manufacturing program" "Removed language referencing permitting of manufacturers and requiring that licenses be issued to Southern University and Louisiana State University; licenses were transferred to the former permit-holders contracted by the universities in 2024"

Current licensees (LDH page, opened 25 Oct 2026):

"There are two licensed medical marijuana manufacturers in the state of Louisiana–Advanced Biomedics LLC dba Ilera Holistic Healthcare and Good Day Farm Louisiana LLC."

The LDH Act 150 Report 2025 (covering 1 Jan–31 Dec 2025) uses the same two names and adds that Ilera "distributed their first approved medical cannabis products to authorized medical marijuana retailers in July of 2020" and that Good Day Farm Louisiana's production is at its Ruston facility. Source: https://ldh.la.gov/assets/oph/Center-EH/sanitarian/Act-150-Report.2025.pdf

What the licence covers: one licence = cultivate + extract + process + produce + transport therapeutic marijuana (R.S. 40:1046(H)(1)(a), verbatim above). There is no separate processor-only medical licence in the current statute text opened.

Renewal, replacement, and disqualifiers (verbatim, same statute):

"(c) Upon each renewal period, a license in force shall be renewed by the department for the next succeeding period upon proper application for renewal and payment of license fees as required by law and the rules and regulations of the department." "(d) Subject to the limitation of no more than two licenses … the department shall select a new licensee through a competitive bid process in accordance with … the Louisiana Procurement Code, R.S. 39:1551 et seq., if … (i) After written notice … and failure … to cure within thirty days … a licensee fails to comply with the proper application for renewal and payment of license fees … and the license is revoked. (ii) A license is voluntarily returned or remitted … prior to the expiration of the licensure period." "(3) No company that has made a contribution to a candidate in a Louisiana election governed by the provisions of the Campaign Finance Disclosure Act within the five years prior to bidding for the license, or is controlled wholly or in part by a person who made such a contribution within the five years prior to the company bidding for the license, may be eligible for the license."

Fees (verbatim, R.S. 40:1046(H)(4), same legis.la.gov link):

"(a) Establish and collect an annual license fee of one hundred thousand dollars from each licensee permitted to cultivate, extract, process, produce, and transport therapeutic marijuana." "(b) Collect a nonrefundable application fee of ten thousand dollars." "(c) Assess a fee of seven percent of the gross sales of therapeutic marijuana. The fee shall be reported and paid by the licensee. The fee shall be collected by the Department of Revenue … The Department of Revenue shall transfer monthly to the state treasury for deposit into the Disability Services Fund, as established in R.S. 28:826, the amount of revenues collected in accordance with this Subparagraph."

Note on the 7% fee's destination: the Act 150 (2024) digest states "Proposed law changes the dedication of the funds" (from the earlier Community and Family Support System Fund framing found in older secondary summaries). The current statute text above — Disability Services Fund, R.S. 28:826 — governs. Older summaries naming the Community and Family Support System Fund should be treated as superseded for current dedication. Source for digest: https://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1384639

Sunset: R.S. 40:1046(M): "The provisions of this Section shall terminate on July 1, 2030." (Same legis.la.gov link; Act 150 extended the sunset from 1 January 2025 to 1 July 2030.)

No sale/transfer/conversion of a production licence to a third party was found in an official source. The only transfer mechanism in the current statute is the competitive-bid replacement on revocation or voluntary return (quoted above), plus the one-off 1 July 2024 transfer to the 1 January 2024 contractors. Any claim that a production licence was sold on the open market is [Verify — no official record located].

Requirements beyond fees: LDH must collect annually from each licensee: (i) gross marijuana produced; (ii) production-cost details (seed, fertilizer, labor, advisory services, construction, irrigation); (iii) subcontractor items/services and costs; (iv) therapeutic chemicals produced; (v) therapeutic marijuana distributed to each retail permit holder — and must report the prior calendar year's information to the Legislature by 1 February each year and publish it online (R.S. 40:1046(H)(2), same link). That report is the Act 150 Report used in Part 6. THC levels "shall be reduced to the lowest acceptable therapeutic levels available through scientifically accepted methods" (R.S. 40:1046(I)). Research: LSU AgCenter, Southern University AgCenter, and the University of Louisiana at Monroe "may conduct research on marijuana for therapeutic use" (R.S. 40:1046(L)) — this is a research permission, not a production licence, after Act 150.

Official info pages: - LDH medical marijuana hub: https://ldh.la.gov/page/medical-marijuana (includes final rule published January 2026, emergency rule 28 March 2025, Act 150 and Act 693 links) - Current statute: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=96986 — caveat: LDH's own page warns "note that this online version has not yet been updated with 2024 changes" on its linked copy; the legis.la.gov Law.aspx text opened for this research DOES contain the Act 150/Act 693/2025 amendments (it cites Acts 2024 No. 150, No. 693 and Acts 2025 No. 513, No. 514 in its history line), so the Law.aspx text, not LDH's older linked copy, was used for quotations.

4.1.3 Industrial hemp cultivation/processing — LDAF (non-consumable only since Act 336, 2021)

See also Part 5 for the licensee list. LDAF's licensing page (opened 25 Oct 2026, https://www.ldaf.la.gov/plants/industrial-hemp/hemp-licensing) lists four types on one application:

LDAF licence What it authorises (LDAF page wording)
Grower License Produce hemp
Processor License Process non-consumable hemp
Handler License Transport, harvest, clean, package, and test hemp
Seed Producer License Produce, transport, and sell hemp seed
  • Fee: $500 each; renewals due by 30 November each year. Source: same LDAF licensing page — "Licenses cost $500 each, and renewals are due by November 30 of each year." Repeated on the LDAF regulations page: https://www.ldaf.la.gov/plants/industrial-hemp/regulations
  • No cap, no minimum acreage: same regulations page — "There is no limit to the number of licenses Louisiana issues, and there is no minimum number of production acres to be a licensed grower. You can grow industrial hemp plants in your yard as long as you're licensed." Permanent Resident Card (Green Card) holders are eligible.
  • Before applying: review the industrial hemp law, rules and regulations, and compliance checklist; complete a state and federal background check (one set suffices for multiple licence types if performed within 60 days of the application being received by LDAF); create a colour photographic map for each growing, storage, handling, or processing location. Source: LDAF licensing page, same link.
  • Historic contract-carrier type: a 2019 LDAF announcement listed a fourth historic type, "Contract Carrier — authorizes the licensee to transport industrial hemp; required when the transporter is not the licensed grower or processor," with a then-illustrative $250 fee in a legislative fiscal note. Source (secondary/dated): Louisiana Farm Bureau News, 27 Dec 2019: https://lafarmbureaunews.com/news/2019/12/27/louisiana-among-the-first-states-to-get-federal-approval-of-state-industrial-hemp-plan — The current LDAF licensing page does not list a separate contract-carrier licence; transport is folded into Grower/Processor/Handler. Treat the standalone contract-carrier type as historic/superseded [Verify against current LDAF forms].
  • USDA-approved state plan: Louisiana runs its own USDA-approved state plan, not the USDA direct programme. USDA approved Louisiana's plan on 27 December 2019 (LSU AgCenter Staff Report No. 2020-53, Sept 2020: https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1605805806025 — "On December 23, 2019, Louisiana's state industrial hemp plan was approved by the USDA" [date discrepancy: 23 vs 27 Dec — see Gaps]; Farm Bureau announcement dated 27 Dec 2019: https://lafarmbureaunews.com/news/2019/12/27/louisiana-among-the-first-states-to-get-federal-approval-of-state-industrial-hemp-plan). LDAF began accepting applications 27 December 2019 / early February 2020 (sources differ on the exact application-open date; see Gaps).
  • Consumable processors moved away from LDAF: "As a result of Act 336 of the 2021 Regular Legislative Session, LDAF is no longer authorized to license or regulate processors of 'consumable' hemp as defined by R.S. 3:1481. Anyone interested in processing consumable hemp should go through the Louisiana Department of Health." Source: LDAF regulations page, same link above.

4.2 Marijuana pharmacies / retailers

4.2.1 Cap, regions, satellites — current statute (verbatim)

R.S. 40:1046(G) (legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=96986):

"(1)(a) The department shall issue an annual retail permit to sell recommended marijuana for therapeutic use and, except as provided in Paragraph (3) of this Subsection, shall limit the number of retail permits granted in the state to no more than ten." "(2) For the purposes of this Subsection, the regions among which the marijuana retail permits are allocated shall correspond to the sets of parishes comprising, respectively, the administrative regions of the Louisiana Department of Health as those regions existed on August 1, 2022. On and after October 1, 2022, at least one marijuana retailer shall be located in each region." "(3)(a) After three thousand five hundred active, qualified patients are identified in a region, the department shall notify and allow the marijuana retail permit holder in that region to open one additional retail location as a satellite location in that region." "(3)(b) After seven thousand active, qualified patients are identified in a region, the department shall notify and allow the marijuana retail permit holder in that region to open one additional marijuana retail location as a second satellite location in that region." "(4)(a) The total number of marijuana retail locations, including satellite locations, approved by the department pursuant to Paragraph (3) of this Subsection shall not be greater than thirty locations." "(4)(b) … shall not be construed to authorize a marijuana retail permit holder to open more than two satellite locations in a single region." "(6)(a) No marijuana retail permit holder shall locate within a fifteen-mile radius of another retail permit holder's marijuana retail location." — with 10-mile (parish >350,000 population) and 5-mile (municipality >350,000) variants in (6)(b)–(c), waivable by written mutual agreement of all affected holders under (6)(d).

Patient-count mechanics (current, as amended by Act 150): the count is "conducted and reviewed on a quarterly basis using the preceding twenty-four-month period" (R.S. 40:1046(G)(3)(e) as shown in the current text), and "active, qualified patient" means "a patient who has acquired a therapeutic marijuana product at least once" (G)(8). A satellite applicant must apply within 90 days of LDH notification and the satellite must be operational within 310 days of approval (extensions for circumstances beyond the holder's control). If a holder declines a satellite, LDH may issue an additional retail permit in that region in lieu of that satellite. No closure is required if the patient count later falls below 3,500. All from R.S. 40:1046(G)(3)–(5), same link.

History of the count: the 10th base permit was added effective 1 August 2022 for the region comprising Jefferson, Orleans, Plaquemines, and St. Bernard parishes (Act 491/492/628 of 2022 framework; secondary summary: Butler Snow, JD Supra, "Louisiana's Medical Marijuana Law Amended Effective August 1, 2022": https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/louisiana-s-medical-marijuana-law-8389319/ — secondary, used only for the 2022 narrative; the current cap of 10 is confirmed in the current statute text above).

4.2.2 Regulator transfer — Act 693 (2024), effective 1 January 2025

LDH page (https://ldh.la.gov/page/medical-marijuana):

"Act 693 of the 2024 Regular Legislature transferred authority over marijuana retailers from the Louisiana Board of Pharmacy to the Louisiana Department of Health. LDH's Cannabis Program began regulating these retail sites on January 1, 2025."

LDH now calls them retailers, not dispensaries: "Retailers are now referenced as such and not as 'dispensaries'" (Emergency Rule summary, April 2025 Louisiana Register, effective 28 March 2025, same LDH page). Retailers may only sell products manufactured by firms licensed in Louisiana; may not deliver outside Louisiana; patients remain restricted to 71 g (2.5 oz) of flower per 14 days (same page).

Board of Pharmacy records are historic only for retail permitting after 1 January 2025. The pharmacist requirement survives in a different form: each retail permit holder must appoint at least one Louisiana-residing pharmacist with an active unrestricted Louisiana Board of Pharmacy licence, designated as responsible for the primary location and satellites, on duty when accessible by telephone during open hours and available by telephone/video for patient consultation during open hours (R.S. 40:1046(F)(1)(b), same legis.la.gov link).

4.2.3 Fees, renewal, and whether new permits are open

  • Annual retail permit fee: $22,500 per retail permit holder (verbatim, R.S. 40:1046(G)(1)(b)): "The department shall charge an annual retail permit fee in the amount of twenty-two thousand five hundred dollars to each of the ten retail permit holders authorized in Subparagraph (a) of this Paragraph to sell recommended marijuana for therapeutic use." Source: same legis.la.gov link. The fee was added by HB 657 (2025 Regular Session); BillTrack50 records it as signed/enacted 1 July 2025, effective 1 August 2025: https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1887931 — Act number for HB 657 is [Verify — the current statute history line cites Acts 2025 No. 513 and No. 514 without mapping them to bill numbers in the text opened; do not assign an Act number to HB 657 without checking legis.la.gov's bill page].
  • Renewal: "Upon each annual renewal period, a retail permit in force shall be renewed by the department for the next succeeding period upon proper application for renewal and payment of permit fees as required by law and the rules and regulations of the department." (R.S. 40:1046(G)(1)(b), same link.)
  • New permit holder selection — closed except on vacancy: LDH "shall select a new retail permit holder through a competitive bid process in accordance with … the Louisiana Procurement Code, R.S. 39:1551 et seq., only if" (i) a permit is revoked after written notice and a 30-day cure failure for non-renewal/non-payment, or (ii) a permit is voluntarily returned before expiry (R.S. 40:1046(G)(1)(c), same link).
  • Membership-interest transfer needs no LDH approval: "The transfer of a membership interest in an entity that holds a marijuana retail permit may be conducted without approval of the department." (R.S. 40:1046(G)(1)(d), same link.)
  • New non-satellite permits: CLOSED at the time of access. LDH page, Applications section: "Application for a New Marijuana Retailer Permit - NOTE: No new permits may be issued for non-satellite locations at this time. See the table of active permits for additional information." (https://ldh.la.gov/page/medical-marijuana)
  • Satellite applications: LDH lists an application form for satellites implicitly through the same permitting process; the statute's 90-day/310-day satellite timetable is in §4.2.1 above. A separate satellite fee, if any, was not found in the sources opened — [Verify: whether the $22,500 fee is per permit holder (covering satellites) or per location]. The statute says "to each of the ten retail permit holders," which reads as per holder, but LDH's fee practice was not confirmed on a fee schedule page.

4.4 Consumable hemp permits

4.4.1 The three-agency split (current)

  • LDAF: industrial hemp growing/handling/processing of non-consumable hemp only (see §4.1.3).
  • LDH (Office of Public Health, Bureau of Sanitarian Services / Food and Drug Unit): consumable hemp processor permits and per-product registration. Source: LDH hemp registration page: https://ldh.la.gov/page/hemp-registration; LDH primer: https://ldh.la.gov/assets/oph/Center-EH/sanitarian/A_Primer_for_Selling_Consumable_Hemp_Products_2023.pdf — "Wholesale Manufacturing: A facility in the state of Louisiana that wishes to manufacture Consumable Hemp for ingestion under the authority of Act 498 of the 2022 Louisiana Legislature must obtain a Permit to Operate with the Louisiana Department of Health / Food and Drug Unit."
  • ATC: consumable hemp wholesaler, retailer (per place of business / per domain), and special-event permits. Source: La. R.S. 3:1484; ATC wholesale application form: https://atc.louisiana.gov/media/idcpj45s/application-for-consumable-hemp-wholesale-permit_a11y.pdf

4.4.2 LDH consumable hemp processor permit — fees, requirements

Statute: La. R.S. 3:1483(A)(1) (legis.la.gov, https://legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=1147994 — opened via search result; the fee schedule text below is verbatim from that statute page):

"Each consumable hemp processor shall obtain an annual consumable hemp processor permit issued by the department. The department shall charge and collect an annual consumable hemp processor permit fee. The fee shall be for each separate processing facility and shall be based on the annual sales of such facility according to the following schedule: Annual Sales / Annual Fee — Under $500,000 / $175.00; $500,001 - $1,000,000 / $475.00; $1,000,001 - $2,500,000 / $775.00; $2,500,001 - $5,000,000 / $1,075.00; Over $5,000,000 / $1,375.00"

Additional statutory processor duties in the same section (summarised, not quoted in full): potency test of the distillate/concentrate used; batch test showing disaggregated THC components by percentage, serving size, total THC mg per serving, and solvents/pesticides/microbials/heavy metals; retain test records minimum 3 years; adhere to department sanitary regulations.

In-state vs out-of-state processor (LDH page, current after Act 752):

"NOTE: Due to changes resulting from Act 752 of the 2024 Regular Legislature, any consumable hemp product to be registered must be submitted through a permitted in-state hemp products processor OR a permitted out-of-state hemp processor. A list of in-state firms that may sponsor out-of-state products may be found here." (https://ldh.la.gov/page/hemp-registration)

Out-of-state permit application requirements (same LDH page): $175 application fee ("fees are based on a sliding scale but the department will assess additional fees if applicable at a later point in time"); FD-99a application form; list of stakeholders with >5% stake and percentages; notarised attestation of good character of major stakeholders (specifically no felony conviction by the U.S. or any state/territory, and no convictions for soliciting for prostitution, pandering, letting premises for prostitution, contributing to delinquency of juveniles, keeping/letting a disorderly place, or illegally dealing in controlled dangerous substances); sole proprietors must also supply a state-issued photo ID showing date of birth.

Act 752 (HB 952, 2024) — effective 1 January 2025 — what changed for processors/retailers (official Act text): Act 752 enrolled text: https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1382781 — key provisions verified in that text: retailer must maintain all consumable hemp products except beverages in a location inaccessible to the public without employee assistance; no sale at a retail location also authorised to sell gasoline/motor fuel (facility licensed under R.S. 27:417 exempt — i.e. qualified truck stops); no processing/distribution/sale of any alcoholic beverage containing a consumable hemp product, any consumable hemp product for inhalation without a required licence/permit, or any floral hemp material for retail use. Secondary summaries (American Bar Association article; MJBizDaily, June 2024: https://mjbizdaily.com/news/louisiana-bans-thca-flower-sale-of-hemp-products-at-gas-stations/392264/) add: 5 mg THC per serving (down from 8 mg), 40 mg per package cap, 21+ for all consumable hemp (up from 18, with the adult-use category repealed), no new bar/restaurant permits (c. 220 grandfathered), 12-oz minimum for beverages, max 4 containers per beverage package — these numeric limits are secondary-summary figures; the Act 752 enrolled text itself was opened but not read line-by-line for every THC number in this run, so the 5 mg / 40 mg figures are marked [Verify against enrolled Act 752 text / current R.S. 3:1481–1484] in the parent's Part 1 work, and are repeated here only as context for why retailer counts fell after 1 Jan 2025. The 21+ age and ID-verification requirement is corroborated in current statute: R.S. 14:93.16–93.17 (Acts 2025, No. 233) — sale to under-21 unlawful; under-21 purchase/possession fined not more than $100 by citation, not on criminal history record.

4.4.3 LDH consumable hemp product registration — $50 per product

LDH hemp registration page (https://ldh.la.gov/page/hemp-registration), requirements to upload to the portal: - Labels for each product; Certificates of Analysis from accredited labs for each product; completed application form for each product (FD-10); laboratory accreditation verification (ISO-IEC 17025); attestation the product was produced from hemp; photographs/renderings of each product including accessories; detailed written description of how individual servings will be packaged/marketed; complete list of the firm's previously registered products. - "Administrative Coordinators will send an invoice ($50 per product submitted for registration) once every product has been accepted for registration" — payable by money order, cashier's check, or online through the portal, payable to LDH. - "Each product must be renewed between July 1 and August 15 of every year" — firms may, with department permission, attest/certify the product has not changed in lieu of repeat submission. - Review clock: "Each time the Administrative Coordinator asks for more documentation, and upon each response to LDH, the 60-day period for Administrative Coordinators to register or decline to register a product begins anew" (60 business days; excludes weekends, legal holidays, state office closures). If LDH does not hear back within 60 business days after requesting more information, LDH will close the file. - On registration, the product is placed on the "Louisiana Department of Health Database for Registered Consumable Hemp Products" and the applicant receives a Certificate of Consumable Hemp Product Registration (FD-8a). - The older rule text (LAC 49:I §517, via Justia: https://regulations.justia.com/states/louisiana/title-49/part-i/chapter-5/section-i-517/) states the same $50 figure and adds that a product not receiving a written response within 60 business days of initial submission may be sold after the 60th business day by any permitted wholesaler/retailer until LDH accepts or rejects it — note the clock discrepancy: the current LDH page describes a 60-day register-or-decline clock that resets on each request, while the older rule excerpt describes a 15-business-day feedback window in a 2023 LDH memo; the current page governs, and the memo/rule history is [Verify] for the parent's Part 1. - In-state manufacturing permit to operate: facilities manufacturing consumable hemp for ingestion in Louisiana must obtain a Permit to Operate with LDH Food and Drug Unit (LDH primer, Act 498 of 2022 authority — see §4.4.1). A separate fee for that Permit to Operate, if any beyond the processor permit fee, was not found [Verify].

4.4.4 ATC permits — wholesaler, retailer, remote retailer, special event

Statute: La. R.S. 3:1484 (Justia reproduction of 2022 text: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2022/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1484/; current text should be re-checked on legis.la.gov for Act 752 amendments):

"A.(1) Each wholesaler of consumable hemp products shall apply for and obtain a permit from the office of alcohol and tobacco control." "(2) The commissioner may establish and collect an annual wholesaler permit fee. The amount of the wholesaler permit fee shall be based on the cost of the regulatory functions performed and shall not exceed five hundred dollars per year." "B.(1)(a) Each person who sells or is about to engage in the business of selling at retail any consumable hemp product shall first apply for and obtain a permit for each place of business from the office of alcohol and tobacco control." "(b) For purposes of this Section, each individually registered domain name owned or leased by or on behalf of a remote retailer shall be considered a place of business. No person or entity shall be required to have a physical place of business in the state of Louisiana in order to sell consumable hemp products at retail." "(2) Prior to selling consumable hemp products at a special event, the retailer shall request and promptly receive an annual special event permit from the commissioner. … The permittee shall notify the commissioner in writing of any special event the permittee will be attending prior to the event. Failure to notify the commissioner shall be grounds for revocation of the permit." "C.(1) The commissioner may establish and collect an annual retail permit fee and an annual special event permit fee. The amount of each permit fee … shall be based on the cost of the regulatory functions performed and shall not exceed one hundred seventy-five dollars per year."

Actual ATC charges found: - Wholesaler application fee: $500.00 (ATC form, https://atc.louisiana.gov/media/idcpj45s/application-for-consumable-hemp-wholesale-permit_a11y.pdf — "Consumable Hemp Wholesale Application Fee $500.00"; "all application and permit fees are nonrefundable"; payment by personal/business check, cashier's check, money order, or credit card). - Retail / special-event fee: capped at $175/year by statute (above); the ATC retail application form itself was not opened in this run — [Verify: current ATC retail application fee actually charged, and whether it is $175]. - ATC online licensing system (from the wholesale form): https://laatcabc.atc.la.gov/laatcprod/pub/Login.aspx — applicants are recommended to register there and submit online; paper applications may be mailed to 7979 Independence Blvd., Suite 101, Baton Rouge, LA 70896-6404 / P.O. Box 66404, Baton Rouge, LA 70896, or submitted in person at ATC offices. ATC contact on the form: telephone (225) 925-4041, www.atc.la.gov. - Wholesale application checklist (same form): coloured copy of driver's licence for each owner/member/director/officer; corporate documents (articles as filed with the Secretary of State, notarised partnership agreement, etc.); proof of registration and good standing with the Louisiana Secretary of State; Louisiana Tax Clearance certificate from the Department of Revenue; application fees. - Retailer sourcing rule (Act 752 context): a retailer permitted under R.S. 3:1484 must obtain consumable hemp products to sell at retail only from a wholesaler permitted under the same section (per the House floor amendment text for SB 237, legis.la.gov: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1381220 — this is an amendment document, not the enrolled Act 752 text; the sourcing rule is [Verify against current R.S. 3:1484]). - Bar/restaurant and gasoline bars since 1 Jan 2025: no new hemp retail permits to businesses also licensed as bars/restaurants (secondary: LegalClarity summary of HB 952 advisory; corroborated by the Act 752 gasoline/alcohol-location prohibitions above and by the ABA article's "c. 220 grandfathered" figure — the 220 figure is secondary [Verify against ATC permit data]). Gasoline retailers are barred except qualified truck stops (R.S. 27:417 licensees) per Act 752 text above. - Department of Revenue overlay: every wholesaler and retailer must hold the ATC permit; retailers must obtain a licence for each place of business and each individually registered domain name for remote retail. Source: Louisiana Department of Revenue FAQ: https://revenue.louisiana.gov/tax-education-and-faqs/faqs/excise-taxes/consumable-hemp-products/do-i-have-to-have-a-permit-to-sell-consumable-hemp-products/

4.4.5 Other hemp permits

  • No separate Louisiana "transporter" licence on the current LDAF page (see historic contract carrier in §4.1.3).
  • Seed dealer overlay: distributors of hemp seed must possess a current Louisiana Seed Dealer License (LDAF seed acquisition form, 2020 — secondary/dated, [Verify current requirement]).
  • No hemp retailer licence issued by LDAF or LDH — retail is ATC only. A business that grows hemp (LDAF), processes it into a consumable (LDH), and sells it at retail (ATC) needs all three agencies' authorisations for the respective activities; one licence does not cover the others.

4.5 Social equity, minority, and small-business provisions

Finding: No enacted Louisiana social-equity, minority set-aside, or small-business preference programme for cannabis or hemp licensing was located in any official source opened.

  • The most authoritative secondary check located (CannBus Louisiana Legal Summary Q3 2026, https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/la_lsum.html, citing the Minority Cannabis Business Association State Equity Map) states: "Louisiana does not offer a state social equity program for medical cannabis licensing. There are no state-level licensing priorities, set-asides, or fee waivers/reductions for applicants from communities disproportionately affected by cannabis prohibition." CannBus's market report (https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/la_cannmir.html) repeats: "Social equity program: N/A: none found" and "No cannabis-specific grant, loan or fee-waiver program was found at Louisiana Economic Development or LDH." These are secondary; the absence is consistent with the statute text opened (R.S. 40:1046 contains no equity preference; R.S. 3:1465/1483/1484 contain no equity preference), but absence-of-text is not a quotable statute — mark as [No programme found in official sources checked; Verify by a legis.la.gov full-text search for "social equity" before the parent asserts this absolutely].
  • Proposed, not enacted: HB 637 (2021 Regular Session) proposed a social-equity chapter (R.S. 26:941 et seq. in the original; committee amendments recast it as R.S. 3:4761 et seq.) declaring that "a program of social equity should be established" with financial assistance and licence-application benefits. Sources: legis.la.gov original: http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1212341 and committee amendments: http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1223731. HB 637 did not become law (it was part of the failed 2021 adult-use package). It must be listed only as PROPOSED, never as current law.
  • Contradictory secondary sources — rejected: StateRegsToday pages claim Louisiana grants "priority licensing to minority-owned businesses," "reduced fees," an ATC "Equity Score," and a "Community Reinvestment Fund" (https://www.stateregstoday.com/health/marijuana-legalization/social-equity-programs-in-louisiana and https://www.stateregstoday.com/business/cannabis-grower-license-in-louisiana). No statute, rule, or agency page corroborates any of these, and they contradict the closed 2-licence/10-permit structure (there is no open round in which a priority could operate). These claims are treated as unreliable and are NOT adopted. The same site's claim of a $1,000 industrial hemp licence fee and $10,000 therapeutic cultivation application fee structure is likewise not adopted where it conflicts with the official $500 LDAF fee and the $10,000 figure that IS in R.S. 40:1046(H)(4)(b) — the $10,000 figure coincides, but the site's other fee claims do not.
  • General small-business programmes (not cannabis-specific): Louisiana Economic Development (LED) general programmes (e.g. Enterprise Zone, Quality Jobs) were not found to contain a cannabis-specific carve-out in the sources checked; whether a hemp or medical business could qualify for a general programme is [Verify with LED — no cannabis-specific eligibility statement located].
  • Banking-adjacent equity note: Act 100 (HB 211, 2020), R.S. 6:121.1.1, prohibits the Commissioner of the Office of Financial Institutions from prohibiting/discouraging or penalising a state bank or credit union solely for providing financial services to a "cannabis-related legitimate business" or service provider. Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1180955. This is a banking-protection provision, not a licensing equity provision, and it does not name any bank. See §6.7.

LDH consumable hemp product registration $50 per product per year LDH hemp page
ATC consumable hemp wholesaler $500 application (nonrefundable) ATC wholesale form
ATC consumable hemp retailer / special event Statutory cap $175/year each; actual charged fee [Verify] R.S. 3:1484(C)
Louisiana entity formation (general, not cannabis-specific) LLC articles $100; corporation articles $75; annual report $30 (LLC/corp) — secondary summary of SOS fee schedule, [Verify on sos.la.gov] Secondary: https://sosbusinesssearch.com/louisiana-secretary-of-state-office

(b) Reported operator costs (official Act 150 Report 2025 — these are the licensees' own reported 2025 figures, NOT a startup quote)

Good Day Farm Louisiana, calendar 2025 (LDH Act 150 Report 2025, https://ldh.la.gov/assets/oph/Center-EH/sanitarian/Act-150-Report.2025.pdf): - Construction $27,700,000; Licenses, Fees, Permits & Taxes $138,200; Production, Manufacturing, Equipment $3,300,000; Wages, Employee Benefits & Payroll Taxes $11,800,000; Utilities $2,900,000; Security Personnel & Monitoring $379,000; Professional Services (Accounting, Legal, Banking) $169,000. - Note: the report does not state whether "Construction $27,700,000" is cumulative investment or 2025-only spend — [Verify before quoting as a single-year cost].

Ilera Holistic Healthcare (Advanced Biomedics LLC), calendar 2025 (same report): - Construction $12,439,400 (report footnote: "Construction Investment amount includes capital invested by Licensee property owner and leased to Licensee for use in Therapeutic Marijuana Production"); Licenses, Fees, Permits & Taxes $1,580,900; Production, Manufacturing, Equipment $6,770,000; Wages, Employee Benefits & Payroll Taxes $3,628,300; Utilities $396,100; Security Personnel & Monitoring $156,900; Professional Services $232,000; plus transdermal-patch subcontract $25,400 (manufactured on Ilera's site with Ilera distillate). - Good Day Farm reported no subcontracting for cultivation/extraction/processing/production in 2025.

These figures show the order of magnitude of an operating, vertically integrated medical producer in Louisiana (multi-million-dollar construction and seven-figure annual payroll), but they are not a startup-cost estimate for a new entrant — and, crucially, a new entrant cannot enter medical production or retail at all unless a vacancy opens (see §§4.1–4.2).

(c) Non-official estimates — marked as such, use with caution

  • Hemp farming/processing: No credible, dated, Louisiana-specific startup estimate was located in an official or reputable secondary source in this run. Generic national hemp business-plan templates (e.g. hempcbdbusinessplans.com) were found but are not adopted — they are sales material, not Louisiana cost data. The honest statement for the parent's report is: no reliable Louisiana hemp startup-cost estimate located [Verify / gap].
  • Medical retail build-out: No official or reputable secondary Louisiana-specific retail startup estimate was located. Secondary price guides (Elevate Holistics, ARCannabisClinic) discuss product prices, not build-out costs, and are not used for startup costs.
  • Patient-side costs (for context, not business startup): Louisiana charges patients no state registration/card fee (secondary: MMJ.com 2026 renewal guide, https://www.mmj.com/louisiana-medical-marijuana-card/renewals/ — "$0 (Louisiana charges patients no registration or card fees)"; the $149.99 figure on that page is that clinic's own telehealth evaluation fee, not a state fee). Physician/clinic evaluation fees are private-market prices and vary.

5.11 Patient statistics — what exists and what does not

  • No LDH patient registry or patient-count dashboard was located. Louisiana issues no patient card (secondary: MMJ.com — "Louisiana does not issue a patient registration card"; "no patient-facing portal; dispensing is tracked in the LDH-run LMMTS"). The LMMTS (Louisiana Medical Marijuana Tracking System) is the seed-to-sale/patient-dispensing database, but it is not public — retailers and labs must use it; patients and the public have no LMMTS login.
  • Patient counts therefore come only from: (a) the statutory satellite thresholds (3,500 / 7,000 active qualified patients per region — a trigger, not a published count); (b) operator/press statements (see §6.2); (c) the Act 150 Reports, which contain no patient counts.
  • Enforcement/compliance actions (medical): No published LDH violation/suspension list for manufacturers, retailers, or labs was located [Unavailable].

PART 6 — MARKET DATA

Read this first — wholesale vs retail confusion (affects every sales figure below): Louisiana's only official money series is the 7% fee on producers' gross (wholesale) sales, collected by the Department of Revenue. Dividing fee collections by 7% gives producer-to-pharmacy wholesale value, NOT retail sales to patients. Secondary dashboards that report a single "Louisiana cannabis sales" number mix these concepts: one secondary site reports $61.0M "2025 retail sales" while the wholesale series implies $90.9M wholesale for FY2025 — retail cannot be below wholesale. At least one of those two numbers is wrong or differently defined. Both are carried below with their definitions and conflicts flagged; neither is presented as an official retail-sales total, because no official retail-sales total was located.

6.1 Medical sales by year — official fee series (wholesale basis)

Source for the fee series: secondary compilation citing Louisiana Department of Revenue (2026) — The Motley Fool, "Marijuana Tax Revenue by State" (accessed via search 25 Oct 2026): https://www.fool.com/research/marijuana-tax-revenue-by-state/ — secondary compilation; the underlying Department of Revenue reports were not opened directly [Verify against LDR annual reports / revenue.louisiana.gov].

Fiscal year 7% fee collections (Fool / LDR-cited) Implied producer gross sales (collections ÷ 7%)
FY2020 $76,794 ~$1.10M
FY2021 $286,963 ~$4.10M
FY2022 $1,066,243 ~$15.23M
FY2023 $2,309,603 ~$32.99M
FY2024 $3,602,620 ~$51.47M
FY2025 $6,362,786 ~$90.90M

Cross-check: independent secondary analysis (CannBus Q3 2026, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/la_cannmir.html, and Shreveport-Bossier Advocate, 2026, https://www.shreveportbossieradvocate.com/business/louisiana-marijuana-tax-cut-280e/article_6917d21e-5682-58c9-b33a-84c0582919d0.html) independently gives the same FY2025 wholesale figure — "$90.9 million worth of cannabis to dispensaries in the year ending June 30, 2025, a 77% increase compared with the prior fiscal year, according to Louisiana Department of Revenue reports" (Advocate). The 77% growth rate is consistent with $51.47M → $90.90M (+76.6%). The FY2025 figure is therefore well-corroborated as a wholesale figure, even though the primary LDR table was not opened.

What is NOT available: calendar-year retail sales to patients; sales by product form at retail; sales by region or by retailer; average transaction value. The Act 150 Reports give volumes (lbs/units), not dollars (see §6.3).

Earlier history (secondary, for context): MJBizDaily's Marijuana Business Factbook estimated 2019 Louisiana sales at $1M–$1.5M (MJBizDaily, 2020: https://mjbizdaily.com/news/louisiana-lawmakers-approve-medical-cannabis-reform-bills/205832/) — consistent with the FY2020 fee-implied ~$1.10M wholesale figure, and with first sales in August 2019. MJBizDaily (2019, pre-launch) had projected $6M–$12M in 2019 and $15M–$30M within 3–5 years — those projections were not met on that timetable.

6.7 Cannabis-friendly banks and credit unions

  • Law (official): Act 100 (HB 211, 2020), R.S. 6:121.1.1 — the Commissioner of the Office of Financial Institutions "shall not" prohibit/discourage or penalise a state bank or credit union solely for providing financial services to a cannabis-related legitimate business or service provider, or its employees/owners/operators, solely because of that status (with an "egregious violations" exception). Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1180955
  • Named institutions: No official list of Louisiana banks or credit unions serving cannabis businesses was located, and no institution is named here. One secondary commentary (Cannabis Law Report, undated) claims Louisiana "has no banking protections" — that claim is wrong on the statute (Act 100 exists) and is rejected; it appears to confuse "no state lending programme" with "no protections." The correct statement is: Louisiana has a state banking-protection statute (Act 100) but no state cannabis lending/grant programme and no published roster of cannabis-serving institutions [Verify with the Office of Financial Institutions].
  • Federal context (given baseline): No federal cannabis banking law exists; Schedule III medical status (28 Apr 2026) does not by itself create a federal banking safe harbour. Secondary press (Shreveport-Bossier Advocate, 2026) quotes Good Day Farm's president as calling rescheduling's operational impact "premature to speculate" and Ilera as "still evaluating" — operator caution, not a banking announcement.

R.S. 3:1465 and La. R.S. 3:1483 on legis.la.gov; and the 420Property Louisiana hub page.
