9.2.1 The 1978 law — what it was, and what it was not

Louisiana's first therapeutic law is consistently described in secondary histories as Act 725 of 1978, sponsored by Senator Tony (Troy) Guarisco, covering glaucoma and chemotherapy, with a Marijuana Prescription Review Board that was never effectively staffed and no supply route, so no patient ever lawfully obtained marijuana under it. The Reason history puts it this way (secondary, 14 Nov 2019): "Louisiana first legalized medical marijuana back in 1978. It amended the law in 1991, then left the program to wither on the regulatory vine, with the Department of Health failing to appoint a Marijuana Prescription Review Board or to draw up contracts with national groups for production and distribution." — https://reason.com/2019/11/14/the-cajun-cannabis-conundrum/?itm_source=parsely-api (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026). The 1978 Act number, sponsor name spelling (Tony vs Troy Guarisco in different secondary sources), and board name (Marijuana Prescription Review Board vs Marijuana Control Board in one secondary source) are all [VERIFY] against the 1978 session law before any of them is cited as confirmed. Do not present 1978 as the start of an operating programme — it was a law on the books with no operating programme.

9.2.2 The 1991 amendment — Act 874

The R.S. 40:1046 history line's first entry is "Acts 1991, No. 874, §1" (legis.la.gov, search-indexed, [VERIFY] by direct open). Secondary histories agree the 1991 amendment added spastic quadriplegia to the 1978 law's conditions. No operating programme followed in 1991 either. The often-repeated secondary claim that the 1991 bill "failed to pass" (StateRegsToday timeline) is WRONG on the history line's own terms — Act 874 exists in the statute history — and is flagged as CONFLICT C-3 in §10.3; do not repeat it.

9.2.3 The 2015 Act — Act 261 (SB 143, Alison Neustrom Act)

Governor Bobby Jindal signed SB 143 on 29 June 2015; it became Act 261, effective 29 June 2015 (TrackBill history, secondary tracker, accessed 25 Oct 2026). It created the modern R.S. 40:1046 framework but with the two defects that made it inoperable in practice: physicians had to "prescribe" a Schedule I substance (federally impermissible), and the condition list was confined to glaucoma, spastic quadriplegia, and chemotherapy effects, in non-inhalation, non-raw forms only. The 2016 Acts fixed the first defect and widened the second.

9.2.4 The 2016 Acts — Act 96 (SB 271) and Act 567 (SB 180)

Governor John Bel Edwards signed SB 271 (Act 96, effective 19 May 2016) and SB 180 (Act 567). SB 271 changed "prescribe" to "recommend", expanded conditions, and gave LSU and Southern AgCenters the right of first refusal for production licensing. The R.S. 40:1046 history line confirms both Acts and the 19 May 2016 effective date for Act 96 (legis.la.gov, search-indexed, [VERIFY] by direct open). A secondary summary (NORML/The Weed Blog, May 2016) states SB 271 required the two AgCenters to decide whether to seek licensing by 2 September 2016 — secondary-only, [VERIFY] against the enrolled Act 96 text if the deadline matters.

9.2.5 Pharmacy permitting under the Board — and the 10-permit structure

Under the Board of Pharmacy era, marijuana pharmacies were permitted per LDH administrative region, with a 10-permit structure that survives in LDH's current "maximum 10" base-permit table. The LDH page's current table lists 10 base permits (Region 1 has two entries — H & W Acquisition Company LLC, New Orleans, and Crescent City Therapeutics, LLC, Kenner — and Regions 2–9 one each) and 19 satellite locations (LDH page, accessed 25 Oct 2026). The oft-repeated secondary figure of "nine dispensaries" for 2019 reflects the nine licensed pharmacies operating at first sales (see §9.2.6), not a 9-permit cap; the 10th base permit (Region 1's second permit) is the point most secondary timelines blur. [VERIFY] the date the 10th base permit was issued, if a precise 9→10 history is required — it was not established in this run.

9.2.6 First sales — 6 August 2019

Verbatim from the LSU AgCenter announcement (official university source, via search-indexed text): "Therapeutic cannabis products developed through a partnership between the LSU AgCenter and GB Sciences Louisiana were made available for sale for the first time in Louisiana Tuesday, Aug. 6." and "This initial batch of products includes three formulations of sublingual tinctures in 30-milliliter bottles." and "People can obtain the products if they have one of the 16 qualifying medical conditions and receive a certified physician's recommendation for therapeutic cannabis. The products are available at nine licensed pharmacies in the state." — LSU AgCenter, 6 Aug 2019, https://www.lsuagcenter.com/profiles/rbogren/articles/page1565103258096 (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026; [VERIFY] by direct open). The secondary claim in one timeline that sales "officially began" in February 2022 is WRONG and is flagged as CONFLICT C-4 in §10.3; February 2022 is, at most, a garbled reference to smokable-flower sales starting in January 2022 (see §9.2.9). Contemporary reporting two weeks after first sales put the patient count at "about 5,000" (GB Sciences Louisiana president, via AP/Medical Xpress, 19 Aug 2019, https://medicalxpress.com/news/2019-08-grower-louisiana-medical-marijuana.html, secondary, accessed 25 Oct 2026) — a dated secondary figure, not an official LDH count, and superseded for current purposes by Run 1 Part 6 (no official LDH patient count located; ~150,000 operator statement via press, Feb 2026, secondary).

9.2.7 Expansion to physician discretion — Act 286 (HB 819), effective 1 August 2020

Verbatim from HB 819 Engrossed (legis.la.gov document, via search-indexed text): the bill adds to the debilitating-condition list "(10) Any condition not otherwise specified in present law or proposed law that a physician, in his medical opinion, considers debilitating to an individual patient and is qualified through his medical education and training to treat." — https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1169717 (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026; [VERIFY] the enrolled Act 286 text by direct open). The same document lists the other additions: Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, Lewy body dementia, motor neuron disease, spinal muscular atrophy, chronic pain associated with fibromyalgia, chronic pain associated with sickle cell disease, and any condition for which a patient is receiving hospice or palliative care. Secondary reporting of the votes (House 77–15 on 15 May 2020; Senate 28–6 on 27 May 2020; effective 1 August 2020) is from NORML/Tenth Amendment Center summaries (accessed 25 Oct 2026) and is [VERIFY] against the legis.la.gov bill history if vote counts are to be cited as confirmed. Later, the authorised-clinician class was widened beyond physicians to nurse practitioners with prescriptive authority and medical psychologists (Run 1 anchor; Board Authorized Clinicians page, accessed 25 Oct 2026, §9.1.4) — the precise Act for that widening was not established in this run and is [VERIFY] (one secondary source attributes it to a 2024 Act; do not assert an Act number here).

9.2.8 The 14-gram decriminalisation — Act 247 (HB 652), effective 1 August 2021

Verbatim from the Act 247 Résumé Digest (legis.la.gov document, via search-indexed text): "ACT 247 (HB 652) 2021 Regular Session Glover Prior law provided for a fine of up to $300, imprisonment for not more than 15 days, or both, with regard to a first conviction for possession of marijuana when the offender possessed 14 grams or less and provided for enhanced penalties for subsequent convictions. New law provides that the penalty for possession of 14 grams or less of marijuana for first or subsequent convictions is a fine of up to $100." and "New law further provides that if an offender upon whom a fine has been imposed for possession of 14 grams or less alleges indigency or otherwise fails to pay the imposed fine, the court shall determine whether the defendant has willfully refused to pay or has made bona fide efforts to legally acquire resources to pay." and "New law provides for enforcement of new law for possession of 14 grams or less by use of summons. Effective August 1, 2021. (Amends R.S. 40:966(C)(2)(a), (d), (e)(i), and (f)(i))" — https://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1236895 (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026; [VERIFY] the enrolled Act 247 text by direct open). This is NOT legalisation: possession of ≤14 g remains a misdemeanour offence punishable by a fine; possession of >14 g retains jail exposure (Run 1 Part 1 §1.3). Governor John Bel Edwards signed HB 652 on 15 June 2021 (secondary reporting of the signing statement, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — [VERIFY] against the Governor's bill-action page if the signing date is to be cited as confirmed). The bill's House author was Representative Cedric Glover of Shreveport, and secondary reporting notes the bill was modelled in part on a Shreveport local ordinance — secondary-only, [VERIFY] if that provenance matters.

9.2.9 Smokable flower legalisation — Act 424 (HB 391), effective 1 January 2022

Verbatim from Act 424 Enrolled (HB 391, legis.la.gov document, via search-indexed text): "(5)(a) No pharmacy authorized to dispense marijuana for therapeutic use in accordance with the provisions of this Section shall dispense more than two and one half ounces, or seventy-one grams, of raw or crude marijuana every fourteen days to any individual patient." and "(b) No pharmacy authorized to dispense marijuana for therapeutic use in accordance with the provisions of this Section shall dispense raw or crude marijuana to any person under twenty-one years of age without a recommendation from a physician specifically recommending marijuana in raw or crude form for that person." and "Section 2. This Act shall become effective on January 1, 2022." — https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1235925 (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026; [VERIFY] the enrolled text by direct open). The bill was signed by Governor Edwards on 22 June 2021 (Cannabis Business Times, June 2021, secondary, accessed 25 Oct 2026). Before 1 January 2022, inhalation was permitted only via a "metered-dose inhaler" (a device that "delivers a specific amount of medication to the lungs, in the form of a short burst of medicine that is usually self-administered by the patient via inhalation" — Act 424 enrolled text, same source). Contemporary reporting of the January 2022 rollout (Cannabis Business Times, Jan 2022, secondary) records flower at $440–$480/ounce at one West Monroe retailer and $35–$80 per eighth-ounce across the state — dated secondary price points, NOT official price data (Run 1 Part 6: no official price series located).

9.2.11 Changes to the university licence model — from first refusal to exit

  • 2016: LSU and Southern AgCenters given the right of first refusal for production licensing (Act 96, §9.2.4). Both opted in, each with a private contractor (LSU/GB Sciences Louisiana; Southern/Advanced Biomedics, later Ilera Holistic Healthcare).
  • 2019–2024: The two licensees operated through their contractors. Secondary reporting (Cannabis Business Times, 2019) notes Southern "originally partnered with a Louisiana company called Advanced Biomedics before later aligning itself with Pennsylvania-based Ilera Holistic Healthcare, which has since been acquired by TerrAscend Corp." — secondary-only, and the TerrAscend acquisition point is [VERIFY] and is NOT needed for the licence-model history.
  • 2024: Act 150 (SB 228) removed the universities from the manufacturing programme. Verbatim LDH summary: "Act 150 of the 2024 Legislature - extended the sunset date of the medical marijuana program to 2030, changed the basis for calculating patient numbers for reporting purposes, and removed the universities from the manufacturing program" — LDH page, https://ldh.la.gov/page/medical-marijuana (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Verbatim LDH Emergency Rule summary: "Removed language referencing permitting of manufacturers and requiring that licenses be issued to Southern University and Louisiana State University; licenses were transferred to the former permit-holders contracted by the universities in 2024" — same page. Run 1 anchor (transfer 1 July 2024 to Good Day Farm Louisiana LLC and Advanced Biomedics LLC dba Ilera Holistic Healthcare) is unchanged by anything in this run.
  • Research survives the exit: The current R.S. 40:1046 text as shown in the legis.la.gov search excerpt retains: "L. The Louisiana State University Agricultural Center, the Southern University Agricultural Center, and the University of Louisiana at Monroe may conduct research on marijuana for therapeutic use." — legis.la.gov law page, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=96986 (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026; [VERIFY] current text). The universities' exit is from manufacturing, not from research. Whether any university research licence or project is currently active was not established in this run — [VERIFY] against LSU AgCenter / Southern University Agricultural Center research pages (Part 11 territory, not decided here).

9.3 Ballot history and public opinion polling

9.3.1 No statewide citizen initiative — confirmed, with the mechanism

Louisiana has no statewide citizen initiative and no statewide citizen referendum for statutes or constitutional amendments. The only route for a constitutional amendment to reach voters is a joint resolution passed by two-thirds of each legislative chamber in one session; amendments do not require the Governor's signature to be referred. Secondary confirmation (Ballotpedia, accessed 25 Oct 2026): "In Louisiana, citizens do not have the power to initiate statewide initiatives or referendums. As of 2021, voters of Louisiana had never voted on a ballot measure to authorize a statewide initiative and referendum process." and "The Louisiana Constitution requires a two-thirds vote in each legislative chamber during one legislative session to refer a constitutional amendment to the ballot. That amounts to a minimum of 70 votes in the Louisiana House of Representatives and 26 votes in the Louisiana State Senate, assuming no vacancies." — https://ballotpedia.org/Louisiana_2026_ballot_measures (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026). Official-text check still required: the governing provisions are Louisiana Constitution Article XIII, §1 (amendments) and Article XIII, §2 (convention) — the constitution text itself was NOT opened in this run, so the two-thirds mechanism is secondary-confirmed here and marked [VERIFY] against the official constitution text on legis.la.gov before it is cited as confirmed law. 10.1.2 The legal framework with the state — what federal recognition does and does not do here

  • Government-to-government relationship: Federally recognised tribes maintain a government-to-government relationship with the United States and are eligible for Bureau of Indian Affairs funding and services, with federal reservations operating outside state jurisdiction for many purposes (LSU Libraries guide, secondary-academic, https://guides.lib.lsu.edu/c.php?g=1095533&p=7990161, accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026). This general statement is NOT a Louisiana cannabis rule and must not be cited as one.
  • State-recognised tribes are different in kind: The same LSU guide states state-recognised tribes "may be allotted state reservations. These reservations are exempt from state tax, but are subject to state law." — same source. That distinction matters for cannabis: a state-recognised tribe has no federal-recognition sovereignty shield for a marijuana programme, and Louisiana's medical and consumable-hemp statutes apply to it on the same terms as to any other Louisiana person or business, unless a specific state law says otherwise (none was located in this run — [VERIFY] against R.S. 25:1301 et seq., the Louisiana Indian affairs statutes, if a state-recognition legal effect is to be asserted).
  • No Louisiana tribal-state cannabis compact located: No compact, memorandum of understanding, or agreement between Louisiana and any federally recognised tribe covering cannabis or hemp cultivation, retail, taxation, or enforcement was located in official state or tribal sources searched in this run. Louisiana's well-known tribal-state gaming compacts (under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act) are a different subject and do NOT cover cannabis; do not cite a gaming compact as cannabis authority. [UNAVAILABLE — no cannabis compact found; follow-up: Governor's Office of Indian Affairs + each tribe's government office, and a legis.la.gov full-text search for tribal cannabis provisions.]
  • No Louisiana tribal cannabis ordinance located: No tribal code, ordinance, resolution, or regulation of any Louisiana tribe authorising, prohibiting, or regulating cannabis or hemp was located in official tribal sources searched in this run. Tribal codes are generally published by the tribe itself (or not published at all); the absence finding here means "none located in the sources searched", not a proven universal negative. Follow-up route is in the Gaps list.
  • Federal law frame (given baseline + general federal law, not Louisiana law): Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I federally (given baseline), so a tribal adult-use programme would face the same federal-law problem as any other adult-use programme, plus the additional question of federal trust-land jurisdiction. State-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III on 28 April 2026 (given baseline) — but that change is framed in terms of state licensing; whether and how it would apply to a tribally licensed medical programme with no state licence was NOT established in this run and is [VERIFY] against federal guidance before any statement is made. Hemp, by contrast, is federally lawful if produced under an approved state, tribal, or USDA plan (see §10.1.4) — the hemp route is the only tribal route with a clear federal plan mechanism, and no Louisiana tribe has used it (see §10.1.4).

10.2 Interstate issues

10.2.1 The governing distinction — transit through vs sale into vs personal transport

Three different interstate acts must not be conflated:

  1. Transit/shipment through a state of lawfully produced hemp/hemp products is federally protected (see §10.2.2).
  2. Sale into a state is governed by the destination state's retail law, even if the product lawfully transited other states (see §10.2.3).
  3. Personal transport of marijuana across a state line by an individual is a different act again, governed by federal controlled-substances law and by the destination state's possession law, and is NOT protected by the hemp transit rule (see §10.2.4).

10.2.2 Hemp shipments — federal transit protection, and Louisiana's own hemp-transport rules

Federal transit rule (verbatim, 2018 Farm Bill §10114, via USDA guidance summaries): "No State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with subtitle G of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (as added by section 10113) through the State or the territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable." — quoted in USDA guidance summary, Arnold & Porter, https://www.arnoldporter.com/en/perspectives/advisories/2019/05/usda-issues-guidance-on-hemp?pdf=1 (secondary law-firm summary of USDA guidance, accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026), and in the USDA hemp rule's federalism discussion (7 CFR §990.63: "No State or Indian Tribe may prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products lawfully produced under a State or Tribal plan approved under subpart B of this part, under a license issued under subpart C of this part, or under 7 U.S.C. 5940 through the State or territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable" — via FMCSA-hosted white paper quoting the rule, https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/sites/fmcsa.dot.gov/files/2020-07/White_Paper_from_GenCanna_Global_Regarding_Transport_of_Hemp.pdf, accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026). Caveat: the federal rule protects hemp "produced in accordance with" an approved plan. A shipment that exceeds the federal hemp definition — including, after 11 December 2026 on the given baseline, a product above the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap — would fall outside that protection on the given baseline's own terms. That is the interstate consequence of the federal hemp cliff for Louisiana shippers: a Louisiana-compliant 5 mg product that is lawful to sell in Louisiana (as written) would, after 11 December 2026, no longer be federal "hemp" and would lose Farm Bill transit protection, even though Louisiana law as written had not changed. No Louisiana state response to that cliff was located in Run 1 or in this run ([UNAVAILABLE] in both runs).

Louisiana hemp-transport rules (state law, secondary summary of statute — [VERIFY] current R.S. 3:1461–1471 text): Louisiana's Industrial Hemp Law (R.S. 3:1461–1471, Act 164 of 2019) authorises licensed cultivation, processing, handling and transportation of industrial hemp, defined (pre-Act 752 framework, via secondary summaries) as Cannabis sativa L. with delta-9 THC ≤0.3% on a dry-weight basis; material above that threshold is marijuana, not hemp, and handling/transporting it outside the destruction exception is unlawful under R.S. 3:1471 (per the 2020 bill text excerpt, legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1173252, accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026 — bill text, not current statute, [VERIFY] current text). LDAF's hemp pages describe "guidelines for the safe and legal movement of hemp" and required reporting for production and acquisition (LDAF page, https://www.ldaf.la.gov/plants/industrial-hemp, accessed 25 Oct 2026) — the movement-guideline document itself was not opened in this run, [VERIFY]. Practical documentation for a hemp shipment (licence, manifest, certificate of analysis) is industry/USDA-guidance practice, not a Louisiana statute quoted here; do not cite a Louisiana manifest statute that was not located.

Louisiana hemp coming in from other states: Industrial hemp lawfully produced under another approved state/tribal/USDA plan may transit Louisiana under the federal rule above. But to be sold in Louisiana as a consumable hemp product, it must additionally satisfy Louisiana's sale rules (see §10.2.3) — transit protection is not a sale licence.

10.2.3 What can legally be brought into Louisiana — and what cannot

Consumable hemp products from other states (including Texas, Arkansas, and Mississippi hemp products): A consumable hemp product may be sold in Louisiana only if it is LDH-registered (through a permitted in-state or out-of-state processor — LDH Hemp Registration page, https://ldh.la.gov/page/hemp-registration, accessed 25 Oct 2026), sold by an ATC-permitted retailer/wholesaler/remote retailer, and compliant with Louisiana's product rules as written (Run 1 anchors: 5 mg/serving, 40 mg/package, beverages 5 mg/≥12 oz, age 21+, no inhalables/floral hemp at retail, no hemp alcohol, behind-employee-assistance display for non-beverage products). Origin does not save a non-compliant product: a Texas, Arkansas, or Mississippi hemp product that is lawful in its home state but exceeds Louisiana's caps, is an inhalable/floral product, or is unregistered in Louisiana cannot lawfully be sold at retail in Louisiana, even if it could lawfully transit Louisiana to another destination. Conversely, a product that meets Louisiana's rules and is properly registered and ATC-permitted may be sold in Louisiana regardless of where the hemp was grown, provided the processor route (in-state or out-of-state LDH permit) is satisfied. The LDH page's out-of-state processor route (FD-99a application, $175 initial fee on a sliding scale, >5% stakeholder list, good-character attestation) is the mechanism for out-of-state product entry — LDH Hemp Registration page, accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Remote / shipped sales into Louisiana: Louisiana law defines a "remote retailer" as "a person or entity who offers any consumable hemp product for sale at retail through a digital application, catalog, or the internet that can be purchased and delivered directly to a consumer in Louisiana" (R.S. 3:1481(7), Justia republication, https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1481/, accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026; [VERIFY] current legis.la.gov text). Remote retailers require ATC permitting per place of business / per domain (Run 1 Part 4 §4.4.4 anchor). An unpermitted out-of-state website shipping consumable hemp directly to Louisiana consumers is therefore not a lawful Louisiana retail channel on the sources located, even if the product is hemp under federal law.

Medical marijuana from other states — cannot lawfully be brought in by the patient: There is no Louisiana law authorising a patient to import marijuana purchased in another state, and no interstate medical-marijuana import agreement was located. Federal law independently prohibits interstate transport of marijuana except as authorised by federal law, and the given baseline keeps adult-use marijuana in Schedule I and frames Schedule III around state-licensed medical activity — it does not create a personal interstate-transport right. The lawful route for a visiting patient is to purchase in Louisiana under R.S. 40:1046.1 (see §10.2.4), not to carry product across the border. The same applies in reverse: a Louisiana patient cannot lawfully carry Louisiana-purchased medical marijuana into Mississippi, Arkansas, or Texas and expect that state's law to protect it (see §10.2.5 for each neighbour's position). LDH's retailer rule reinforces the boundary from the seller's side: "Retailers may not deliver to addresses located outside of the state of Louisiana" (LDH page, accessed 25 Oct 2026).

Non-medical marijuana from other states: Adult-use marijuana is illegal in Louisiana regardless of where it was lawfully purchased (e.g. in an adult-use state). Possession in Louisiana is governed by R.S. 40:966 (Run 1 Part 1 §1.3), including the ≤14 g fine-only tier and the >14 g tiers. Lawful purchase elsewhere is not a defence in Louisiana on any source located.

Industrial (non-consumable) hemp from other states: Lawfully produced industrial hemp may be transported into/through Louisiana under the federal transit rule and Louisiana's hemp framework, subject to LDAF licensing/reporting for Louisiana handling (see §10.2.2). Material above the hemp THC threshold is marijuana for Louisiana purposes and is not protected.

10.2.4 Visiting patients — Louisiana's inbound route (and its limits)

Louisiana DOES accept visiting qualifying patients for in-state purchase — this is Run 1's anchor and is confirmed by the statute text. Verbatim from R.S. 40:1046.1 (Justia 2022 republication, via search-indexed text; [VERIFY] current legis.la.gov text): "A visiting qualifying patient may obtain medical marijuana from a marijuana pharmacy upon producing evidence of his valid medical marijuana registry identification card, or its equivalent, which has been issued under the medical marijuana laws of another state, district, territory, commonwealth, or insular possession of the United States." and "A marijuana pharmacy shall require each visiting qualifying patient to certify on a form approved by the board that he has been diagnosed by a licensed physician with one or more debilitating medical conditions." and the pharmacy must retain the registry card/equivalent, a government photo ID, and the signed form, and the dispensing pharmacist must review the patient's prescription monitoring programme records before dispensing — https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2022/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046-1/ (accessed via search-indexed text 25 Oct 2026). The authorising Acts are Act 438 (HB 135) and Act 439 (HB 137) of 2022, effective 1 August 2022 (MPP 2022 session summary, secondary, https://www.mpp.org/states/louisiana/louisiana-2022-legislative-session-cannabis-bills/, accessed 25 Oct 2026; Act 439 also provides visiting-patient immunity from prosecution for certain Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law violations). Limits: (a) the visiting-patient route authorises purchase from a Louisiana retailer, not importation of out-of-state product; (b) the "board" in the 2022 text is the Board of Pharmacy — after the Act 693 transfer, which body approves the form now is [VERIFY] (LDH presumably, but the current form-approver was not confirmed in this run); (c) secondary sources that still say "Louisiana lacks reciprocity / does not accept out-of-state cards" (e.g. Bluebird Wellness, Bloom Legal) are stale pre-2022 material and are flagged as CONFLICT C-6 in §10.3 — do not use them. Run 1's visiting-patient statement stands.

Run 1 anchors are 5 mg/serving and 40 mg/package under Act 752, and the LDH hemp pages are consistent with a 5 mg regime. Louisiana Cannabis and Hemp — Run 2, PART 11 ONLY: Operations Rules

Scope note. This is part of the combined Louisiana dossier (Parts 0–12), as corrected in the 28 October 2026 audit. See Part 1 (audit) at the top of this file for corrections and items still unverified.

How to read this file. Each of the 9 headings is treated separately for (a) medical (therapeutic) marijuana licensees/permit holders/laboratories and (b) hemp / consumable hemp businesses, where the rules differ. Where a rule is the same, that is stated rather than repeated. "Medical" means therapeutic marijuana under La. R.S. 40:1046 et seq. "Hemp" means industrial hemp under La. R.S. 3:1461 et seq. (LDAF) and "consumable hemp" means consumable hemp products under La. R.S. 3:1481–1485 (LDH + ATC). Louisiana has parishes, not counties; "parish" is used throughout.

Run 1 anchors kept consistent (NOT re-decided here). Medical only; no adult-use law. LDH regulates production/laboratories (Acts 491/492 of 2022, effective 1 August 2022) and retailers (Act 693 of 2024, effective 1 January 2025). Act 150 of 2024 transferred the two cultivation licences on 1 July 2024 to Good Day Farm Louisiana LLC and Advanced Biomedics LLC dba Ilera Holistic Healthcare, sunset 1 July 2030 (R.S. 40:1046(M)). 10 base retail permits + up to 20 satellites (30 locations total); retail fee $22,500/year; cultivation licence $100,000/year + $10,000 application fee + 7% gross-sales fee. No patient card/registry for residents; clinician-discretion qualification; flower 71 g / 14 days; no home grow; ≤14 g fine-only ≤$100. Consumable hemp (Act 752 of 2024, effective 1 January 2025): 5 mg total THC/serving, 40 mg/package (beverages 5 mg/≥12 oz, tinctures 1 mg/mL), age 21+, LDH registration + ATC permits; medical exempt from state AND local sales tax; consumable hemp excise 3%. Employment protection in Run 1 was state-employer only (R.S. 49:1016). Those anchors are repeated only where an operations rule touches them; this file does not re-litigate them.

Federal baseline (given, NOT re-researched in this run; only contradictions flagged). State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; IRS §280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical only; hemp PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-lab hemp testing delayed to 31 December 2026; federal medical rider through 11 December 2026; no federal banking law. No contradiction to that baseline was found in the operations sources opened for this file. One interaction is flagged, not resolved, in §11.1.6 and §11.9: Louisiana's state operations rules as written on 25 October 2026 still use the state 5 mg / 40 mg consumable limits and the state 0.3% hemp plant test; no Louisiana conforming rule, LDH rule, ATC guidance, or LDAF guidance responding to the 11 December 2026 federal dates was located in this run.

Sourcing method note — read first. Official pages opened and read directly in this run: LDH Medical Marijuana page; LDH Hemp Registration page; LDH consumable hemp final rule, Louisiana Register Vol. 52, No. 1 (20 January 2026), LR 52:54–58 (LAC Title 49, Part I, Chapter 5, §§501, 516–519, 521, 533–535, 539) as published in the LDH PDF; LDH medical marijuana Notice of Intent, Louisiana Register Vol. 51, No. 5 (20 May 2025), LR 51:717–722 (LAC Title 51, Part XXIX, Subpart 1 Chapters 1, 5, 7, 9 and Subpart 2 Chapters 21, 23, 25); La. R.S. 40:1046, 40:1046.2, 40:1046.3, 40:1046.4, and 3:1465 on legis.la.gov / Justia republications of the Louisiana Laws; LDAF industrial hemp regulations and reporting/forms pages. Where a rule text was read only in the May 2025 Notice of Intent (NOI) and not line-by-line in the January 2026 final rule (LR 52:59), that is flagged as [Verify — NOI-to-final survival]; the January 2026 final rule was confirmed to reenact/amend Part XXIX and enact Subpart 2 (Marijuana Retailers), but the Register excerpt opened for the final rule ran only through LAC 51:XXIX §505, so later chapters (notably Chapter 25 retailer operations) are cited to the NOI text with that flag. Secondary sources (notably a software vendor's Louisiana state page synthesising the January 2026 final rule, and LSU AgCenter extension pages) are labelled as secondary and are NEVER used as the sole authority for a rule; they are used only to point to a rule section that is then quoted from the official text, or to describe university research activity. No personal phone numbers or emails of individuals are reproduced; official public business addresses already published by LDH are reproduced because they are official public listings.

Rule-citation shorthand used below. LAC 51:XXIX = Louisiana Administrative Code Title 51, Part XXIX (Public Health — Sanitary Code, Medical Marijuana). LAC 49:I Ch. 5 = Title 49, Part I, Chapter 5 (Registration of Foods, Drugs, Cosmetics and Prophylactic Devices — consumable hemp). LAC 7:XIII = Title 7, Part XIII (LDAF industrial hemp rules, cited via Cornell LII for the USDA-reporting section only). LMMTS = Louisiana Medical Marijuana Tracking System.

11.1 Testing: required tests, sampling rules, failed tests and recalls, list of licensed labs

11.1.1 Medical — the testing statute: every batch, independent lab, 24-hour certificate of analysis

La. R.S. 40:1046.4, "Testing; sample collection; minimum standards; reporting; remediation" (Acts 2022, No. 491, §1; Acts 2024, No. 150, §1, eff. 22 May 2024; Acts 2024, No. 693, §1, eff. 1 January 2025), opened on legis.la.gov 25 October 2026 (https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=1295746):

"A.(1) Each licensee authorized to cultivate, extract, process, produce, and transport therapeutic marijuana pursuant to this Part shall comply with approved minimum standards by making each batch of therapeutic marijuana subject to random selection, sampling, and analysis conducted by an independent approved laboratory collector in a volume sufficient to ensure compliance." "A.(2) Each therapeutic marijuana laboratory licensed according to this Part shall maintain test results for no less than three years." "A.(3) The laboratory shall record test results in the Louisiana Medical Marijuana Tracking System and produce a certificate of analysis to be delivered to the Louisiana Department of Health and licensee permitted to cultivate, extract, process, produce, and transport therapeutic marijuana within twenty-four hours of test completion."

Required panels — R.S. 40:1046.4(B), verbatim (same source):

"Each batch of medical marijuana finished product shall pass all applicable testing standards, including appropriate microbial and fungal limits, acceptable standards for pesticide chemical residues, appropriate residual solvent and heavy metals limits, homogeneity for concentrates and extracts, and complete active ingredient analysis or potency analysis prior to transportation to a medical marijuana retail permit holder. The administrative rules of the Louisiana Department of Health shall allow for a variance of no greater than plus fifteen percent or minus fifteen percent from the labeled amount of active ingredients in the ingredient analysis or potency analysis."

No batch may be released before it passes — R.S. 40:1046.4(C)(1), verbatim (same source):

"Neither a licensee nor an approved laboratory authorized pursuant to this Part shall release or approve a therapeutic marijuana product for delivery or sale until a sample from the applicable product batch has complied with all required testing standards."

LDH's own summary is to the same effect — LDH Medical Marijuana page, opened 25 October 2026 (https://ldh.la.gov/page/medical-marijuana): "Each batch of product is tested for purity and to ensure that it does not exceed the THC-content levels prescribed by the Legislature. Product that has been tested and accepted by the licensee may be transported to one of the licensed retailers in the state for distribution to a consumer." Note also R.S. 40:1046(I): "The levels of THC in any marijuana produced pursuant to this Section shall be reduced to the lowest acceptable therapeutic levels available through scientifically accepted methods" — a production standard, not a numeric potency cap; no numeric THC potency cap for medical products was located in §1046 itself (source: same legis.la.gov §1046 page, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=96986, accessed 25 October 2026).

11.1.2 Medical — sampling rule (LAC 51:XXIX §713) and the quality standards

LAC 51:XXIX §713, "Sampling Requirements," as published in the May 2025 NOI (Louisiana Register Vol. 51, No. 5, 20 May 2025, pp. 717–722; LDH PDF https://ldh.la.gov/assets/oph/Center-EH/sanitarian/fooddrug/marijuana/MedicalMarijuanaNoI.Published.5.20.25.pdf, accessed 25 October 2026) — [Verify — NOI-to-final survival in LR 52:59]:

  • §713(A): "Licensees shall sample every batch of product to ensure compliance with the standards of quality outlined below. Licensees shall not release any batch of product for sale until the representative sample has been verified as compliant. Batches may be tested prior to portioning or packaging."
  • §713(B) (paraphrased from the two-column Register text, which interleaves the pesticide table): sample verification is by issuance of a certificate of analysis from the approved laboratory conducting the analysis, issued to LDH and the originating facility no later than 24 hours after testing is complete — consistent with R.S. 40:1046.4(A)(3) above.
  • §713(F) quality standards, microbiological contaminants: "mold/yeast <100,000 CFU/g" (colony-forming units per gram). This is the January 2026 / Emergency Rule change LDH summarises on its medical page as: "Changed the regulatory threshold for mold/yeast from 10,000 colony-forming units per gram (CFU/g) to 100,000 CFU/g" (LDH page, same link as above). The pre-2025 figure of 10,000 CFU/g must NOT be quoted as current.
  • §713(G), Table 1, "Pesticide Residue Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCL) in parts per million (ppm) by dosage form," with separate "Ingested" and "Inhaled" columns. LDH's medical page summarises the change as: "Altered the pesticide testing schedule for marijuana to mirror the one utilized by the state of Oregon" (Emergency Rule summary, April 2025 Louisiana Register, effective 28 March 2025). Examples from the NOI table (ppm, ingested / inhaled): Abamectin 0.5 / 0.5; Acephate 0.4 / 0.4; Bifenthrin 0.2 / 0.2; Chlorpyrifos 0.2 / 0.2; DDVP (Dichlorvos) 0.1 / 0.1; Imidacloprid 0.4 / 0.4; Myclobutanil 0.2 / 0.2; Permethrins 0.2 / 0.2 (measured as cumulative residue of cis- and trans-permethrin isomers); Pyrethrins 1 / 1 (measured as cumulative residue of pyrethrin 1, cinerin 1, and jasmolin 1). 11.1.3 Medical — failed tests, remediation (once only), destruction, and recalls

Statute — R.S. 40:1046.4(C)(2)–(4), verbatim (legis.la.gov, same link as §11.1.1, accessed 25 October 2026):

"(2) A licensee may resubmit to an approved laboratory any sample that fails one or more initial tests required by this Part. The sample may be released for delivery and sale only if it passes all tests conducted by an approved laboratory in duplicate. The sample may be remediated according to any reasonably acceptable industry methods if it fails one or more tests conducted by an approved laboratory." "(3) Any remediated sample shall pass remediation testing in duplicate prior to approval for delivery and sale." "(4) A product may be remediated only once, and any product failing remediation testing shall be destroyed within sixty days of the failed test, in addition to the timely destruction of the entire batch from which the sample was collected."

Rule — LAC 51:XXIX §713(C), NOI text (same LDH PDF, [Verify — NOI-to-final survival]): "Any batch with a sample failing one or more of the tests (by exceeding allowable limits for contaminants or residues) shall be remediated or destroyed, at the option of the licensee. A batch shall only be remediated once, and if subsequent sampling fails to correct the exceedance, the affected batch shall be destroyed." Read together with the statute: one remediation, duplicate passing tests required after remediation, 60-day destruction deadline for a product failing remediation testing, plus timely destruction of the entire batch.

Recalls — manufacturer level: a recall plan is a required application element. LAC 51:XXIX §505(B)(6) (NOI text; also visible in the January 2026 final-rule Register excerpt, LR 52:59, in the LDH combined January 2026 PDF https://ldh.la.gov/assets/oph/Center-EH/sanitarian/fooddrug/hemp/Hemp_Final_Rule_1_2026.pdf, accessed 25 October 2026): applications for licensure must include, among other items, "6. a recall plan." No standalone medical recall procedure — no LDH recall-notification deadline, patient-notification method, or recall-class scheme — was located in R.S. 40:1046, R.S. 40:1046.2, R.S. 40:1046.4, or the LAC 51:XXIX sections opened. The operational recall levers that ARE located are: (i) the LMMTS chain (seed → lab → wholesale → retailer → sale → destruction, R.S. 40:1046(F)(1)(a)), which makes a batch traceable to retailers and patients; (ii) retailer refusal of a misbranded/adulterated/expired/nonsaleable delivery, recorded in the POS system and LMMTS (LAC 51:XXIX §2507(A), NOI text, [Verify — NOI-to-final survival]); and (iii) LDH inspection/enforcement (see §11.2.5). A secondary vendor synthesis (Flourish Software, Louisiana state page, https://www.flourishsoftware.com/states/louisiana, accessed 25 October 2026) states the same three points ("complete recall plan" as an application item; "Batches failing one or more tests may be remediated once; if a subsequent sample still fails, the batch must be destroyed") but adds no recall timeline and is NOT relied on for any timeline. [Verify: whether the January 2026 final rule adds a recall-execution section beyond the §505 application requirement.] A low-quality secondary page claiming "No… system in place for tracking and recalling unsafe marijuana products in Louisiana" (foodhandlersguide.com, accessed via search 25 October 2026) is REJECTED: it contradicts the LMMTS statute and the recall-plan requirement and appears to describe the illicit market, not the licensed programme.

11.1.4 Medical — licensed laboratories: licence, accreditation, independence, and the CURRENT list (Orion vs Ceres RESOLVED as a list question)

Licence statute — La. R.S. 40:1046.3, "Therapeutic marijuana laboratory; licensure and renewal requirements" (Acts 2022, No. 491, §1), opened on legis.la.gov 25 October 2026 (https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=1295745):

"A.(1) Prior to analyzing, testing, or handling therapeutic marijuana in Louisiana, an applicant for a therapeutic marijuana laboratory license shall submit an initial license application on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Louisiana Department of Health…" "A.(2) Approved laboratories may include the Department of Agriculture and Forestry agricultural chemistry laboratory; the colleges, universities, other institutions, and systems governed by the Louisiana Board of Regents; public-private partnerships involving the systems, colleges, and universities governed by the Louisiana Board of Regents and private laboratories; and private laboratories. The Department of Agriculture and Forestry agricultural chemistry laboratory shall be exempt from the application process and deemed approved but shall comply with Subparagraphs (d) and (e) of this Paragraph."

Other licensure conditions in §1046.3(A)(2) (same source): (a) proof of accreditation by "the National Institute on Drug Abuse, the National Environmental Laboratory Accreditation Conference, the International Organization for Standardization, or other accrediting entity approved by the department," maintained "in active and good standing… for the duration of licensure" — OR, alternatively, documentation of operating a state-approved active medical marijuana laboratory in another state for at least the past 12 months plus ISO (or LDH-approved) accreditation or a pending ISO application (if accreditation is not achieved within nine months of LDH inspection, LDH "shall not accept any additional certificates of analysis from the laboratory until the accreditation is received"); (b) employ/hire a laboratory director or other qualifying individual, and any person involved in testing or with access to restricted limited-access areas "shall obtain a permit in accordance with the requirements of R.S. 40:1047" (see §11.8); (c) at least one on-site facility inspection by LDH prior to licensure; (d) implement/utilise LMMTS to post accurate analyses/results, at the laboratory's exclusive cost; (e) demonstrate acceptable laboratory performance standards (accuracy, precision, proficiency, reportable ranges, specificity, quality controls).

Renewal — §1046.3(B) (same source): "Each therapeutic marijuana laboratory license shall be effective for one year and shall be renewed on or before December thirty-first annually"; renewal application "on or before October thirty-first each year"; a licence not timely renewed "shall expire on December thirty-first at midnight. Upon expiration of the license, the laboratory shall cease all operations and destroy all marijuana or marijuana products physically remaining at its location"; before renewal LDH must ensure continued compliance and Secretary of State good standing, and may conduct an out-of-cycle inspection. R.S. 40:1046 [or successor legislation]) and the current rules referenced above." 11.1.5 Consumable hemp — two testing layers: distillate/concentrate potency test + batch test, ISO/IEC 17025 labs, COA contents

Statute — La. R.S. 3:1483(A)(3)–(5) and (E)–(F), as summarised in Run 1 §1.6.7 and confirmed in the January 2026 rule text below: the processor must test the distillate/concentrate used; test each batch for disaggregated THC components by percentage, serving size, total THC mg per serving, and solvents/pesticides/microbials/heavy metals; retain test records at least 3 years; adhere to LDH sanitary regulations. (Full current §1483 text: https://legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=1147994, accessed 25 October 2026 in Run 1; re-opened in this run via the §1483(G) text returned by search, which confirms the 60-business-day review clock and the LDH list/scan duties in §1483(G)(1)–(3).)

Rule — LAC 49:I Ch. 5, §521, "Distillate Potency Test; Batch Testing; Certificates of Analysis" (LR 52:57, January 2026; LDH final-rule PDF, same link as above, accessed 25 October 2026):

  • §521(A): "A consumable hemp processor or manufacturer shall obtain a certificate of analysis (COA) of the distillate or concentrate used to produce any consumable hemp product," including the information required by §519(C)(5).
  • §521(B): "A manufacturer shall obtain a COA of each batch of consumable hemp product that it manufactures," including the information required by §519(C)(1)–(10).
  • §521(C): "A consumable hemp processor or manufacturer shall not sell or distribute in Louisiana any consumable hemp product from a batch whose COA indicates an exceedance of any of the maximum contaminant limits set forth in §519.C.1–10… or indicates that the product otherwise violates any requirements of this Chapter or Part VI of Chapter 10-a of R.S. Title 3." (This is the consumable-hemp failed-test rule: no sale/distribution of a failing batch. There is NO consumable-hemp remediation-and-retest provision in §521 comparable to medical §1046.4(C) — see §11.1.6.)
  • §521(D): "The COAs required by this Section shall be retained for at least three years and shall be made available to the department upon request."

Lab accreditation — LDH Hemp Registration page (https://ldh.la.gov/page/hemp-registration, accessed 25 October 2026): registration uploads must include "Certificates of Analysis (CoA) from accredited labs for each product" and "Laboratory accreditation verification documentation (ISO-IEC 17025)." Run 1 §1.6.1 adds the statutory independence requirement: the COA laboratory must be ISO-accredited or department-approved and independent, with no direct/indirect interest in a grower/processor/wholesaler/retailer (R.S. 3:1483(F)(1) as summarised there) — the January 2026 rule text opened does not restate the independence sentence in §521, so the independence point is carried from Run 1 with a [Verify against current §1483(F)] flag. The University of Louisiana at Monroe-affiliated laboratory preference in §1483(F)(2) (Run 1 §1.6.1) is likewise carried, not re-verified here.

COA contents — LAC 49:I §519(C) (LR 52:57, January 2026; LDH final-rule PDF). The Register excerpt shows subsections only in part ("B.–C.4. …", "6.–9. …"), so the full §519(C)(1)–(10) list could NOT be transcribed complete from the PDF opened. Items confirmed in the excerpt: a scannable barcode, QR code, or web address linked to the COA (§519(A)); a cannabinoid profile for the finished product "listing all major cannabinoid constituents by percentage of dry weight" (§519(C)(5)); a cannabinoid profile for the "active ingredient" (cannabinoid-containing distillate or isolate used in formulating the finished product) by percentage of dry weight (§519(C)(11) as numbered in the excerpt); heavy-metal detections in parts per million, which "may not meet or exceed" arsenic 10 ppm, cadmium 4.1 ppm, lead 10 ppm, mercury 2 ppm (§519(C)(10)). Run 1 §1.6.1/§1.6.7 lists the fuller statutory COA contents (batch ID, product name, dates, method, solvents/pesticides/microbials/heavy metals, cannabinoid profile by % weight, potency: serving size, total THC/serving, servings, total THC/package in mg/g) from R.S. 3:1483(E). [Verify: complete §519(C)(1)–(10) list, including the solvent and pesticide numeric limits, against a clean copy of LAC 49:I §519.] Secondary lab-marketing pages (e.g. ACS Laboratory, Louisiana hemp compliance page, accessed via search 25 October 2026) claim screens for 21 residual solvents (butane 800 ppm, benzene 1 ppm, ethanol 5,000 ppm in another secondary summary) and 66 pesticides; those numbers are NOT adopted here because they were not found in the official §519 excerpt opened — do not publish them as Louisiana limits without the §519 verification above.

Labelling/packaging limits that the COA must prove (LAC 49:I §533, LR 52:57, January 2026; LDH final-rule PDF): labels must "clearly indicate the amount of THC per serving…, the serving size, and the number of servings per package" (§533(A)); beverages: serving ≥12 fluid ounces, ≤5 mg THC, one serving per container, tamper-evident container, ≤4 containers per package (§533(B)); tinctures: serving 1 mL, ≤1 mg THC, container ≤30 mL, dropper dispensing precisely one serving, oil-based only, no concentrated water-soluble liquid consumable directly or added to food/beverage, child-resistant (§533(C)); other products: serving ≤5 mg THC, package ≤40 mg THC, child-resistant, each serving a discrete unit (§533(D)); no child-appealing naming/branding/logo (§533(E)); THC-containing labels must bear "a disclaimer that consumption of such products may cause the user to fail a preemployment or routine drug screen" (§533(F)); nonedible topicals are not subject to §533 (§533(G)). Label accuracy variance: "Labels on consumable hemp products must accurately reflect the contents of the packaging with a variation of no greater than fifteen percent. This fifteen percent variance allowance shall not be construed to allow a product to exceed the THC content maximum limits" (LAC 49:I §534(A), LR 52:58, January 2026; same PDF) — paralleling the medical ±15% potency variance in §1046.4(B), but with the express no-exceedance qualifier for hemp.

11.1.6 Consumable hemp — failed tests, market surveillance, registration revocation, and what "recall" means for hemp

No remediation: unlike medical §1046.4(C), LAC 49:I §521 contains no "remediate once and retest in duplicate" pathway. A batch whose COA shows a contaminant exceedance or other violation "shall not [be sold or distributed] in Louisiana" (§521(C)). Whether a failing batch may be reworked into a new batch and retested as a new batch is NOT stated in §521 as opened — [Verify; do not assume a rework right].

Market surveillance and revocation — LAC 49:I §539, "Additional Enforcement Provisions" (LR 52:58, January 2026; LDH final-rule PDF, accessed 25 October 2026):

  • §539(A): "The department may, randomly or based upon a complaint, procure a COA on a specimen of any registered consumable hemp product offered for sale in Louisiana to determine compliance… An appropriate Chain of Custody document shall be utilized for such purpose."
  • §539(B): if that COA "shows that the product does not meet the requirements of this Chapter or Part VI of Chapter 10-a of R.S. Title 3, the registration of such product may be revoked by order issued pursuant to §518…, which order shall note the costs paid to procure the COA, including laboratory and shipping costs. Such product shall not thereafter be registered by any person for two years."
  • §539(C): if revocation becomes final, "the registration holder shall reimburse the department for the costs paid to procure the COA within 30 days"; if not reimbursed within 30 days, "the registration holder shall additionally owe… a civil penalty equal to three times the costs"; if that penalty is not paid within 30 days of demand, "the department may revoke all other product registrations held by the registration holder."
  • §539(D)–(F) (three-year bars): if LDH revokes more than two product registrations of a person within a two-year period, LDH "may revoke all other consumable hemp product registrations held by [that] person" and for three years thereafter "shall not accept any product registrations from such person or related entity, nor register any product manufactured by such person or related entity" (§539(D)); the same three-year processor-permit bar applies to a person with more than two revocations in two years (§539(E)); if more than two registrations of products produced by one manufacturer are revoked in two years, all other products of that manufacturer may be revoked and none registered for three years (§539(F)). §539(G): a revocation "solely due to a change in law shall not be considered a revocation" for §§539(D)–(F) purposes.
  • §518, "Revocation of a Consumable Hemp Product Registration" (LR 52:56–57, January 2026; same PDF): LDH "may revoke" a registration if, among other grounds shown in part (grounds 1–2 elided in the excerpt; grounds 3–6 confirmed): the product/accessories are materially modified so submitted photographs/renderings/specimens are no longer accurate; the product/label/packaging/marketing no longer complies with registration prerequisites or any provision of the Chapter or Part VI; the manufacturer fails to comply with any Chapter requirement concerning the product, including §521; or sale in Louisiana is prohibited under Part VI (particularly R.S. 3:1484(A)(3), (B)(1)(b)(iii), (B)(4)). Revocation is by Order Revoking Registration stating the violation(s) with citations; the registrant has 20 calendar days from receipt to request an administrative hearing (forwarded to the Louisiana Division of Administrative Law); the Order is stayed pending decision unless the State Health Officer finds the product a nuisance dangerous to public health / danger to public life, health, or safety, in which case it is an emergency order not stayed. (Procedure summarised from §518(B)–(D) as returned by search of the July 2023 emergency-rule text of §518, which the January 2026 rule re-adopts in substance — [Verify §518(B)–(E) pinpoint in LR 52:56–57].)
  • Penalties for registration violations: LAC 49:I §535(A) (LR 52:58, January 2026): "Any person who violates the provisions requiring registration of consumable hemp products is subject to the penalties provided for by R.S. 3:1482 and other sanctions as provided for by the State Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Law."

There is NO hemp "recall" procedure (consumer notification, retrieval, LDH recall order) in LAC 49:I Chapter 5 as opened; the hemp enforcement model is registration revocation + the 2-year / 3-year re-registration bars above, plus ATC permit action (see §11.2.6) and the general State Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Law. Do NOT describe a hemp recall system as existing. Note the interaction flagged for the parent: because a Louisiana-compliant 5 mg beverage / 40 mg package exceeds the post-11 December 2026 federal 0.4 mg-per-container cap by 12.5× / 100× (Run 1 §1.6.9 arithmetic), a future federal-law change could in principle trigger §539(G)'s "change in law" revocation carve-out — but no Louisiana rule or guidance applying §539(G) to the federal dates was located, so this is a flag, not a finding.

11.1.7 Industrial hemp (cultivation) — pre-harvest sampling, performance-based sampling, random inspection

Statute — La. R.S. 3:1468, "Testing; inspections" (current text via FindLaw republication, https://codes.findlaw.com/la/revised-statutes/la-rev-stat-tit-3-sect-1468/, accessed 25 October 2026; legis.la.gov current text to be re-opened before publication — the 2020 Act 344 text, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1182597, still shows the older 15-day window and must NOT be quoted as current):

"A.(1) The department shall collect samples to test all industrial hemp crops, except those crops produced by licensees approved by the department for performance-based sampling, prior to harvest to ensure the THC concentration does not exceed a total delta-9 THC concentration of 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis. The grower shall harvest his approved industrial hemp plants not more than thirty days following the date of sample collection by the department, unless specifically authorized in writing by the department."

Change to note: the harvest window is now 30 days, not the 15 days in the 2020 Act 344 text and in older LDAF/LSU AgCenter guidance (which still says "Must harvest within 15 days of sampling" and "Harvested material must stay onsite until result reported"). The parent must use 30 days as current and must NOT carry the 15-day figure forward except as history. Performance-based sampling eligibility — §1468(A)(2): LDAF must ensure one or more of: (a) variety/strain is AOSCA Certified Seed or has consistently demonstrated compliant results under LDAF sampling/testing; (b) hemp produced for grain or fiber with no leaf/floral material harvested; (c) producer conducting industrial hemp research; (d) producer has consistently produced compliant plants over an extended period; (e) producer growing immature plants from seed of known compliant varieties, harvested prior to flowering. LDAF may contract with any public postsecondary education institution for THC testing (§1468(A)(3)).

Random inspection — §1468(B) (same source, text truncated in the excerpt at "take a representative composite sample for THC concentration analysis if the department has reason to believe a violation has occurred"; full paragraph to be re-opened): LDAF may randomly inspect any hemp crop/product in the possession of a grower, processor, handler, or seed-producer licensee and take a representative composite sample if it has reason to believe a violation has occurred. The 2020 text adds the consequence (detain, seize, destroy, or embargo a crop/product exceeding the hemp THC level) — [Verify the current §1468(B) consequence sentence on legis.la.gov].

LDAF's own testing description (LDAF industrial hemp regulations page, https://www.ldaf.la.gov/plants/industrial-hemp/regulations, accessed 25 October 2026): "In Louisiana, LDAF samples and tests industrial hemp to evaluate Total THC concentration levels prior to harvest"; "THC is measured post-decarboxylation… The values for THC and THCa (adjusted for molecular weight conversion) are added together. Final answers are subject to a further adjustment for uncertainty… The uncertainty value used in Louisiana is 0.104%. Hemp samples are dried and ground into a homogenous powder… extracted using methanol and analyzed by HPLC-UV technology." And: "If hemp has more than 0.3% of THC, it is considered marijuana and is not in compliance. This will result in LDAF issuing a stop order. Anything testing over 1.0% THC will result in LDAF taking further regulatory action." The 0.3% vs 1.0% distinction and the stop-order mechanism are developed in §11.5.3. Note the terminology tension preserved from Run 1: §1468 as republished says "total delta-9 THC concentration of 0.3 percent," while the LDAF page says "Total THC"; the federal baseline after 11 December 2026 uses a total-THC definition — the parent should NOT collapse these three wordings into one without the legis.la.gov check flagged above. USDA DEA-registered-lab testing: the given baseline delays USDA DEA-lab enforcement to 31 December 2026; Louisiana's pre-harvest testing as described by LDAF is an LDAF/state-lab process, not stated to be a DEA-lab process — do not conflate them.

11.2 Licence rules: transfers and sales, ownership changes, renewal requirements and timelines, ownership caps, relocation, surrender/revocation, required insurance or bonding minimums

11.2.1 Medical cultivation licences — nontransferable, annual 1 July renewal, replacement ONLY by competitive bid on revocation-for-nonrenewal or voluntary return

Statute — R.S. 40:1046(H)(1) (legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=96986, accessed 25 October 2026), verbatim in relevant part:

"(a) The Louisiana Department of Health shall issue no more than two licenses to cultivate, extract, process, produce, and transport therapeutic marijuana in this state. Each license shall be issued on July first and shall be effective for a period of one year." "(c) Upon each renewal period, a license in force shall be renewed by the department for the next succeeding period upon proper application for renewal and payment of license fees as required by law and the rules and regulations of the department." "(d) Subject to the limitation of no more than two licenses… the department shall select a new licensee through a competitive bid process in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Louisiana Procurement Code, R.S. 39:1551 et seq., if any of the following occur: (i) After written notice from the department and failure of the licensee to cure within thirty days following receipt of written notice, a licensee fails to comply with the proper application for renewal and payment of license fees as required by law and the rules and regulations of the department, and the license is revoked. (ii) A license is voluntarily returned or remitted to the department prior to the expiration of the licensure period."

Rule — LAC 51:XXIX §501 (January 2026 final rule, LR 52:59; LDH combined January 2026 PDF, accessed 25 October 2026; also NOI LR 51:717): "The department shall issue a nontransferable license to the licensees successfully completing the application process referenced in §505… Such license shall be renewable annually on July 1"; "Only a total of two licenses may be issued for the production of medical marijuana"; "Each license is subject to an annual administration fee of $100,000.00"; new licences "only" on voluntary surrender or failure to renew timely (revocable in the latter case only if the licensee "fails to respond to a written notification by the department with the necessary documentation and fees within a thirty-day timeframe"); "New licenses shall be awarded by means of a competitive bid process in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Procurement Code (R.S. 39:1551 et seq.)."

Consequences, stated plainly:

  • No sale of a cultivation licence. There is no licence-sale, assignment, or transfer mechanism in §1046(H) or LAC 51:XXIX §501 as opened. A would-be buyer cannot acquire the licence; it can only (a) acquire the licensee entity itself — which is a corporate transaction, NOT a licence transfer, and whose LDH treatment is not stated in the statute/rule opened (see ownership-change note below) — or (b) wait for a vacancy and win the competitive bid. Run 1 Part 4–6 reached the same conclusion ("No sale/transfer/conversion of a production licence to a third party was found in an official source").
  • Renewal information duty: as a condition of renewal, the licensee "shall supply the following additional information in writing to the department by January 10 of the renewal year," including (in the excerpt, item 4 confirmed) "the total quantity of medical marijuana generated as a finished product within that year and the quantity distributed to each licensed marijuana retailer" (LAC 51:XXIX §505(C), NOI text and January 2026 excerpt; items 1–3 and 5–6 elided as "…" — [Verify full §505(C) list in LR 52:59]). Separately, LDH must collect annual production/cost/subcontractor/distribution data from each licensee and report the prior calendar year's information to the Legislature by 1 February each year and publish it online (R.S. 40:1046(H)(2); same legis.la.gov page).
  • Ownership cap / eligibility bar: there is NO percentage ownership cap (e.g. "no person may own more than X%") in §1046(H) as opened. The only bidder-eligibility bar located is the campaign-finance bar, R.S. 40:1046(H)(3), verbatim (same page): "No company that has made a contribution to a candidate in a Louisiana election governed by the provisions of the Campaign Finance Disclosure Act within the five years prior to bidding for the license, or is controlled wholly or in part by a person who made such a contribution within the five years prior to the company bidding for the license, may be eligible for the license." Note the bar is phrased for "bidding" — i.e. it bites on a competitive-bid vacancy, and its application to a mere change in the ownership of an existing licensee is NOT stated in the text opened. [Verify: LDH treatment of a change in control / membership-interest transfer of an existing cultivation licensee — no rule located in §1046(H), §1046.2, or LAC 51:XXIX §§501/505 as opened.] Contrast retailers (§11.2.2), where the statute expressly allows membership-interest transfer without LDH approval; no parallel sentence exists for cultivation licensees in the text opened, and the parent must NOT import the retailer rule into the cultivation rule.
  • Relocation: no relocation procedure for a cultivation facility was located in §1046(H), §1046.2, or LAC 51:XXIX §§501/505 as opened. What IS located is facility-specific: initial inspection is "limited strictly to a determination" of, among other things, building enclosure, plans/elevation drawings of "all operational areas," and a written operations plan for "each facility production area" (§1046.2(B)(1); see §11.3.1), and LMMTS tracking is by "each authorized location" (§1046.2(G)(1)). A new site would therefore on its face require a new initial inspection and plan review, but no relocation application, fee, or timeline is stated — [Verify: LDH relocation / additional-site procedure for licensees].

11.2.2 Medical retail permits — nontransferable to location or owner, BUT membership-interest transfer without approval; calendar-year renewal with Dec 1 / Dec 31 / Mar 1 deadlines; surrender/change-of-ownership packet path

Statute — R.S. 40:1046(G)(1) (same legis.la.gov page, accessed 25 October 2026):

  • Renewal: "(b) Upon each annual renewal period, a retail permit in force shall be renewed by the department for the next succeeding period upon proper application for renewal and payment of permit fees as required by law and the rules and regulations of the department. The department shall charge an annual retail permit fee in the amount of twenty-two thousand five hundred dollars to each of the ten retail permit holders…"
  • Replacement only on vacancy: "(c) … the department shall select a new retail permit holder through a competitive bid process in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Louisiana Procurement Code, R.S. 39:1551 et seq., only if… (i) After written notice… and failure… to cure within thirty days…, a retail permit holder fails to comply with the proper application for renewal and payment of permit fees…, and the retail permit is revoked. (ii) A retail permit is voluntarily returned or remitted… prior to the expiration of the permit period."
  • Membership-interest transfer: "(d) The transfer of a membership interest in an entity that holds a marijuana retail permit may be conducted without approval of the department." This is the CURRENT rule and it directly supersedes the historic Board of Pharmacy position (see below). It does NOT say the permit itself is transferable — it says a membership interest in the holder entity may transfer without approval.

Rule — LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 23 (NOI text, LR 51:720–721; [Verify — NOI-to-final survival in LR 52:59]):

  • §2303(A)–(B): "In accordance with the statutory limits provided for in R.S. 40:1046(G), the department may issue no more than thirty permits for therapeutic marijuana retailers and their approved satellite locations." "Permits are not transferable to other locations or owners."
  • §2303(C): "In the circumstance that one of the existing permitholders for a primary retailer location or its satellite chooses to surrender that permit or the facility undergoes a change-of-ownership, an applicant may submit a packet for review to include the following: 1. a completed application form provided by the department; 2. detailed plans of the facility, including a site plan and plumbing, electrical, mechanical, HVAC, and drainage schedules as well as a schedule of finishes for floors, walls, and ceilings in all areas; plans should include measures to secure the area where marijuana product is being held to prevent the entry of unauthorized personnel; 3. proposed hours of operation, anticipated staffing levels, and a list of other goods and services to be provided on the premises; 4. the name and contact telephone number and email address of the registered pharmacist designated to be available to the retailer; and 5. a notarized, sworn affidavit that the proposed location meets the separation distance requirements stipulated in R.S. 40:1046(G)(6) and that any applicable zoning requirements have been met." Note the tension to flag, not resolve by paraphrase: §2303(C) provides a packet path on "change-of-ownership" even though §2303(B) says permits are not transferable to other owners and §1046(G)(1)(d) allows membership-interest transfer without approval. The coherent reading — a new packet is needed when the permit itself is surrendered and reissued to a new holder, while a mere membership-interest transfer within the same holder entity needs no approval — is the natural reconciliation, but LDH has not stated it in the text opened. [Verify: LDH guidance distinguishing §1046(G)(1)(d) membership transfers from §2303(C) change-of-ownership packets.] A secondary vendor synthesis (Flourish, same page as above) states the same operational consequence ("Any change of ownership at a retail location requires the surrender of the existing permit and submission of a new application packet…") but does not reconcile it with §1046(G)(1)(d); it is not relied on for the reconciliation.
  • §2303(E)–(F) (conditions of permitting): each permitted facility must supply LDH "with registered patient counts based on the previous 24-month period on a quarterly basis" (the satellite-threshold count, R.S. 40:1046(G)(3)(e)); each facility must designate at least one registered pharmacist available to the primary site and satellites by physical presence or telephone/videoconference during hours of operation (R.S. 40:1046(F)(1)(b)).
  • §2305, "Renewal, Suspension, and Revocation" (NOI text, [Verify — NOI-to-final survival]): "(A) A marijuana retailer permit shall be subject to renewal on a calendar-year basis utilizing a form supplied by [LDH]. (B) Renewal packets (to include ancillary documentation required by the renewal form) must be submitted to LDH no later than December 1 to renew for the following year. (C) Permits that are not renewed by December 31 are subject to suspension until such time as the proper packet has been submitted, reviewed, and accepted by LDH. (D) Permits that have not been renewed by March 1 of the subsequent calendar year or whose holders have been documented to be in violation of any provisions of this Subpart may be subject to revocation in accordance with the applicable provisions of LAC 51:I.113." (Note: LAC 51:I.113 is the general LDH enforcement/adjudication provision; its text was not opened — [Verify §2305(D) cross-reference and any hearing right].)
  • §2307, "Renovations" (NOI text): "substantial renovations (per LAC 51.I:101) must submit plans for review and approval to [LDH]. The department must approve the plans prior to the onset of construction/substantial renovations to the existing facility." This is the closest located analogue to a relocation/alteration rule for retailers; a full relocation is governed by §2303(B)'s nontransferability to other locations, i.e. a move is a new-permit event, not a relocation of the old permit — subject to the §2303(C) packet path on surrender.
  • Satellite timing (statute, R.S. 40:1046(G)(3)(c)): satellite application "no later than ninety days after receipt of the notification" from LDH; satellite "operational within three hundred ten days of the approval," with LDH extensions for circumstances beyond the holder's control; if the holder declines, LDH may issue an additional retail permit in that region in lieu of that satellite. No separate satellite fee was located (Run 1 Part 4–6 gap 9, carried forward: statute says the $22,500 fee is charged "to each of the ten retail permit holders," reading as per holder, not per location — [Verify LDH fee practice]).
  • Historic Board rule — DO NOT quote as current: former LAC Title 46, Part LIII, §2445(E)–(F) (Board of Pharmacy, via Cornell LII, https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/louisiana/La-Admin-Code-tit-46-SS-LIII-2445, accessed 25 October 2026) provided a marijuana pharmacy permit was "non-transferable from one owner to another owner, and moreover, in the event the ownership… changes by 50 percent or more, then the ownership will be deemed sufficiently different as to require a new marijuana pharmacy permit," with <50% changes requiring prior notice and Board approval, and §2447 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/louisiana/La-Admin-Code-tit-46-SS-LIII-2447) requiring a new-location application and Board approval before operating at a new location. Those provisions are HISTORIC after the Act 693 transfer (1 January 2025). The current LDH rule (§2303(B)) retains nontransferability to owners/locations but the statute (§1046(G)(1)(d)) has replaced the Board's 50% regime with "without approval" for membership-interest transfers. The parent must not present the 50% rule as current LDH law.

11.2.3 Medical laboratories — renewal Oct 31 / Dec 31, expiry = cease operations + destroy remaining product

See §11.1.4: licence effective one year, renewal application on or before 31 October each year, renewal on or before 31 December; untimely renewal = expiry at midnight 31 December, "the laboratory shall cease all operations and destroy all marijuana or marijuana products physically remaining at its location" (R.S. 40:1046.3(B)(3)). No transfer/sale provision for a laboratory licence was located in §1046.3 as opened — [Verify: LDH lab-licence transfer / change-of-ownership treatment]. No ownership cap for labs was located. Note the lab-licence calendar (Oct 31 / Dec 31) differs from the cultivation licence calendar (1 July) and the retailer calendar (Dec 1 / Dec 31 / Mar 1); do not harmonise them.

11.2.4 Medical — surrender and revocation generally

  • Cultivation: surrender = voluntary return/remittance before expiry (§1046(H)(1)(d)(ii)); revocation in the renewal context = failure to cure within 30 days after written notice of failure to apply/pay, then revocation (§1046(H)(1)(d)(i)). No general "revocation for violation" paragraph for cultivation licences was located in §1046(H) as opened — but LDH's general inspection/enforcement authority (§1046.2, LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 7 inspections at least twice per fiscal year, complaint inspections without prior notice during business hours) and the general LDH adjudication provision (LAC 51:I.113, cited in retailer §2305(D)) are the enforcement backdrop. [Verify: general revocation grounds/procedure for cultivation licences and laboratories beyond the renewal-failure mechanism.]
  • Retailers: suspension for non-renewal by 31 December; revocation exposure for non-renewal by 1 March or documented Subpart violation (§2305(C)–(D), NOI text). General LDH permit revocation procedure (LAC 51:I.113) not opened — [Verify].
  • Sunset: the whole of R.S. 40:1046 "shall terminate on July 1, 2030" (§1046(M)). Every medical licence/permit described here therefore terminates with the section unless the Legislature extends it; this is a surrender-by-operation-of-law date, not a renewal deadline.

11.2.5 Medical — inspections as the enforcement spine (for the revocation context)

  • Cultivation licensees: LDH "shall inspect each facility at least twice annually" after production commences, verifying plans/drawings, current written operations plan, LMMTS connection, operational alarm/video systems, secure locks, limited-access controls, current personnel records, and biannual inventory reports (R.S. 40:1046.2(C)(2)). Initial inspection before commencement is "limited strictly to" the §1046.2(B)(1) determinations (see §11.3.1). LAC 51:XXIX §701 (NOI text): preoperational/initial inspection after plan review/acceptance; as a licence condition the licensee must allow the State Health Officer/designee to review all records relevant to operations/management; "Routine inspections… shall occur no less frequently than twice per fiscal year. Complaint-based inspections may be conducted at any time during business hours and without prior notice."
  • Retailers: "Permitted facilities are required to be inspected at least once annually" (§2501(A), NOI text); complaint inspections "at any time during business hours and without prior notice" (§2501(C)); as a permit condition the permittee must allow the Surgeon General/designee to review all records relevant to operations/management (§2501(B)).
