Permits must be displayed prominently (Flourish synthesis, secondary — [Verify in final rule]; the NOI §2501 excerpt opened does not show a display sentence, so it is NOT asserted here as rule text).
  • Laboratories: "subject to reasonable inspection by the department as a condition of their license" (Flourish synthesis of LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 9, secondary — the §1046.3(A)(2)(c) pre-licensure inspection and §1046.3(B)(4) out-of-cycle inspection are the statutory anchors actually opened; a general "reasonable inspection" rule sentence was not verified in the NOI excerpt — [Verify]).

11.2.6 Hemp — transfers, renewals, caps, relocation, surrender/revocation, by agency

LDAF industrial hemp licences (grower / processor (non-consumable) / handler / seed producer) — R.S. 3:1465, LDAF pages:

  • Annual licences: "Each seed producer shall obtain an annual license"; "A grower… shall obtain an annual license… to possess, store, cultivate, trim, dry, cure, and transport industrial hemp"; processor (non-consumable) annual licence "to possess, store, process, and transport"; handler annual licence "to handle industrial hemp" (R.S. 3:1465(A)(1)–(4), Justia 2025 text, https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1465/, accessed 25 October 2026). Fee $500 each; "renewals are due yearly by November 30" (LDAF regulations page, https://www.ldaf.la.gov/plants/industrial-hemp/regulations, accessed 25 October 2026; also LDAF licensing page, Run 1 Part 4). No cap, no minimum acreage (same LDAF page).
  • Transfer/sale: no transfer provision was located in §1465 as opened. The licence is applied for on a commissioner-prescribed form and "must be obtained before a person purchases or obtains any industrial hemp seeds" (§1465(B)). Changes to required application information must be resubmitted "within fifteen days" (§1465(C)(2)). Site changes use LDAF's Site Modification form (add/remove field, greenhouse, or indoor locations with farm name, own/rent, physical address, parish, legal description, GPS latitude/longitude, acres, Location ID) — LDAF industrial hemp forms page (https://www.ldaf.la.gov/plants/industrial-hemp/industrial-hemp-forms, accessed via search 25 October 2026) lists the Site Modification form (paper + online) among licence forms. Whether a licence itself may be assigned on sale of the farm/business is NOT stated — [Verify; do not assume transferability].
  • No ownership cap was located in §1465. The applicant is "responsible for any employee working under the applicant's license" (§1465(E)).
  • Revocation/suspension: LDAF may detain/seize/destroy/embargo non-compliant crops/products (see §11.5.3); criminal penalties for unlicensed/out-of-scope/over-limit cultivation/handling/processing/transport are in R.S. 3:1471 (1–20 years hard labour + ≤$50,000, Run 1 §1.6.6/§11.5.3 context); civil penalty up to $500 per violation per day is stated in the 2019 Act 164 digest (secondary summary of the Act, via search) — [Verify current civil-penalty provision and any LDAF licence-revocation procedure in current §§1470–1472 on legis.la.gov]. Stop orders: R.S. 3:1472 — a stop order "shall prohibit further sale, exchange, movement, processing, or distribution" of the listed plants/parts until the commissioner is satisfied of compliance and issues a written release; the recipient has 30 days to comply and obtain a written release or be subject to Part penalties (Act 344 of 2020 text, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1182597, accessed via search 25 October 2026 — [Verify current §1472 text]).

LDH consumable hemp processor permits — LAC 49:I §516 (LR 52:54–55, January 2026; LDH final-rule PDF, accessed 25 October 2026):

  • Separate annual permit per facility: "Any person seeking to manufacture or process consumable hemp products in Louisiana must first obtain from the department a separate annual consumable hemp processor permit for each facility in which such manufacturing or processing will occur. No person shall process or manufacture any consumable hemp product in Louisiana at a facility for which a current valid annual consumable hemp processor permit has not been issued" (§516(A)).
  • In-state issuance conditions (§516(B)): compliance with LAC Title 51, Part VI, §103 (food-manufacturing sanitary requirements); payment of the R.S. 3:1483(A)(1) fee ($175–$1,375 by sales tier, Run 1 Part 4); disclosure of legal name and ownership interest of each person owning more than 5%; prescribed application form; compliance with Part VI of Chapter 10-a of Title 3, §516, and Chapter 5.
  • Out-of-state issuance by endorsement (§516(C)): applicant must hold a current valid permit from its home state's health department or equivalent agency under a scheme with pre-issuance inspection and substantially equivalent sanitary/manufacturing requirements (LAC 51, Part VI), pay the §1483(A)(1) fee, disclose >5% owners, file the prescribed form, comply with Title 3 Part VI / §516 / Chapter 5, and consent to Louisiana court/administrative jurisdiction.
  • Term and renewal (§516(D)): "Annual consumable hemp processor permits shall be issued on a fiscal year basis, expiring on June 30 of the fiscal year of issuance. The department shall prorate the annual fee for permits applied for and issued subsequent to July 1 of a fiscal year. Permit renewal applications, together with the required fee, must be submitted to the department no later than 30 days prior to permit expiration. The provisions of R.S. 49:977.3(B) shall apply to a timely-submitted renewal application." (R.S. 49:977.3(B) is the Administrative Procedure Act timely-renewal provision; its text was not opened — the practical point is that a renewal filed ≥30 days before 30 June is timely.)
  • Character attestation (§516(E)–(F)): individuals must prove age ≥21 and give a notarised attestation under penalty of perjury of no felony conviction (U.S., Louisiana, any other state or country) and no conviction for soliciting for prostitution, pandering, letting premises for prostitution, contributing to delinquency of juveniles, keeping/letting a disorderly place, or illegally dealing in controlled dangerous substances. Juridical entities must give a notarised attestation by the secretary/managing member/authorized individual that no officer or shareholder/member owning >5% has such a conviction. Note the difference from LDAF: §516 states NO time limit (no "within 10 years" qualifier) — on its face any prior felony disqualifies a processor applicant/owner, whereas LDAF bars only a felony within 10 years / drug misdemeanor within 2 years (see §11.8.3). The parent must NOT harmonise them.
  • Denial, suspension, revocation (§516(G)–(I)): notice of final denial must state specific reasons and notice of the right to an administrative hearing, expiring unless a written hearing request is filed within 20 calendar days of receipt (forwarded to the Division of Administrative Law); service may be by email to an address provided in permitting/registration, effective even if returned undeliverable. LDH "may revoke or suspend a consumable hemp processor permit if the permit holder, or the facility for which the permit was issued, no longer complies with the prerequisites and conditions for obtaining or holding such permit," by Order Revoking/Suspending Permit in accordance with §518(B)–(C), except that if the State Health Officer finds immediate implementation necessary to abate a potential danger to public life, health, or safety, the order is an emergency order not stayed pending Division of Administrative Law decision (§516(H)). An endorsement permit "shall be automatically suspended or revoked if the out-of-state permit upon which it is based lapses, expires, or is suspended or revoked," and the holder has an affirmative duty to inform LDH (§516(I)).
  • Sponsor route (§517(J), LR 52:56, January 2026): a product manufactured in a facility WITHOUT an LDH processor permit "may be registered only by a person holding a consumable hemp processing permit issued by the department for a facility located in Louisiana," who must ensure the manufacturer meets §516, the facility meets substantially equivalent LAC 51, Part VI sanitary/manufacturing requirements, and the product meets Chapter 5 and Title 3 Part VI; the sponsor "must have access to and retain for at least three years the records required by §521" and make them available on request. Any pre-existing registration for a product from an unpermitted facility "shall be deemed to meet the criteria for revocation under an Emergency Order pursuant to §518.D" (effective 15 July 2025, §517(I)).
  • Transfer/sale/relocation of a processor permit: no transfer provision was located in §516 as opened. Because the permit is "for each facility" and issuance turns on that facility's compliance, a new facility on its face needs a new permit, and a change of facility ownership is not addressed — [Verify: LDH processor-permit transfer / change-of-ownership / relocation procedure]. No ownership cap was located in §516 (only >5% disclosure).
  • Product registration renewal (distinct from the permit): "Each product must be renewed between July 1 and August 15 of every year," with attestation/certification of no change permitted with LDH permission in lieu of repeat submission (LDH Hemp Registration page, same link as above). Note the two different hemp calendars: processor permit = fiscal year to 30 June, renewal ≥30 days before expiry; product registration = 1 July–15 August window. Do not conflate them.

ATC consumable hemp permits (wholesaler / retailer per place of business / per domain / special event) — R.S. 3:1484:

  • Fees/caps (2022 text, Justia, https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2022/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1484/, accessed via search 25 October 2026 — [Verify current §1484 text after Act 752]): wholesaler fee "based on the cost of the regulatory functions performed and shall not exceed five hundred dollars per year"; retail and special-event fees each "based on the cost of the regulatory functions performed and shall not exceed one hundred seventy-five dollars per year." Actual ATC wholesale application fee $500 (ATC form, Run 1 Part 4); actual retail fee charged [Verify — Run 1 Part 4–6 gap 1].
  • Special events: annual special-event permit; the permittee "shall notify the commissioner in writing of any special event the permittee will be attending prior to the event. Failure to notify the commissioner shall be grounds for revocation of the permit" (2022 text, same source).
  • Suspension/revocation and fines (2022 text, same source): "Any fine imposed pursuant to this Part or the revocation or suspension of a permit is in addition to and is not in lieu of or a limitation on the imposition of any other penalty provided by law"; fines for selling at retail without a permit: first offense ≤$300, second ≤$1,000, third or subsequent $500–$3,000 (as shown in the Act 344 / 2020 engrossed text of §1484(C) returned by search — [Verify current paragraph lettering after Act 752]). Tax suspension: "the secretary of the Department of Revenue shall order the commissioner to immediately suspend the retailer's permit if the secretary determines that a consumable hemp product retailer has failed to timely file returns or pay taxes as required by R.S. 47:1693… until the returns have been filed and the taxes are paid. No permit shall be suspended for taxes which have been properly protested or appealed… pursuant to R.S. 47:1565 or 1567" (§1484(F) in the 2022 text). ATC "shall investigate any report of a violation of this Part and report any criminal violation to the appropriate law enforcement agency" (§1484(G)).
  • No ATC renewal deadline, transfer provision, or relocation procedure was located in the §1484 text opened. ATC permits are per place of business and per domain name for remote retailers (R.S. 3:1484(B)(1)(b), Run 1 §1.6.6), so a new place of business or new domain on its face needs a new permit — but that inference is flagged, not stated as rule text. [Verify: current ATC renewal cycle, transfer, and relocation rules.] No ownership cap for ATC permits was located.
  • ATC rulemaking limits (important for §11.8): §1484(H) (2022 text): "The rules shall not include any fees or penalties for any permit not provided for in this Section, or any requirements for proof of Louisiana residency, criminal background checks, diagrams of retail premises, or proof of lease or ownership of any retail establishment."

11.2.7 Insurance or bonding minimums — what was and was NOT found

  • Medical cultivation licences, retail permits, laboratories (current law): NO insurance minimum and NO bond/surety minimum was located in R.S. 40:1046, R.S. 40:1046.2, R.S. 40:1046.3, R.S. 40:1046.4, or the LAC 51:XXIX sections opened (Chapters 1, 5, 7, 9, 21, 23, 25). The parent must NOT publish an insurance or bond figure for current LDH licensees/permit holders on the evidence in this file.
  • Historic / secondary-only $100,000 pharmacy bond — NOT adopted as current law: multiple surety-vendor pages (Surety One, Surety Bond Authority, ProSure Group, ZipBonds — all accessed via search 25 October 2026, all secondary, all undated or dated 2026) list a "Louisiana Marijuana Pharmacy Permit Bond" of $100,000, described as ensuring the pharmacy "successfully completes the construction of the pharmacy in a timely manner" and operates "in compliance with… Subchapter E. Marijuana Pharmacy, of the Louisiana Administrative Code" — i.e. the former Board of Pharmacy regime (LAC Title 46, Part LIII). No current LDH rule, statute, or LDH application form requiring a $100,000 bond was located. [Verify: whether any bond requirement survived the Act 693 transfer into LAC 51:XXIX Subpart 2; until verified, the $100,000 figure must be labelled historic/secondary only.] A historic financial-capacity item also exists: the 2021 §1046 text (Justia 2021) contemplated Board rules requiring an applicant to demonstrate financial capacity and "the ability to maintain an escrow account in a financial institution headquartered in Louisiana in an amount of two million dollars, if required by the Louisiana Board of Pharmacy" — the "if required" qualifier and the Board's loss of jurisdiction mean this is NOT a current LDH requirement on the evidence opened. [Verify: no current escrow requirement located.]
  • Transport insurance (historic, narrow): a 2019 LDAF-era emergency rule excerpt (Fox Rothschild republication, accessed via search 25 October 2026) for medical transport required the transporter to "have a valid Louisiana driver's license and be insured above the legal requirements in Louisiana" and to be "capable of securing (locking) medical marijuana and product items during transportation." That text predates the LDH regime and the current §1046.2(I) transport rule (see §11.4.1), which does NOT restate an insurance-above-minimums requirement in the text opened. [Verify survival in current LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 7, §711.] General Louisiana motor-vehicle compulsory insurance (La. R.S. 32:861 et seq.) applies to any transport vehicle as a matter of general law and is not cannabis-specific; it is noted here only to prevent the error of stating that medical transport is uninsured.
  • Hemp (LDAF / LDH processor / ATC): NO insurance minimum and NO bond minimum was located in R.S. 3:1465, R.S. 3:1483, R.S. 3:1484, LAC 49:I Chapter 5 (§§516–539), or the LDAF pages opened. General business insurance, workers' compensation (Title 23 generally), and vehicle insurance apply as general law, not as hemp-licence conditions located here. [Verify: ATC application forms for any insurance attestation not in the statute/rule text.]

11.3 Cultivation rules: indoor/outdoor/greenhouse, canopy, plant counts; hemp plot registration and pre-harvest sampling

11.3.1 Medical cultivation — effectively indoor, enclosed-building standard; NO canopy limit and NO plant count located

Building standard — R.S. 40:1046.2(B)(1)(a) (legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=1295736, accessed 25 October 2026), verbatim in relevant part: the initial inspection must determine that the facility "(i) Is within a building that has a complete roof enclosure supported by connecting walls, constructed of solid materials, that extend from the ground to the roof. (ii) Has a foundation, slab, or equivalent base to which the floor is securely attached. (iii) Meets performance standards ensuring that cultivation and processing activities cannot be and are not reasonably perceptible from the structure in terms of common visual observation, odors, smell, fragrances, or other olfactory stimulus, light pollution, glare, brightness, adequate ventilation to prevent mold, and noise. (iv) Provides complete visual screening. (v) Meets the standards of any applicable state and local electrical, fire, plumbing, and building specification codes."

Practical consequence: a medical cultivation facility must be a fully enclosed, solid-walled, roofed building on a foundation/slab, with complete visual screening and with odour, light, glare, and noise not reasonably perceptible from outside, plus ventilation adequate to prevent mold. The statute does not use the words "indoor," "outdoor," or "greenhouse," and does not authorise an open-field medical grow; an unenclosed outdoor grow cannot satisfy (i)–(iv) on its face. Whether a greenhouse with solid walls, complete roof enclosure, and complete visual screening could satisfy the standard is NOT stated — [Verify: LDH interpretation for greenhouse structures]. No separate greenhouse rule for medical cultivation was located.

Canopy and plant counts: NO canopy-size limit (square feet), NO plant-count limit, and NO mature/immature plant distinction with a numeric cap was located in R.S. 40:1046, R.S. 40:1046.2, or the LAC 51:XXIX sections opened. What exists instead is inventory control without a numeric cap: "Each licensee shall maintain a comprehensive inventory of all marijuana, including without limitation usable marijuana available for sale, mature marijuana plants, and seedlings at each authorized location. Following an initial inventory, all marijuana shall be inventoried on a weekly basis" (R.S. 40:1046.2(G)(1)); LMMTS tagging of "each plant and product with a unique identification number" (§1046.2(F)(1)); and LAC 51:XXIX §707 (NOI text): "Licensed facilities shall maintain an inventory of medical marijuana, including medical marijuana waste, on their premises and update these records no less frequently than once per week." The parent must state the absence ("no canopy/plant-count cap located") rather than importing another state's canopy rule or inferring a cap from the two-licence limit. Production is instead constrained by the two-licence cap, the annual $100,000 fee, the 7% gross-sales fee, the THC "lowest acceptable therapeutic levels" standard (§1046(I)), testing, and LMMTS traceability.

Other cultivation-operations duties located (medical): written operations plan limited to SOPs for cultivation in each facility production area, instructions for making each product, equipment manuals, safety-check procedures, sanitisation procedures for surfaces/equipment, quality-control procedures, and emergency preparedness (§1046.2(B)(1)(c)); detailed plans and elevation drawings of all operational areas (§1046.2(B)(1)(b)); MSDS and pesticide-application logging (see §11.6.1); LMMTS recording within 24 hours of seed/plant/derivative acquisition, sale/transfer/transport, and disposal (§1046.2(F)(2)); records retention "for at least the current year and the three preceding calendar years" (§1046.2(F)(3)).

11.3.2 Hemp cultivation — field, greenhouse, and indoor growing all contemplated; plot registration by legal description + GPS; reporting cadence

Licence scope — R.S. 3:1465(A)(2) (same Justia source as §11.2.6): a grower licence authorises the licensee "to possess, store, cultivate, trim, dry, cure, and transport industrial hemp in this state." No indoor/outdoor restriction is stated in §1465. The LDAF programme structure confirms all three settings: LDAF forms distinguish "Field Locations" from "Greenhouse / Indoor Growing Locations" (Site Modification form, via search 25 October 2026: greenhouse/indoor types include "Transplants only," "Stock plants, year round," and "Year-round production with intent to harvest indoor plants"); LAC 7:XIII §1332 (USDA reporting, via Cornell LII, https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/louisiana/La-Admin-Code-tit-7-SS-XIII-1332, accessed via search 25 October 2026) requires "legal description and GPS coordinates for each field, greenhouse, indoor growing structure, or site where industrial hemp will be cultivated, handled, or stored." LDAF's regulations page states: "You can grow industrial hemp plants in your yard as long as you're licensed" (same LDAF page) — i.e. no minimum acreage and no field-only limitation.

Plot registration (application contents) — R.S. 3:1465(C) (same Justia source): the application for any grower, processor, handler, or seed-producer licence must include "(a) The name and address of the applicant. (b) The name and address of the designated responsible party, if the applicant is a business entity. (c) If applicable, the legal description and global positioning coordinates of the land area to be used to produce or process industrial hemp." Changes: "If any changes are made to the required information in Paragraph (1)…, the applicant shall resubmit the application to the department within fifteen days" (§1465(C)(2)). LDAF licensing practice (Run 1 Part 4, LDAF licensing page): "create a colour photographic map for each growing, storage, handling, or processing location" before applying; a colour photographic map is therefore a programme requirement in addition to the statutory legal-description/GPS requirement — the map checklist is on the LDAF forms page ("Checklist for Map Requirements").

Signage (programme requirement, LSU AgCenter growers-rules summary, https://www.lsuagcenter.com/sitecore/content/lih/rules-and-regulations/growers-rules-and-regulations, accessed via search 25 October 2026 — university extension summary of LDAF rules, label as secondary/official-extension, [Verify in LAC 7:XIII]): "All licensed seed producers and growers are required to post an 18'' x 24'' sign at the main entrance of each field, and an 8.5'' x 11'' sign at the main entrance of each greenhouse, or indoor growing structure that contains… 'Louisiana Industrial Hemp Program', their industrial hemp license number, and the LDAF industrial hemp program's phone number." Sign templates are provided by LDAF at licensing (same source). Do not quote the sign dimensions as statute text; they are programme guidance as sourced.

Reporting — LDAF required reporting (LDAF reporting page, https://www.ldaf.la.gov/plants/industrial-hemp/required-reporting, accessed via search 25 October 2026; LDAF forms page, same source):

  • Seed Acquisition Request Form (before obtaining seed; purchaser must ask for seller's licence documentation and a lab COA stating ≤0.3% THC, with the lab accredited/affiliated with a national organisation such as ISO or DEA — LDAF purchase/transport page, https://www.ldaf.state.la.us/plants/industrial-hemp/purchase-transport, accessed via search 25 October 2026).
  • 1st Report of Planting (online) and Quarterly Planting Report; Annual Production Report; Harvest Report; Destruction Report; Site Modification form. LSU AgCenter growers-rules summary adds the cadence: "All commercial oil, fiber and seed production must be reported on a First Report of Planting form for each field, greenhouse, or growing structure to LDAF within 15 days of planting. All production and inventory of vegetative stock plants must be reported on a quarterly planting report… by March 31st, June 30th, September 30th, and December 31st." The LDAF reporting page adds: "If you do not intend to plant at one of your approved locations, report as 'No Planting.'" And for harvest: "At least several days prior to harvesting, submit a harvest report… for each planting address. LDAF will then contact you about collecting samples. Harvest is not allowed until you receive approval from LDAF."
  • FSA reporting: growers/seed producers "are also required to report their hemp crop acreage to the USDA Farm Service Agency and provide the assigned FSA Lot ID numbers to LDAF at time of planting" (LSU AgCenter summary, same source); LDAF's forms page lists "Reporting Hemp Acreage to FSA" as a form/guide.
  • Canopy/plant counts for hemp: NO canopy limit and NO plant-count limit for industrial hemp was located in R.S. 3:1461 et seq. or the LDAF pages opened. Hemp is regulated by licensed location (legal description + GPS + Location ID/FSA Lot No.), variety designation (LDAF Variety Designation List, as of 15 January 2026, LDAF regulations page), pre-harvest THC testing, and acreage reporting — not by plant numbers. The Location ID "will become part of the license record and should be used to identify the field in all reports to LDAF" (Site Modification form, via search).

Pre-harvest sampling: see §11.1.7 (30-day harvest window, performance-based sampling, random inspection). Note the interaction with the harvest report: LDAF sampling is triggered by the harvest report ("Triggered by Harvest/Crop Destruction Report; All growing sites/lots will [be] sampled" — LDAF/LSU AgCenter sampling presentation, via search 25 October 2026, older guidance showing the 15-day window; the window figure is superseded by the current 30-day statute, but the trigger mechanism — harvest report → LDAF contact → sampling → approval before harvest — is consistent with the current LDAF reporting page quoted above).

11.4 Security requirements: cameras, alarms, storage, transport

11.4.1 Medical cultivation facilities — statute-grade security (R.S. 40:1046.2(D)–(E))

R.S. 40:1046.2(D) (legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=1295736, accessed 25 October 2026), verbatim in substance (paragraphing condensed only for line breaks):

"(1) Any facility alarm or surveillance system shall include the following: (a) A panic device that sounds an audible alarm and notifies law enforcement. (b) Surveillance system coverage for all points of ingress and egress to the facility, including but not limited to doorways, windows, and loading bays. (c) 'Duress' or 'hold up' features to enable activation of a silent alarm. (d) Date- and time-stamped recording of all points of ingress and egress, any limited access areas including rooms containing a safe, any room in which any part of the disposal process occurs, and any room or area used to cultivate, extract, process, produce, or store therapeutic marijuana. (e) Capabilities including continuous recording, archiving, and at least one on-site display monitor connected to the system." "(2) Each facility shall maintain on-site security personnel, at a minimum, during standard United States business hours of eight o'clock a.m. to five o'clock p.m. and shall maintain off-site, electronic security monitoring at all other times." "(3) All surveillance recordings shall be maintained for a minimum of thirty days and access to surveillance controls and monitoring shall be limited to specifically authorized personnel." "(4) Each licensee shall limit access to and post limited-access signage where marijuana is cultivated, extracted, processed, produced, or stored. Limited access areas shall remain locked and accessible only by authorized personnel." "(5) Each employee, supervisor, or agent of each licensee shall keep a current identification card, in a form approved by the department, on his person when present at a facility."

Initial-inspection security check: "security against unauthorized entry via the presence of operational alarm and video surveillance systems, limited access areas, secure locking systems, and door controls throughout the facility" (§1046.2(B)(1)(e)); ongoing inspections verify "Operational alarm and video surveillance systems," "Secure locks throughout the facility," and "Controls to limited access areas" (§1046.2(C)(2)(d)–(f)).

Visitors — §1046.2(E) (same source): persons without a licensee identification card "shall be issued a visitor identification badge after signing a log maintained by the licensee that properly identifies the visitor to the premises," must wear the badge, and "shall not be left unaccompanied in any area where marijuana or marijuana products are present" — except: a repair/maintenance visitor may be left unaccompanied outside a limited-access area; inside a limited-access area, the visitor must remain accompanied while work is done if marijuana/products are present, but may be left unaccompanied if no marijuana/products are present while the visitor is there, provided the visitor "is under video surveillance for the duration."

Rule overlay — LAC 51:XXIX §703, "Product and Site Security" (NOI text, LR 51:717–718): "Licensed facilities shall maintain an onsite security system that includes, at a minimum, the following components:" followed in the Register excerpt by "A.1.–D. …" (elided) — the NOI excerpt does NOT reproduce the §703 component list, so the statute above is the citable security list for manufacturers and §703 is cited only for the existence of a rule-level security duty. [Verify full §703(A)–(D) in LR 52:59; do not import the retailer §2503 list into the manufacturer rule.]

Storage (manufacturer): marijuana and waste are stored in limited-access areas (§1046.2(D)(4); waste specifically "stored in a limited access area of a facility until rendered unusable," §1046.2(G)(2) — see §11.5.1). No safe/vault specification (e.g. safe rating, vault construction) beyond "rooms containing a safe" being within surveillance coverage (§1046.2(D)(1)(d)) was located — [Verify any safe/vault standard in LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 7].

Transport (manufacturer → retailer / laboratory / other licensee / disposal) — R.S. 40:1046.2(I) (same source), verbatim in substance:

"(1) Prior to transporting therapeutic marijuana, a licensee shall generate an inventory manifest in the LMMTS, including: (a) the name of the licensee originating the transport; (b) the name of the licensee, approved laboratory, or retail permit holder receiving the transport; (c) the quantity by weight or unit of each type of therapeutic marijuana product contained in the transport; (d) the date and approximate departure and arrival times; (e) the identity of the agent or agents accompanying the transport; (f) the make, model, and license plate number of the transport delivery vehicle." "(2) The licensee originating the transport shall provide the… receiving [party] with a copy of the LMMTS inventory manifest, which shall not be altered after departing the originating licensee's facility." "(3) The… receiving [party] shall record the quantities of all therapeutic marijuana products in the LMMTS. However, any licensee, approved laboratory, or retail permit holder receiving a therapeutic marijuana transport shall refuse the transport if it is not accompanied by an unaltered LMMTS inventory manifest."

LAC 51:XXIX §711, "Transportation of Medical Marijuana" (NOI text, LR 51:718): "Licensed facilities shall generate an inventory manifest prior to transporting any medical marijuana to a licensed marijuana retailer, laboratory, contractor or disposal site." (Manifest contents in the NOI are shown as "A.1.–D. …" — the statute list above governs.) Note the destinations: manufacturer transport is ONLY to a retailer, laboratory, contractor, or disposal site (rule) / licensee, laboratory, or retail permit holder (statute) — there is no manufacturer-to-patient transport; patient delivery is a retailer function (see §11.4.2). No vehicle specification (unmarked vehicle, GPS, two-person crew, locked compartment standard beyond the historic "capable of securing (locking)" language in §11.2.7) was located in the current §1046.2(I) or §711 excerpt — [Verify vehicle/crew/GPS requirements in LR 52:59 Chapter 7]. Do NOT import another state's transport-vehicle rules.

11.4.2 Medical retailers — rule-grade security (LAC 51:XXIX §2503) and delivery security

LAC 51:XXIX §2503, "Product and Site Security" (NOI text, LR 51:721; [Verify — NOI-to-final survival in LR 52:59]):

"A. Permitted facilities shall maintain an onsite security system that includes, at a minimum, the following components: 1. secured locks on doors throughout the facility; 2. audible alarms and a system of audio and video surveillance cameras that cover points of entry and egress as well as restricted-access areas; 3. restricted-access areas denoted by suitable signage and protected by means of secured-access locks where marijuana products are held and provided to patients or caregivers." "Access to areas where marijuana inventory is stored and orders are fulfilled shall meet the following requirements: a. be restricted to authorized personnel and not allowed to the general public; b. be secured by suitable physical barriers and monitored by the facility's security system; c. be inaccessible to any nonemployee unless that person remains under the constant supervision of an employee authorized to be in the secure area." "B. The security system shall be documented in detail in the firm's security plan and subject to review during inspection by the department."

Differences from the manufacturer statute to note (do not merge them): the retailer rule as excerpted does NOT state a 30-day recording-retention period, a panic/duress device, an on-site display monitor, or 8 a.m.–5 p.m. on-site security personnel — those are §1046.2(D) manufacturer provisions. Whether the final retailer rule (LR 52:59) adds retention/personnel provisions is [Verify]. The retailer rule DOES add a written security plan subject to inspection review, which the manufacturer statute phrases as a written operations plan (§1046.2(B)(1)(c)).

Retailer storage: inventory areas restricted to authorised personnel, secured by physical barriers, monitored (§2503(A) above); waste held in "secure storage while pending disposal" (§2511(B)(2), NOI text); packages/containers/labelling storage and "secure storage of marijuana products pending order fulfillment" must be accommodated in facility sizing (§2511(B)(3), (6)). Packaging: "Marijuana products, whether provided on- or off-premises, must be packaged in tightly-sealed and light-impermeable packaging" (§2507(E), NOI text).

Retailer delivery (security-relevant): products "may be issued… on the premises or by delivery to the patient's or caregiver's home address" (§2507(B), NOI text); "Deliveries must be made available upon request at least once per month per ZIP code serviced by the retailer; however, no delivery may be made outside the state of Louisiana" (§2507(C)); "Any marijuana product that is part of a delivery that is not completed must be returned to the retailer of origin, and if the packaging integrity cannot be verified by retailer staff, it must be disposed of by a department-approved method and that disposal documented in the firm's POS system" (§2507(D)). Statutory delivery duty: "Each marijuana retail permit holder shall offer delivery to patients in each zip code within its region at least once per month" (R.S. 40:1046(G)(7)). No delivery-vehicle, delivery-agent credential, signature-on-delivery, or ID-at-door rule was located in §2507 as excerpted — [Verify delivery-agent/vehicle rules in LR 52:59 Chapter 25]. Retailer refusal of inbound product: a retailer "may refuse delivery from a manufacturing facility… if it is determined at receiving that the product is misbranded, adulterated, expired, or otherwise in a nonsaleable condition. Such refusals shall be recorded in the POS system and the [LMMTS]" (§2507(A), NOI text).

Historic Board pharmacy security (for contrast only, NOT current): former LAC 46:LIII pharmacy rules required, at minimum, a perimeter alarm, motion detector, video cameras in all areas that may contain marijuana and at all entry/exit points (angled to capture clear identification), 24-hour recordings retained at least 30 days (longer if relevant to a pending investigation), exportable still images/video, and erasure before disposal/sale of the pharmacy (Board draft, https://www.pharmacy.la.gov/assets/docs/Cmtes/RegRev/RegProp2022-O_MarijuanaPharmacy_Draft1.pdf, accessed via search 25 October 2026). The 30-day retention figure in that historic rule must NOT be attributed to the current retailer rule, where retention was not located.

11.4.3 Medical laboratories — security

No standalone laboratory security section was located in §1046.3 or LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 9 as opened, beyond: (i) persons involved in testing or with access to restricted limited-access areas must hold a permit under R.S. 40:1047 (§1046.3(A)(2)(b)); (ii) the general LMMTS and inspection duties (§1046.3(A)(2)(c)–(d), (B)(4)). Whether laboratories are subject to the §1046.2(D) manufacturer security standards by rule is [Verify in LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 9].

11.4.4 Hemp — no camera/alarm/storage/transport security code equivalent to the medical code was located

  • LDAF industrial hemp: no camera, alarm, safe, or security-personnel requirement was located in R.S. 3:1461 et seq. or the LDAF pages opened. The located controls are location-based, not security-system-based: licensed locations by legal description/GPS/Location ID (§1465(C)); LDAF "unrestricted access to all industrial hemp plants and all land and buildings that are used in the cultivation, handling, processing, and storage of industrial hemp" and authority to "sample and test any industrial hemp material at any time if LDAF believes a violation has occurred" (LSU AgCenter growers-rules summary, secondary/extension — [Verify in LAC 7:XIII]); field/greenhouse signage (see §11.3.2); harvested material must remain on the licensee's location unless transported directly to a Louisiana licensed contracted processor (2020 Harvest/Destruction Report form instruction, via search 25 October 2026 — form-dated, [Verify current transport instruction]).
  • Hemp transport documentation: LDAF provides a Voluntary Driver Reporting Form and a Transportation Information Sheet (LDAF forms page, same link as §11.3.2). The form is described as "voluntary" — i.e. NOT a mandatory manifest on the evidence opened — in contrast to the mandatory LMMTS medical manifest (§1046.2(I)). The parent must NOT describe the voluntary driver form as a mandatory hemp manifest. Seed transport requires LDAF-approved Seed Acquisition Request (see §11.3.2).
  • LDH consumable hemp processors: no camera/alarm/storage security section was located in LAC 49:I Chapter 5 (§§516–539) as opened. The located facility duties are sanitary/manufacturing: compliance with LAC Title 51, Part VI, §103 (in-state permits, §516(B)(1)) and with requirements "substantially equivalent to those set forth in LAC 51, Part VI" for sponsored out-of-state facilities (§517(J)). General food-manufacturing premises standards (LAC 51, Part VI) were not opened — [Verify any locked-storage / restricted-area provision in LAC 51, Part VI, §103].
  • ATC retailers/wholesalers: no camera/alarm/storage rule was located in R.S. 3:1484 as opened. The located retail controls are permit-per-location/domain, age verification, employee-assistance display (non-beverage products "in a location that is inaccessible to the public without the assistance of an employee," R.S. 3:1482(A)(2), Run 1 §1.6.4), and the gasoline/alcohol-premises location bans (Run 1 §1.6.6). The employee-assistance display rule is the hemp analogue of "restricted access," but it is NOT a camera/alarm rule and must not be described as one. Note also §1484(H)'s bar on ATC rules requiring "diagrams of retail premises" (see §11.2.6) — ATC cannot impose a premises-diagram security review by rule on the current text.

11.5 Waste disposal rules, including non-compliant hemp destruction

11.5.1 Medical manufacturer waste — weighed, LMMTS-recorded, limited-access storage until rendered unusable

R.S. 40:1046.2(G)(2) (legis.la.gov, same link as §11.4.1, accessed 25 October 2026): "Any therapeutic marijuana waste product shall be properly weighed and recorded in the LMMTS and stored in a limited access area of a facility until rendered unusable." LAC 51:XXIX §707 (NOI text): inventory records "including medical marijuana waste" updated "no less frequently than once per week." Disposal itself must be recorded in LMMTS within 24 hours of the disposal event (§1046.2(F)(2)(c): "The disposal of therapeutic marijuana" recorded within 24 hours). No rendering recipe (e.g. the retailer's 50%-mix rule, §11.5.2) is stated for manufacturer waste in §1046.2 as opened — the statute says only "until rendered unusable." Whether LAC 51:XXIX Chapter 7 prescribes a manufacturer rendering method is [Verify in LR 52:59 Chapter 7]. Failed-batch destruction (60 days + entire batch) is in §11.1.3; expired laboratory product destruction on licence expiry is in §11.2.3.

11.5.2 Medical retailer waste — 30-day morgue, 50%-by-volume rendering, three disposal methods, POS documentation

LAC 51:XXIX §2509, "Disposal of Marijuana Product Waste" (NOI text, LR 51:721–722; [Verify — NOI-to-final survival in LR 52:59]), verbatim in substance:

"A. Marijuana product in inventory that is no longer suitable for sale due to deterioration, expiration or other conditions rendering the product unsaleable shall be stored in a temporary morgue area pending disposal. Waste products may not be held on the premises longer than thirty days." "B. Waste products must be rendered into a nonusable state by grinding and mixing with nonmarijuana waste products such that the end product is at least 50% nonmarijuana waste by volume, and this end product may then be transported from the premises and disposed of by means of the following processes: 1. composting; 2. incineration; or 3. compaction and subsurface burial." "C. Acceptable materials for mixing include yard waste; paper or cardboard waste; plastic waste; or soil." "D. Retailer personnel must document every disposal activity in the facility's POS system, including the identifying characteristics of the waste, the quantity of waste, and the method of its disposal."

Related retailer waste duties: POS/LMMTS tracking expressly includes waste disposal (§2505(A): seed-to-sale tracking of "all medical marijuana transactions (including home deliveries and waste disposal) conducted at the facility"); perpetual inventory of products "received, held, sold, and disposed of" with semiannual reconciliations retained on premises at least two calendar years (§2505(D)); facility sizing must allow "holding of waste products in secure storage while pending disposal" (§2511(B)(2)); refuse/non-marijuana waste conveyance/storage/disposal must minimise odours, vermin attraction/harborage, and contamination of products, surfaces, grounds, or water supplies (§2511(F)); undelivered product with unverifiable packaging integrity "must be disposed of by a department-approved method" with POS documentation (§2507(D) — see §11.4.2).

11.5.3 Industrial hemp — non-compliant ("hot") crop destruction, stop orders, volunteer plants, ordinary crop-failure destruction

Statutory consequence — R.S. 3:1468(B) (2020 text, consequence sentence; current-text verification flagged in §11.1.7): if a crop/product "contains a THC concentration that exceeds… the federally defined THC level for hemp, the department may detain, seize, destroy, or embargo" it. LDAF page (same link as §11.1.7, accessed 25 October 2026): over 0.3% = "considered marijuana and is not in compliance. This will result in LDAF issuing a stop order. Anything testing over 1.0% THC will result in LDAF taking further regulatory action." The 1.0% threshold's legal source (USDA's former negligence threshold concept) is NOT stated on the LDAF page — [Verify the 1.0% rule's current statutory/regulatory basis; do not present it as a Louisiana statute without that check]. In particular, do NOT state that a crop at 0.4% or 0.9% "may be kept" — on the LDAF page it is non-compliant and stop-ordered; the 1.0% sentence describes "further regulatory action," not permission.

Stop order — R.S. 3:1472 (Act 344 of 2020 text, via search; [Verify current text]): a stop order "shall prohibit further sale, exchange, movement, processing, or distribution of all Cannabis plants or plant parts included in the order until the commissioner is satisfied that this Part and rules and regulations… have been complied with and the commissioner has issued a written release." The recipient has 30 days to comply and obtain a written release or be subject to Part penalties. LDAF's "Stop Order 'Dos & Don'ts' Information Sheet" is listed on the LDAF forms page (same link as §11.3.2) — its contents were not opened. [Verify the current Dos & Don'ts sheet.]

Destruction procedure (form-level, LDAF Destruction Report) — LDAF forms page lists a Destruction Report (per field/greenhouse/indoor area; separate report per planting address). The LDAF Destruction Report form text (2020 form, via search 25 October 2026 — form-dated, [Verify current form]) provides: "This form must be submitted to and approved by LDAF prior to destruction. You should allow for several days between submittal of this form and approval… No destruction is allowed until you receive written approval from LDAF. Destruction resulting from excessive THC concentration level must be performed under the direct supervision of LDAF and law enforcement representatives. Destruction must be by one of the methods provided on the list of USDA Hemp Disposal Activities." The Harvest/Destruction Report (2020 form, via search) adds: a crop that "has failed due to weather or other agronomic factors" and is to be destroyed requires the same prior LDAF approval (LDAF may inspect and collect a sample), with Location ID matching the approved application/site-modification record. USDA disposal methods (plowing/disking, mulching, composting, burning, etc. under the USDA hemp programme) are federal programme methods referenced by the form, not Louisiana statute text — the parent should cite them as "USDA Hemp Disposal Activities list, as referenced by the LDAF form," not as Louisiana law.

Volunteer plants — LSU AgCenter growers-rules summary (secondary/extension, same source as §11.3.2): "A licensee must destroy any harvested or unharvested industrial hemp plants resulting from either testing hot or other crop failures. Volunteer hemp plants must also be monitored and destroyed for at least three years after cultivation has occurred." [Verify volunteer-plant rule in LAC 7:XIII / current LDAF guidance before publishing as a rule.]

Criminal carve-out for destruction handling — R.S. 3:1471(A)(4) (Act 344 text, via search): it is unlawful to cultivate/handle/process/transport hemp where the plant "would otherwise be industrial hemp… except that it has a… THC concentration that exceeds… the federally defined THC level for hemp. This shall not include handling the plant for destruction as required by the department pursuant to this Part." I.e. destruction handling as directed by LDAF is excepted from the over-limit criminal provision. Research institutions are separately excepted (see §11.9).

11.5.4 Consumable hemp waste / failed product — no rendering recipe; revocation + non-sale is the mechanism

No consumable-hemp waste-rendering rule (grinding/mixing, morgue period, compost/incinerate/bury) was located in LAC 49:I Chapter 5 (§§516–539) as opened. The located mechanisms are: (i) a failing batch "shall not [be sold or distributed] in Louisiana" (§521(C)); (ii) market-surveillance revocation with 2-year re-registration bar (§539(B)) and 3-year bars (§539(D)–(F)); (iii) general State Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Law sanctions (§535(A)). Unsold/expired registered product disposal method, and processor manufacturing-waste disposal, are [Verify — not located in Chapter 5 as opened; check LAC 51, Part VI food-manufacturing waste provisions]. Do NOT import the medical retailer's 50%-mix rule into hemp.

11.6 Environmental rules: water, pesticide limits, energy

11.6.1 Medical — pesticide limits (Oregon-mirror MCL table), pesticide-use logging, MSDS, ventilation/mold, water/plumbing

Pesticide limits: LAC 51:XXIX §713(G) Table 1 (NOI, LR 51:719–720) — see §11.1.2 for the table structure and examples. The table is the operative environmental/contaminant limit for medical cultivation: it sets maximum contaminant levels in ppm separately for ingested and inhaled dosage forms. LDH's summary ("mirror the one utilized by the state of Oregon") is the only provenance statement located; the NOI does not reproduce an Oregon citation. [Verify: final LR 52:59 table identical to NOI table; confirm whether any compound was added/removed between the March 2025 Emergency Rule, the May 2025 NOI, and the January 2026 final rule.]

Pesticide/chemical use and records — R.S. 40:1046.2(H) (legis.la.gov, same link as §11.4.1, accessed 25 October 2026):

"(1) Any pesticides or chemicals used by a licensee in the production of therapeutic marijuana shall be used and stored according to the licensee's written operations plan." "(2) Each licensee shall maintain a material safety data sheet in each facility area where toxic cleaning compounds, sanitizing agents, solvents used in the production of therapeutic marijuana extracts and concentrates, pesticide chemicals, or other agricultural chemicals are used or stored." "(3) Each licensee shall record the following information when applying a pesticide or other agricultural chemical to therapeutic marijuana at any cultivation stage: (a) The date and time of the pesticide or chemical application. (b) The name of each individual who applied the pesticide or chemical. (c) The identification number of all batches receiving the application. (d) The amount and name of the pesticide or chemical applied, including the United States Environmental Protection Agency registration number, if any."

LAC 51:XXIX §709, "Toxic Chemical Use and Storage" (NOI text, LR 51:718): "Licensed facilities shall handle and store any chemicals for direct or indirect contact with medical marijuana in accordance with its written operations plan and the manufacturer's directions"; licensees "shall maintain records of material safety data sheets (MSDS) for all chemicals currently in use at the facility" (§709(C) as excerpted; §709(D)(1)–(4) elided — [Verify full §709 in LR 52:59]).

Ventilation / mold / odour / light / noise (environmental performance standards): §1046.2(B)(1)(a)(iii) — cultivation/processing "cannot be and are not reasonably perceptible from the structure in terms of common visual observation, odors, smell, fragrances, or other olfactory stimulus, light pollution, glare, brightness, adequate ventilation to prevent mold, and noise" (see §11.3.1). Manufacturer facility finishes: LAC 51:XXIX §715(A) (NOI text, LR 51:719): "Licensed facilities shall provide finishes to floors, walls, and ceilings that are durable, light in color, and easily cleanable" (§715(B)–(I) elided). Retailer environmental provisions: lighting, ventilation, and screening "as needed to… prevent contamination of products in storage with extraneous adulterants" and "minimize dissemination of microorganisms from one area to another" (§2511(C)); plumbing with "no cross-connections between any potable and nonpotable water supply," at least one hand lavatory with hot/cold water, soap, paper towels, and waste receptacle in storage/fulfillment areas, at least one utility sink for mop wastes, and "adequate means of sanitary disposal of wastewater" (§2511(E)); premises maintained free from disused equipment/waste/debris vermin harborage, overgrowth, poorly drained areas, and excessively dusty areas (§2511(H)); toilet rooms per the Uniform Construction Code with security/signage against marijuana use therein (§2511(G)). These are sanitary/building provisions, not water-use or discharge permits.

Water use, wastewater discharge permits, and energy: NO cannabis-specific water-withdrawal, irrigation-water, wastewater-discharge (other than the sanitary-disposal sentence above), or energy-efficiency rule was located in R.S. 40:1046, R.S. 40:1046.2, or the LAC 51:XXIX sections opened. General law (Louisiana water law, DEQ discharge permits, building/electrical codes via §1046.2(B)(1)(a)(v)) applies as general law and is not restated here. The parent must NOT claim a Louisiana cannabis water or energy rule on this evidence. Note for context only (not a rule): LDH collects "irrigation" as a production-cost category from licensees (R.S. 40:1046(H)(2)(a)(ii)) — a reporting category, not a water rule.

11.6.2 Hemp — pesticide: narrow FIFRA 25(b) position (extension/FAQ-level, VERIFY); no water/energy rule located

LDAF/extension FAQ (Louisiana Industrial Hemp programme FAQ, lahemp.net, accessed via search 25 October 2026 — programme FAQ, NOT statute or LAC text; treat as guidance-level, [Verify against current LDAF pesticide list]): "What pesticides can I use on my industrial hemp? The only approved pesticides for industrial hemp are 25b minimum risk products (and one conventional pesticide). There are 59 total approved pesticides, which can be found listed on the EPA website." LSU AgCenter's insecticide-efficacy article (https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1700580862170, accessed via search 25 October 2026) is consistent on the mechanism: minimum-risk (FIFRA §25(b)-exempt) products "can be applied to hemp if state registration permits. Louisiana has approved their use," and notes "Louisiana [LDAF] requires all pesticides, including 25(b) to be registered" (per a pesticide-registration survey summary, also via search). The "59" count and the identity of the "one conventional pesticide" are NOT adopted as current facts — the FAQ is undated in the excerpt (page last crawled ~1,238 days before access in one return) and EPA's hemp pesticide list changes. The citable, durable point is narrower: Louisiana hemp pesticide use is constrained to FIFRA minimum-risk products plus state registration, with no broad conventional-pesticide label for hemp located — and the current LDAF/EPA list must be checked at publication. [Verify: current LDAF approved-pesticide list and whether the one conventional product remains approved.]

Contrast with medical: medical pesticide compliance is by finished-product residue MCLs (§713(G)), not by an approved-product list in the text opened; hemp compliance is by approved-product status plus finished-product COA testing for pesticides (consumable §521/§519) and pre-harvest THC testing (cultivation §1468). Do not merge the two models.

Consumable hemp pesticide testing: each batch COA must address pesticides (§1483(A)(4) / §521(B) / §519(C)), but numeric pesticide limits in §519(C) were not fully readable in the excerpt opened (see §11.1.5 [Verify]). Heavy-metal limits ARE confirmed (§519(C)(10): As 10 ppm, Cd 4.1 ppm, Pb 10 ppm, Hg 2 ppm).

Water/energy (hemp): NO hemp-specific water-use, irrigation, runoff, or energy rule was located in R.S. 3:1461 et seq., LAC 7:XIII as opened, or LAC 49:I Chapter 5. General agricultural law (water, pesticide applicator licensing under R.S. 3:3201 et seq. generally, FSA acreage reporting) applies as general law and was not researched as cannabis-specific here. The LDAF programme does require reporting of acreage to FSA (see §11.3.2), which is an agricultural-administration duty, not an environmental standard.

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions

11.7.1 Medical — "samples" means testing samples; NO patient-sample giveaway rule located in current law; historic ban flagged

  • Testing samples: see §11.1.2 (§713: every batch sampled; representative sample verified compliant before release; COA within 24 hours). "Sample" in current medical law is a testing term. No provision for "sample" as a free product unit for patients was located in §1046, §1046.2, §1046.4, or LAC 51:XXIX Chapters 21/23/25 as opened.
  • Historic ban (Board of Pharmacy, NOT current LDH law unless verified): former LAC 46:LIII marijuana-pharmacy rule: "No person at a marijuana pharmacy shall provide marijuana samples" (Board draft, https://www.pharmacy.la.gov/assets/docs/Cmtes/RegRev/RegProp2022-O_MarijuanaPharmacy_Draft1.pdf, accessed via search 25 October 2026). Whether that sentence survived into LAC 51:XXIX Subpart 2 is [Verify in LR 52:59 Chapter 25] — the NOI Chapter 25 text opened (§§2501–2511) contains no "samples" prohibition in the excerpts read (the only "samples" hit in the NOI is §713 testing samples). The parent must NOT state a current sample ban without that verification, and must NOT state that samples are allowed either.
  • Discounts/promotions: NO medical-specific discount, coupon, loyalty, bundle, or promotion rule was located in the current statute/rule text opened. The hard constraints that bound any promotion are: the 71 g / 14-day flower cap and the clinician-recommendation limit for other forms (R.S. 40:1046(A)(5); LAC 51:XXIX §2505(C) cross-reference + refusal duty); in-state-only sourcing (§2103(A): retailers "may only stock marijuana products obtained from in-state licensed medical marijuana manufacturing facilities"); and LMMTS/POS recording of every transaction (§2505). A discount that caused a sale above the cap/recommendation would violate §2505(C); a discount within the cap is not addressed in the text opened.
  • Advertising: no current LDH medical advertising rule was opened (Run 1 §1.7 reached the same conclusion and rejected an unsourced "Section 13" advertising-restriction claim). General Louisiana law that may bear on promotions, NOT cannabis-specific and flagged for applicability: R.S. 51:411 (untrue/deceptive/misleading advertising prohibited, Justia 2025 text, https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-51/rs-51-411/, accessed via search 25 October 2026); R.S. 51:522 (drug retailer: no inaccurate competitor/price advertising, no secret gifts of value to influence a sale, no below-cost sale, no lottery/gamble condition, no undisclosed manufacturer/distributor demonstrator — Justia 2019 text, https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2019/revised-statutes/title-51/rs-522/, accessed via search 25 October 2026). A secondary advertising-marketing page (mediajel.com, accessed via search 25 October 2026) claims Louisiana pharmacies are "prohibited from using public mediums such as newspapers, billboards, television, radio, internet, or social media" and may use direct mail/brochures to physicians — that claim traces to the former Board-era adult-use/medical advertising proposals and the failed 2021 HB 699 advertising sections (R.S. 26:963 as proposed, never enacted — see legis.la.gov HB 699 original, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1218207, accessed via search 25 October 2026) and is REJECTED as a statement of current law. [Verify: any LDH advertising/promotion rule in LR 52:59.] "Discounts / Promotions: Allowed" on that same secondary page is likewise NOT adopted.

11.7.2 Hemp — no giveaway/discount rule located; promotion bounded by labelling, child-appeal, medical-claims, and registration rules

  • No sampling, giveaway, discount, coupon, or promotion rule for consumable hemp was located in R.S. 3:1481–1485 or LAC 49:I Chapter 5 (§§516–539) as opened. In particular, there is no hemp equivalent of the historic medical sample ban, and no hemp discount ban.
  • What DOES bound hemp promotions (all current, all in §11.1.5/Run 1): (i) distribution only of registered products (§517(E), with the 60-business-day pending-sale exception); (ii) no medical claims on labels (§1483(C)(1)(a), Run 1 §1.6.7); (iii) no child-appealing packaging (§533(E)); (iv) mandatory drug-test-failure disclaimer on THC products (§533(F)); (v) no marketing as dietary (§1483(B)(4), Run 1); (vi) serving/package THC caps that a "buy-one-get-one" or bundled offer cannot evade, because each serving/package must individually comply (§533(B)–(D); §517(G) bars functionally combined servings exceeding 5 mg); (vii) age 21+ verification for every sale (R.S. 3:1482(A)(2)) — a free sample given at retail would still be a retail disposition to a person whose age must be verified, but whether a $0 sample is a "sale" under §1482/§1484 is NOT stated in the text opened. [Verify: LDH/ATC treatment of free samples, tastings, and $0 promotions for consumable hemp.] Do not state that hemp samples are banned or allowed.
  • Sampling for compliance (not for consumers): LDH random/complaint COA procurement with chain of custody (§539(A), see §11.1.6); ATC scan-verification of registration (§1483(G)(3), Run 1). Those are enforcement sampling, not promotional sampling.
  • LDAF hemp (cultivation): no sampling/giveaway/promotion rule located; LDAF sampling is pre-harvest THC sampling (§1468) and random inspection sampling (§1468(B)).

11.8 Drug testing and background check rules for licence holders and staff

11.8.1 Medical — no suitability investigation for the licence; contractor-employee background checks (text still in university-contractor language — tension flagged); lab-staff permits; NO licensee drug-testing mandate located

La. R.S. 40:1047 (FindLaw republication, https://codes.findlaw.com/la/revised-statutes/la-rev-stat-tit-40-sect-1047/, accessed via search 25 October 2026 — [Verify current §1047 text on legis.la.gov; the FindLaw text still uses pre-Act 150 "contractor" language]):

"B.(1) No applicant for a specialty license or permit for the production of recommended marijuana for therapeutic use issued pursuant to R.S. 40:1046(H) or a contractor shall be required to undergo a suitability investigation conducted by any government agency as a prerequisite to obtaining a license or permit." "B.(2) A contractor shall submit to a criminal history background check conducted by a government agency or private entity subject to any applicable terms and conditions of the contract between the university licensee and contractor. The requirement to undergo a criminal history background check shall be limited to employees of a contractor for the production of recommended marijuana for therapeutic use. The government agency designated to regulate licensees for the production of recommended marijuana for therapeutic use pursuant to R.S. 40:1046 shall issue a provisional permit to the contractor and shall be converted to an unconditional permit upon successful completion of the criminal history background check."

Tension to preserve, not silently resolve: §1047 as republished still defines "contractor" as a person "selected by either the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center or the Southern University Agricultural Center through a competitive bid process" and still speaks of a "contract between the university licensee and contractor" — language that predates Act 150 of 2024, which removed the universities as licensees and transferred licences directly to the former contractors. Whether §1047's employee background-check duty now applies, as a matter of LDH practice, to employees of the two direct LDH licensees (Good Day Farm Louisiana LLC, Advanced Biomedics LLC) — and whether the provisional→unconditional permit mechanism still operates — was NOT confirmed in the text opened. The 2022 HB 553 history (legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1256636, accessed via search 25 October 2026) shows the Legislature deliberately narrowed §1047: no government suitability investigation as a licence prerequisite; background checks limited to contractor employees; contractors may consider background-check results in hiring ("nothing in this Section shall be construed to limit or prohibit a contractor from considering the results of a background check of a prospective employee in making the final determination of whether to employ the person"). [Verify: current §1047 on legis.la.gov including any Act 150 conforming amendment, and LDH's current employee background-check practice for licensees.] No disqualifying-offence list and no lookback period for medical employees was located in §1047 as republished — do NOT import the hemp 10-year/2-year bars into medical employment.

Laboratory staff: §1046.3(A)(2)(b) (see §11.1.4) — the laboratory director/qualifying individual and any person involved in testing or with access to restricted limited-access areas "shall obtain a permit in accordance with the requirements of R.S. 40:1047." That cross-reference is the lab-staff permit rule as written; its current operation depends on the §1047 verification above.

Retailer staff: the located staff rule is professional licensing, not background checks: each permit holder must appoint at least one Louisiana-residing pharmacist with an active unrestricted Louisiana Board of Pharmacy licence, designated responsible for the primary location and satellites, on duty when accessible by telephone during open hours and available by telephone/video for patient consultation during open hours (R.S. 40:1046(F)(1)(b)); LAC 51:XXIX §2303(F) (NOI text) repeats the designated-pharmacist duty. No retailer-employee background-check or drug-testing rule was located in §1046(G) or LAC 51:XXIX Chapters 21/23/25 as opened. Retailer personnel records must be current, complete, and accurate as an inspection item for manufacturers (§1046.2(B)(1)(g), (C)(2)(g)); the retailer analogue (personnel records) was not confirmed in the §2501 excerpt — [Verify].

Drug testing of licensee/permit-holder staff: NO rule requiring drug testing of medical licensee, retailer, or laboratory employees was located in the statute/rule text opened. General Louisiana drug-testing law (R.S. 49:1001 et seq., drug testing of state employees / agency policies) is a STATE-EMPLOYER regime, not a cannabis-licensee regime, and is NOT imported here. Patient-side drug-test protection is the state-employer rule in Run 1 (R.S. 49:1016: no negative employment consequences by a STATE employer based solely on a positive marijuana test where the employee/prospective employee has a qualifying diagnosis and a §1046 recommendation, with exclusions for on-premises/during-hours use or impairment, vehicle-operation responsibilities, and EMS/law enforcement/public safety/horse-racing-commission/firefighter roles). R.S. 40:1046(J) separately provides employers/workers'-compensation insurers are NOT obliged to pay for medical marijuana. Those patient-employment rules are Run 1 anchors, repeated here only to prevent confusion with licensee-staff rules.

11.8.2 Medical — personnel identification and records (security-adjacent, included here for completeness)

Manufacturer employees/supervisors/agents must keep a current LDH-approved identification card on their person when present at a facility (§1046.2(D)(5)); visitors get a badge + log (§1046.2(E) — see §11.4.1). Current, complete, and accurate personnel records are an initial- and ongoing-inspection item (§1046.2(B)(1)(g), (C)(2)(g)). Records retention for licensees: current year + three preceding calendar years (§1046.2(F)(3)); for labs: testing records ≥3 years (§1046.4(A)(2), LAC 51:XXIX §907); for retailers: reconciliation documents on premises ≥2 calendar years (§2505(D)), visiting-patient documents ≥3 years (§2507(G), NOI text: "A retailer shall retain all documents required by R.S. 40:1046.1(C)(2) for at least three years").

11.8.3 Hemp — three different background regimes; do NOT merge them

LDAF industrial hemp (R.S. 3:1465(D)) — fingerprint-based, 10-year / 2-year bars, every 3 years:

"D.(1) Upon application for initial licensure and every three years thereafter, each applicant shall be required to submit to a criminal background check… 'applicant' shall mean an applicant or designated responsible party as defined in R.S. 3:1462." "D.(2) The applicant shall submit fingerprints and other identifying information to the Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information for the purpose of obtaining state and national criminal history record information and grant permission to the department to obtain the state and national criminal history information on the applicant." "D.(3)… the bureau shall survey its criminal history records… and make a simultaneous request of the Federal Bureau of Investigation for like information… The bureau may charge the applicant a reasonable processing fee…" "D.(4) Any… criminal history record information… which is not already a matter of public record shall be deemed nonpublic and confidential… restricted to the exclusive use by the department in evaluating the applicant's eligibility or disqualification…" "D.(5) No person shall be eligible to obtain a license if convicted under state or federal law of any of the following: (a) A felony within the ten years immediately preceding the date of application. (b) A drug-related misdemeanor within the two years immediately preceding the date of application."

Source: Justia 2025 text, https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1465/, accessed 25 October 2026 (Acts 2019, No. 164; Acts 2020, No. 344; Acts 2021, No. 336; Acts 2022, No. 498, eff. 16 June 2022). LDAF licensing practice (Run 1 Part 4): state + federal background check; one set suffices for multiple licence types if performed within 60 days of LDAF receiving the application. Note the cadence change: the 2020 Act 344 text required a check on initial licensure AND annual renewal; the current text says initial + "every three years thereafter" — use the current cadence. The applicant "is responsible for any employee working under the applicant's license" (§1465(E)) — a responsibility rule, not an employee background-check mandate in the text opened. Research institutions are exempt from §1465 when performing §1469 research (§1465(F) — see §11.9).

LDH consumable hemp processors (LAC 49:I §516(E)–(F)) — attestation-based, no time limit stated:

See §11.2.6: individuals ≥21 + notarised attestation of no felony (any jurisdiction, no lookback stated) and no listed vice/drug-dealing convictions; juridical entities: notarised attestation for >5% officers/shareholders/members. This is an attestation, not a fingerprint/FBI check, in the rule text opened. Whether LDH also runs a fingerprint check in practice is [Verify — not stated in §516]. Do NOT describe the processor regime as "10-year felony bar" — that is the LDAF regime.

ATC retailers/wholesalers — background checks PROHIBITED as a rule requirement:

R.S. 3:1484(H) (2022 text, via search; [Verify current text]): ATC rules "shall not include any… requirements for… criminal background checks, diagrams of retail premises, or proof of lease or ownership of any retail establishment" (see §11.2.6). An ATC applicant therefore cannot be subjected to a background-check requirement by ATC rule on the current text. (This does not bar a private employer's own hiring checks as general employment law, which was not researched here.)

Drug testing — hemp: NO drug-testing mandate for hemp licensees, processor staff, or ATC permit holders was located in Title 3 Part VI, LAC 49:I Chapter 5, or R.S. 3:1465 as opened. The drug-test point that DOES exist for hemp is consumer-facing: THC-product labels must warn that consumption "may cause the user to fail a preemployment or routine drug screen" (LAC 49:I §533(F), see §11.1.5). General pre-employment drug screening by private employers is general employment law, not a hemp-licence rule, and is not detailed here.

11.9 Research and university cannabis and hemp work (LSU AgCenter, Southern University Agricultural Center, any research licences)

11.9.1 Medical marijuana research — permission, not a production licence; no separate research-licence type located

Statute — R.S. 40:1046(L) (legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=96986, accessed 25 October 2026), verbatim:

"The Louisiana State University Agricultural Center, the Southern University Agricultural Center, and the University of Louisiana at Monroe may conduct research on marijuana for therapeutic use."

Three points must be kept distinct:

  1. This is NOT a production licence. After Act 150 of 2024, the universities are NOT licensees (licences went directly to Good Day Farm Louisiana LLC and Advanced Biomedics LLC on 1 July 2024). Run 1 Part 0 correctly states: "R.S. 40:1046(L) still allows LSU AgCenter, Southern University AgCenter and University of Louisiana at Monroe to 'conduct research on marijuana for therapeutic use' — research is not a production licence." Any source still listing the universities as cultivators is stale (Run 1 Part 4–6, §4.1.1).
  2. LMMTS contemplates delivery to researchers. R.S. 40:1046(F)(1)(a) requires LMMTS connectivity "from seed to delivery to an approved laboratory, to wholesale to permitted retailers, to wholesale to another licensed cultivation facility, to delivery to an authorized researcher, to sale to patients or caregivers by permitted retailers, or to destruction." The term "authorized researcher" is used in the LMMTS chain but NO definition of "authorized researcher," NO research-application procedure, NO research-licence fee, and NO research-quantity limit was located in §1046, §1046.2, §1046.3, §1046.4, or the LAC 51:XXIX sections opened. [Verify: LDH "authorized researcher" designation procedure, if any — no separate research licence type was located, and the parent must not invent one.] Historically (2018 §1046 text, Justia 2018), university research was tied to being "licensed as a production facility" with an annual report to the Senate/House health-and-welfare committees; that linkage does NOT appear in the current §1046(L) sentence and must NOT be carried forward as current law without verification.
  3. No university medical-marijuana research programme, project, publication, or funding figure was located in LDH, LSU AgCenter, Southern University, or ULM sources opened in this run. A secondary advocacy page (louisianamarijuanacard.com, "Researchers Call for Marijuana Research Centers," accessed via search 25 October 2026) correctly quotes §1046(L) and argues Louisiana "already has a foundation" for research, but lists only prospective study topics (dosing, formulations, interactions, outcomes), not existing Louisiana studies. Those topics are NOT Louisiana research findings and must not be presented as such. [Unavailable: current LSU/Southern/ULM therapeutic-marijuana research projects, if any — confirm with the institutions / LDH before asserting activity beyond the §1046(L) permission.]

Laboratory angle: §1046.3(A)(2) provides approved laboratories "may include… the colleges, universities, other institutions, and systems governed by the Louisiana Board of Regents; public-private partnerships involving [those] systems, colleges, and universities… and private laboratories" (see §11.1.4). A university laboratory could therefore be an approved testing laboratory (subject to accreditation, inspection, LMMTS, and §1047 permits for testing staff), which is distinct from conducting therapeutic-use research under §1046(L). No university is on the current LDH approved-lab list (§11.1.4: LDAF, Ceres Scientific, Acre Analytical).

11.9.2 Industrial hemp research — R.S. 3:1469: universities authorised, exempt from licensure/penalties when doing §1469 research

Statute history — R.S. 3:1469 (Act 344 of 2020 text, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1182597, accessed via search 25 October 2026 — [Verify current §1469 text on legis.la.gov]):

  • §1469(A)(1): "The Louisiana State University Agricultural Center and the Southern University Agricultural Center are authorized to cultivate, handle, and process industrial hemp and industrial hemp seeds for research and development of new varieties."
  • §1469(A)(2) (as amended in the Act 344 text): "The universities in Paragraph (1)… may contract with licensed hemp seed producers for development of seed for distribution through a process as determined by the department."
  • §1469(B) (Act 344 text): "The University of Louisiana at Monroe College of Pharmacy is authorized to handle and process industrial hemp for medicinal research and development."
  • Act 336 of 2021 added the University of Louisiana at Monroe Agribusiness Program to the research authorisation (JD Supra summary of Act 336, accessed via search 25 October 2026: Act 336 "empowers the University of Louisiana at Monroe Agribusiness Program to cultivate, handle, and process industrial hemp in connection with product research and development, while also exempting the Monroe Agribusiness Program from industrial hemp licensure requirements" and required LSU AgCenter to develop a centralised industrial hemp website with regulators/stakeholders — the website requirement is noted here as a 2021 Act provision, [Verify whether the centralised website exists / is maintained]).

Exemptions — R.S. 3:1465(F) (current Justia text, same source as §11.8.3): "The provisions of this Section shall not apply to the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center, the Southern University Agricultural Center, the University of Louisiana at Monroe Agribusiness Program, and the University of Louisiana at Monroe College of Pharmacy when performing research and development as provided for in R.S. 3:1469." And R.S. 3:1471(C) (Act 344 text, via search): "The provisions of this Section shall not apply to [LSU AgCenter, Southern University AgCenter, and ULM College of Pharmacy] when performing research and development as provided for in R.S. 3:1469" (criminal-penalty exemption). I.e. §1469 research is exempt from LDAF licensure (§1465) and from the §1471 criminal penalties — but ONLY "when performing research and development as provided for in R.S. 3:1469." Commercial production by a university outside §1469 research is not covered by the exemption on the text opened.

Testing contracts — R.S. 3:1468(A)(3) (see §11.1.7): "The department may enter into contracts, cooperative endeavor agreements, memoranda of understanding, or other agreements with any public postsecondary education institution for the testing of THC levels in industrial hemp crops or industrial hemp products deemed necessary by the commissioner." The 2020 HB 491 digest (legis.la.gov, https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1163095, accessed via search 25 October 2026) names LSU AgCenter, Southern University AgCenter, and ULM as the contemplated testing contractors. Whether any such testing contract is currently in force was NOT located — [Verify with LDAF].

Performance-based sampling research factor: §1468(A)(2)(c) makes "conducting industrial hemp research" a factor for performance-based sampling eligibility (see §11.1.7) — research producers may therefore be sampled differently, but the text does not exempt research crops from THC testing.

11.9.3 What the universities actually did (hemp) — LSU AgCenter work documented; Southern/ULM work NOT located

LSU AgCenter — documented, dated, secondary/university sources (NOT statutes):

  • Field production research, Central Research Station, Baton Rouge, 2020–2021: "Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) cultivation research did not exist in Louisiana prior to 2020 (LSU AgCenter Therapeutic Cannabis Committee, 2020). Therefore, nine cultivars of essential oil-type hemp were evaluated in 2020 and 2021 to determine optimum planting dates, in-row plant spacings and THC compliancy for organic field production in south Louisiana" (LSU master's thesis abstract, Deynzer, August 2022, https://digitalcommons.lsu.edu/gradschool_theses/5608/, accessed via search 25 October 2026).
