Findings as abstracted: in-row spacing of three feet recommended for field-grown hemp until suitable genetics are identified; Berry Blossom, Queen Dream, and Stormy Daniels produced sufficient biomass for commercial production; Berry Blossom, Queen Dream, Oregon White, and Putin's Problem were high-yielding, but "Oregon White was the only cultivar to remain compliant and not exceed 0.3% THC when field grown"; no THC difference between top/middle/bottom portions of field plants. Greenhouse arm: 28 cultivars; Umpqua, Lifter Seedless, Sour Lifter, and White CBG Seedless highest-yielding, but Lifter Seedless and Sour Lifter exceeded 0.3% THC and "should be harvested earlier in the flowering period." LSU AgCenter's own lessons-learned article (Fontenot & Deynzer, https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1702394360572, accessed via search 25 October 2026) confirms the design: nine cultivars, organic practices, Central Research Station, planted 15 April / 15 May / 15 June / 15 July, 3-/4-/5-foot in-row spacings, female plants only (flowers contain the essential oils), photoperiod extended to 18 hours with fixed dual-head halogen lights, vegetative growth 2–3 months then ~2 months reproductive/flower development.
  • Grain/fiber variety trials, summer 2022: "researchers evaluated some of the grain and fiber lines of industrial hemp at LSU AgCenter research stations… Sixteen cultivars of grain and fiber hemp were planted at Red River Research station in Bossier City and Macon Ridge Research Station in Winnsboro," randomised complete block design, four replications, 5 ft × 20 ft plots (LSU AgCenter article, https://www.LSUAGCenter.com/articles/page1702393903109, accessed via search 25 October 2026). The article notes northern/European cultivars' unsuitability to "the hot and humid conditions of the South" as the research rationale.
  • Insecticide efficacy work (LSU AgCenter, https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1700580862170, accessed via search 25 October 2026): minimum-risk insecticides (potassium salts, azadirachtin, Bacillus thuringiensis, GS-omega/kappa-Hxtx-Hv1a spider-venom peptide, essential oils) tested on fall armyworm, beet armyworm, and soybean looper on hemp variety Southern Luck grown in a hoop house at the Plant Materials Center, Doyle Chambers Research Station. This is pest-management research, relevant to §11.6.2, and is university research, not a pesticide approval.

Southern University Agricultural Center — NO specific hemp research project, publication, or trial located in this run. The §1469 authorisation and the §1465/§1471 exemptions apply to Southern on the statute text, and the testing-contract digest names Southern as a contemplated contractor, but no Southern hemp trial, cultivar, or publication was found in LSU AgCenter, LDAF, or Southern sources opened. [Unavailable — do not invent a Southern project.]

University of Louisiana at Monroe — NO specific hemp research project located in this run beyond the statutory authorisations (§1469: Agribusiness Program cultivation/handling/processing for product R&D; College of Pharmacy handling/processing for medicinal R&D) and the §1483(F)(2) "preferred laboratory" reference for the ULM-affiliated lab in consumable-hemp COA testing (Run 1 §1.6.1 — "once it meets requirements and commences operations"; whether it has commenced operations was NOT confirmed in this run — [Verify]).

No other research-licence type: no Louisiana "research licence" for private persons, no cannabis research facility licence, and no hemp research licence for non-university applicants was located in R.S. 40:1046, R.S. 3:1469, LAC 51:XXIX, or LAC 49:I Chapter 5 as opened. A private researcher who is not within §1046(L) (medical) or §1469 (hemp, universities) would need the ordinary licence/permit for the activity (medical licensee, LDAF grower/processor/handler/seed-producer licence, or LDH processor permit) — that is the structural conclusion from the absence of a research-licence provision, flagged as an inference from absence, not as a quoted rule. Louisiana Cannabis and Hemp — Run 2, PART 12 ONLY

Consumer and Social Rules

Scope note. This is part of the combined Louisiana dossier (Parts 0–12), as corrected in the 28 October 2026 audit. See Part 1 (audit) at the top of this file for corrections and items still unverified.

12.0 At a glance — where the three tracks diverge

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke-shop rules

12.1.1 What counts as "drug paraphernalia"

La. R.S. 40:1021(A) (Run 1, quoted from legis.la.gov search text; re-check on legis.la.gov before HTML publication):

"'drug paraphernalia' means and includes but is not limited to: (1) All equipment, products, and materials of any kind which are used, intended for use, or designed for use in planting, propagating, cultivating, growing, harvesting, manufacturing, compounding, converting, producing, processing, preparing, testing, analyzing, packaging, repackaging, storing, containing, concealing, injecting, ingesting, inhaling, or otherwise introducing into the human body a controlled substance in violation of the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law, as scheduled in R.S. 40:964."

  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=96972 (§1021) — accessed 25 Oct 2026 via Run 1; not re-opened in full in this run.
  • The definition turns on use / intended use / design for use with a controlled substance "in violation of" the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law. That wording matters for every distinction below: the same pipe is paraphernalia or not depending on what it is used/intended/designed for, and a device used solely for a lawful purpose (e.g. a lawful hemp product that is not a controlled substance, or a programme patient's authorised form) is not within the definition on its face. No Louisiana court decision or LDH/ATC guidance applying that "in violation of" qualifier to a medical patient's device, or to a hemp-only device, was located in this run — [Verify].
  • Run 1 flagged a secondary claim that "devices used solely for inhaling medical marijuana by a programme patient are excluded from the definition". That exclusion was NOT found in the §1021 text opened. Do not publish it as law. The correct statement is narrower: §1021's own "in violation of" qualifier is the only textual hook, and its application to patients is unverified.

12.1.2 The general paraphernalia offences — and what HB 165 did NOT change

  • Prohibited acts (general). R.S. 40:1023–1024 prohibit, in substance, knowingly selling/lending/renting/leasing/giving/exchanging/distributing drug paraphernalia, manufacturing/delivering paraphernalia, and related transactions. The full current text of §§1023–1024 was not opened in full in this run — [Verify] before quoting. Do not quote §§1023–1024 verbatim from this file.
  • Sale to / presence of minors — a separate, stricter rule that HB 165 did not touch. R.S. 40:1023.1 (Acts 1990, No. 398; Acts 2006, No. 676), opened via legis.la.gov search text and FindLaw republication:

    "A. It is unlawful for any person, corporation, or association to sell, lend, rent, lease, give, exchange, exhibit, display, or distribute to any unmarried person under the age of seventeen any drug paraphernalia." "C. It shall be unlawful to invite or permit any unmarried person under the age of seventeen to be in any commercial establishment that exhibits or displays any item, material, work, or object of any kind that is defined as drug paraphernalia pursuant to this Part." "D. Lack of knowledge of age or marital status shall not constitute a defense, unless the defendant shows that he had reasonable cause to believe that the minor involved was either married or seventeen years of age or more and that the minor exhibited to the defendant a draft card, driver's license, birth certificate, or other official or apparently official document purporting to establish that such person was either married or seventeen years of age or more."

  • Sources: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=96977 ; https://codes.findlaw.com/la/revised-statutes/la-rev-stat-tit-40-sect-1023-1/ — both accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Practical consequence for a smoke shop: a shop that exhibits or displays paraphernalia may not invite or permit an unmarried person under 17 to be in the establishment at all (§1023.1(C)) — this is stricter than a mere "do not sell to minors" rule, and it is distinct from the 21+ consumable-hemp rule (§12.2) and the 21+ tobacco/vapour rule. Whether a shop that sells only hemp products (not paraphernalia as defined) is within §1023.1(C) turns on whether its displayed items meet the §1021 definition — [Verify] for any specific shop layout.
  • General penalties (everything EXCEPT the §1025(E) marijuana-personal-use tier). R.S. 40:1025(A)–(C), as amended by Act 682 (HB 165) of 2024 (see §12.1.3 for the (E) carve-out):

    "A.(1) Except as provided in Subsection E of this Section, the first violation of or failure to comply with any provision of this Part shall subject the offender to a fine not in excess of three hundred dollars, or imprisonment of not more than fifteen days, or both." "B. On a second conviction, except as provided in Subsection E of this Section, the offender shall be fined not more than one thousand dollars, or imprisoned for not more than six months, or both." "C. On a third or subsequent conviction, except as provided in Subsection E of this Section, the offender shall be fined not more than two thousand five hundred dollars, or imprisoned, with or without hard labor, for not more than two years, or both."

  • Source: legis.la.gov LawPrint for §1025, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=410561 — accessed 25 Oct 2026; enrolled HB 165 text, https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1379657 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Note the "Except as provided in Subsection E" qualifier in each paragraph: the (A)–(C) jail exposure survives for paraphernalia that is not within (E) — i.e. paraphernalia for non-marijuana drugs, paraphernalia in quantities exceeding personal use, and (on the enrolled text's wording, which says "possessing") sale/delivery transactions. See §12.1.3.

12.1.3 The marijuana personal-use tier — Act 682 (HB 165) of 2024, effective 1 Aug 2024 — Run 1 Act-number gap RESOLVED

Run 1 left the Act number for HB 165 as [Verify]. It is now resolved:

  • Act 682 (HB 165), 2024 Regular Session (Boyd), effective 1 August 2024. Résumé Digest: "ACT 682 (HB 165) 2024 Regular Session Boyd … New law removes incarceration as a punishment for the possession of certain drug paraphernalia in quantities not exceeding those required for individual personal use. New law provides that the punishment for the possession of certain drug paraphernalia in quantities not exceeding those required for individual personal use is a fine of: (1) $100 on a first conviction. (2) $500 on a second conviction. (3) $2,500 on a third or subsequent conviction. Effective August 1, 2024. (Amends R.S. 40:1025(A)(1), (B), and (C); Adds R.S. 40:1025(E))" — source: https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1385127 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Verbatim operative text, R.S. 40:1025(E) (enrolled HB 165; legis.la.gov LawPrint for §1025, same links as §12.1.2):

    "E. The penalty for possessing drug paraphernalia intended for, or used solely for, the inhalation, ingestion, epidermal or sublingual absorption, or other method of introducing marijuana or marijuana derivatives into the human body are as follows for quantities of paraphernalia not exceeding those required for individual personal use: (1) On a first conviction, a fine of one hundred dollars. (2) On a second conviction, a fine of five hundred dollars. (3) On a third or subsequent conviction, a fine of two thousand five hundred dollars."

  • What this does and does not do — state it plainly, because secondary summaries overstate it: 1. It removes incarceration only for possession of marijuana-only paraphernalia in personal-use quantities. It does not make possession lawful; it is a penalty tier, like the ≤14 g possession tier. 2. It does not on its face cover sale, delivery, manufacture, or distribution of paraphernalia — those remain under (A)–(C) (fine and/or jail). A smoke shop that sells a bong is not within (E)'s "possessing" wording. Do not describe HB 165 / Act 682 as "decriminalising paraphernalia sales". 3. It does not cover paraphernalia for other drugs, or marijuana paraphernalia in wholesale / non-personal-use quantities — those remain under (A)–(C). 4. It does not create a patient-specific paraphernalia exemption. A programme patient and a non-patient possessor face the same (E) tier for personal-use marijuana paraphernalia on the text opened; the patient's programme immunity (§966(F), Run 1 §1.4.7) is about possessing medical marijuana itself, not about paraphernalia as a separate offence — whether §966(F) immunity extends to the device used to consume programme marijuana was not located — [Verify]. 5. Predicate-conviction washout: §1025(A)(2) (2016 text, via HB 267 enrolled digest) provides a conviction under (A) may not be used as a predicate for enhancement under (B)/(C) if the offender has no controlled-substances-law conviction for 2 years from completion of sentence/probation/parole/suspension, once per person. Whether that washout paragraph survives verbatim after Act 682 was not re-opened — [Verify] current §1025(A)(2) on legis.la.gov.
  • Governor action: NORML, 24 June 2024 (secondary, dated): Governor Landry signed HB 165 the same day he vetoed HB 391 (expedited pardons — see §12.4). Source: http://norml.org/blog/2024/06/24/louisiana-governor-signs-legislation-decriminalizing-possession-of-marijuana-paraphernalia/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The Act 682 digest itself confirms enactment; the NORML date is used only for the signing/veto pairing.

12.1.4 Smoke shops — there is NO Louisiana "smoke shop licence"

  • No state licence category called "smoke shop" was located in any official source opened. A Louisiana shop's obligations are the sum of the permits for what it actually sells, not a single smoke-shop permit:
  • If it sells tobacco / alternative nicotine / vapour products at retail: an ATC Tobacco Retail Dealer Permit, $25/year per place of business (plus a $50 Responsible Vendor fee if the location does not already hold a valid alcoholic-beverage permit, per the ATC form), with a separate Tobacconist Permit ($100/year) only for a bona fide tobacco retailer blending bulk smoking tobacco where ≥50% of the preceding 12 months' purchases were tobacco products excluding cigarettes. Source (official ATC form): https://atc.louisiana.gov/media/olydphrh/atc-tobacco-retail-dealer-vending-machine-operator-tobacconist_a11y.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Louisiana Department of Revenue tobacco-permit page confirms the same $25 retail / $75 wholesale / $5 vending-machine figures: https://revenue.la.gov/businesses/excise/tobacco-products-permits/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • If it sells consumable hemp products at retail: an ATC consumable-hemp retail permit for each place of business (and for each domain name for a remote retailer), fee capped at $175/year by R.S. 3:1484(C) (Run 1 Part 4, §4.4.4); plus LDH product registration for every product sold. A shop that sells hemp products without the ATC permit, or sells an unregistered product, is in violation of R.S. 3:1482/1484 regardless of whether it also holds a tobacco permit.
  • If it sells only paraphernalia and no tobacco, vapour, hemp, or alcohol: no ATC permit for paraphernalia alone was located. The shop is still subject to §§1021–1025 (including §1023.1(C)'s under-17 presence ban if it displays paraphernalia), to general local business licensing / occupational licence tax and zoning (Run 1 Part 3), and to the Smoke-Free Air Act's "retail tobacco business" exemption analysis (§12.5) — which turns on whether the business is "utilized primarily for the sale of tobacco products and accessories" (§1291.3(11)), not on calling itself a smoke shop.
  • If it sells alcohol: a separate ATC alcoholic-beverage permit; and, since Act 752, a premises holding an alcohol-beverage permit may not newly obtain a hemp permit unless it obtained a hemp permit on or before 17 June 2024 (Run 1 §1.6.6 — alcohol-premises grandfather paragraph, R.S. 3:1484(B)(5), still [Verify] against current §1484 text; HB 539 (2026) would have repealed it — disposition still [Verify] per Run 1 §1.10, do not state it as dead or pending on this file's authority).
  • Local smoke-shop rules: No statewide smoke-shop zoning buffer, distance-from-school rule for shops, or smoke-shop operating-hours rule was located in state law. Local (parish/municipal) zoning and business-licensing rules may impose them — that is a Part 3 matter and was not re-researched here. Do not import another state's "1,000 feet from a school for a smoke shop" rule.
  • On-premises use / "smoke lounge": No Louisiana statute authorising a commercial smoking lounge for marijuana, or a hemp-smoking lounge, was located. A lounge that permits smoking in an enclosed public place would face the Smoke-Free Air Act (§12.5) and, for marijuana, the drug-free-zone and school rules; a "retail tobacco business" exemption (§1291.11(B)(4)) is a tobacco-business exemption, not a marijuana-consumption authorisation — [Verify] whether any local ordinance or LDH rule has ever treated a marijuana retailer or hemp retailer as a "retail tobacco business" for this purpose (none was located).

12.2 Minimum age for consumable hemp THC products — and the medical contrast

12.2.1 Consumable hemp: 21+ to buy, sell, possess — with criminal penalties added in 2025

  • Retail sale ban, R.S. 3:1482(A)(2) (Run 1 §1.6.4, Act 752 eff. 1 Jan 2025): "No person shall sell or offer for sale at retail any consumable hemp product to any person under the age of twenty-one. A retailer shall verify the age of any person attempting to purchase or receive a consumable hemp product prior to the sales transaction of the product. A retailer shall require a purchaser to produce a valid federal or state issued photo identification card or a digitized identification card as defined in R.S. 51:3211. A retailer shall maintain all consumable hemp products except for consumable hemp beverages in a location that is inaccessible to the public without the assistance of an employee of the retailer."
  • Source: legis.la.gov §1482 text opened in Run 1 — accessed 25 Oct 2026 (Run 1); current text to be re-opened by the parent assembler.
  • History: 18+ before Act 752 (21+ only for the former "adult-use" >0.5 mg/package category under Act 498 of 2022); 21+ for all consumable hemp products from 1 Jan 2025, when the "adult-use consumable hemp product" definition was repealed.
  • Scope question — 0-THC products and topicals: The statute says "any consumable hemp product" without a THC threshold, and the §1481 definition includes products containing "any cannabinoid, including cannabidiol or THC" and expressly includes commercial feed and pet products (§1481(3)(b)). On its face, therefore, the 21+ rule reaches a 0-THC CBD topical and a pet product sold at retail. Whether LDH/ATC enforce it that broadly for 0-THC topicals or pet products was not located in LDH/ATC guidance — [Verify] before stating it as an enforcement position. Do not soften the statute to "21+ only for THC products" without that guidance.
  • Criminal sale offence, R.S. 14:93.16 (Acts 2025, No. 233, §1 — HB 12, Schlegel), opened on legis.la.gov:

    "A. It is unlawful for any person to sell, distribute, dispense, or otherwise deliver any consumable hemp product, as defined in R.S. 3:1481, to any person under twenty-one years of age unless such person is the lawful owner or lawful employee of an establishment to which the sale is being made and is accepting such delivery pursuant to such ownership or employment. Lack of knowledge of the person's age shall not be a defense." "B. Whoever violates the provisions of this Section shall be fined not less than five hundred dollars nor more than one thousand dollars, or imprisoned for not less than thirty days nor more than six months, or both."

  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=1429216 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Notes: (i) The only exception in (A) is the under-21 owner/employee accepting a delivery for the establishment — it is not a "handling in the course of employment" exception for a retail sale to a minor, and it is not a parental-consent exception. (ii) "Lack of knowledge of the person's age shall not be a defense" — strict as to age; the §1482(A)(2) ID-verification duty is the compliance route. (iii) This is in Title 14 (Criminal Code), not Title 3 — a sale to a minor is now both a Title 3 permit violation and a Title 14 crime.
  • Under-21 purchase/possession offence, R.S. 14:93.17 (Acts 2025, No. 233, §1), opened on legis.la.gov:

    "A. It is unlawful for any person under twenty-one years of age to purchase or possess any consumable hemp product as defined in R.S. 3:1481." "B.(1) Whoever violates the provisions of this Section shall be fined not more than one hundred dollars. (2) Any person apprehended while violating the provisions of this Section shall be issued a citation by the apprehending law enforcement officer, which shall be paid in the same manner as provided for the offenders of local traffic violations. A citation issued by a law enforcement officer for such violation shall not be included on the person's criminal history record."

  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=1429218 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Contrast with the seller: the minor's exposure is a $100 citation, expressly not on the criminal history record; the seller's exposure is $500–$1,000 and/or 30 days–6 months. There is no parental-consent, medical-need, or "holding for an adult" exception in §93.17's text opened.
  • Related 2025 change — unlicensed consumable-hemp manufacturing/possession. The same Act 233 (HB 12) engrossed text also enacted R.S. 40:966(A)(4) and (B)(4): a consumable hemp product (in the manufacturing/possession context of that bill) carries 1–10 years and/or a fine up to $50,000. Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1407784 (HB 12 engrossed) — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The precise operative scope of §966(A)(4)/(B)(4) — which unlicensed acts it reaches, and whether it reaches mere retail possession of an unregistered product by a consumer — was NOT opened in final Act 233 text in this run — [Verify] before quoting it as a consumer-possession penalty. Do not use it to suggest an ordinary buyer of a registered product faces 1–10 years.
  • Online / remote sales: The 21+ rule applies to a remote retailer in the same terms (domain = place of business, §1484(B)(1)(b), Run 1). How age verification is to be performed for an online sale (ID upload, third-party verification, delivery-age check) was NOT located in LDH/ATC guidance — [Verify]. Do not state an online-verification method as law.
  • Samples / promotion: No separate Louisiana statute on free samples of consumable hemp to under-21s was located beyond §§93.16 ("distribute, dispense, or otherwise deliver") and 1482 ("sell or offer for sale"). A free sample delivered to a minor falls within §93.16's "otherwise deliver" wording on its face — that is a textual reading, not a located prosecution — [Verify] if the parent wants a samples-specific statement.

12.2.2 Medical marijuana: no flat age floor — and the one express under-21 rule

  • No minimum age in §1046. The statute authorises a recommendation for "any patient clinically diagnosed as suffering from a debilitating medical condition" (§1046(A)(1)) and lists autism-spectrum-associated conditions for patients under 18 with a paediatric-subspecialist consultation requirement (§1046(A)(2)(b)) — i.e. minors are contemplated patients. No 18+ or 21+ floor for programme participation was located in §1046.
  • The one express under-21 rule — flower only. R.S. 40:1046(A)(5)(b) (Run 1 §1.3.5): no sale of raw or crude marijuana to a person under 21 "without a recommendation from an authorized clinician specifically recommending marijuana in raw or crude form for that person". Implication, stated as an implication only: a minor can receive flower with that specific recommendation, and can receive non-flower forms on a general recommendation — but the minor-patient procedure (who presents ID, whether a parent/guardian/caregiver must be present, whether a caregiver must be designated for a minor) was not opened in LDH rules — [Verify] (Run 1 §1.4.5 caregiver gap, carried forward).
  • Caregivers / parents for minors — still unverified. §966(F)(1) immunity expressly covers "a caregiver as defined in R.S. 15:1503" and "any person who is a domiciliary parent of a minor child who possesses medical marijuana on behalf of his minor child" (Run 1 §1.4.7). What §15:1503 requires for caregiver designation (age, residency, background check, patient limit, registration) was not opened — [Verify]. Do not publish the secondary caregiver eligibility list (21+, Louisiana resident, background check, ≤2 patients) as law.
  • Contrast table — age:
  • Buy consumable hemp at retail: 21+, no exception for a clinician recommendation (a medical recommendation does not authorise a hemp purchase by a minor; hemp is not §1046 marijuana).
  • Be a §1046 patient: no age floor; flower under 21 needs a specific raw/crude recommendation.
  • Buy tobacco/vapour: 21+ under federal law and R.S. 14:91.8 (secondary summary, ATC form context — not re-verified as a Part 12 law point; do not quote a tobacco age penalty from this file).
  • Possess marijuana as a non-patient minor: unlawful; juvenile disposition rules are outside this Part — [Verify / out of scope] if the parent wants juvenile penalties.

12.3 THC driving limits and impairment testing

12.3.1 There is NO per se THC limit in Louisiana law

  • Current offence, R.S. 14:98 (renamed "Operating a vehicle while impaired" by Acts 2024, No. 662), opened on legis.la.gov:

    "A.(1) The crime of operating a vehicle while impaired is the operating of any motor vehicle, aircraft, watercraft, vessel, or other means of conveyance when any of the following conditions exist: (a) The operator is impaired by alcoholic beverages. (b) The operator's blood alcohol concentration is 0.08 percent or more by weight based on grams of alcohol per one hundred cubic centimeters of blood. (c) The operator is impaired by any other drug, combination of drugs, or combination of alcohol and drugs. (d), (e) Repealed by Acts 2024, No. 662, §3." "(2) A valid driver's license shall not be an element of the offense, and the lack thereof shall not be a defense to a prosecution for operating a vehicle while impaired." "(3) As used in this Section, the term 'drug' means any substance or combination of substances that, when taken into the human body, can impair the ability of the person to operate a vehicle safely."

  • Source: https://legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?p=y&d=78751 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • What this means, precisely:
  • The only numeric per se threshold in §98(A)(1) is alcohol: 0.08% BAC (paragraph (b)). There is no THC ng/mL figure, no "5 ng/mL" rule, and no metabolite threshold anywhere in §98(A)(1) as opened. The 0.02% (under-21) and 0.04% (commercial) figures in secondary DWI guides are alcohol thresholds, not THC thresholds — do not apply them to THC.
  • For drugs, the element is impairment — "impaired by any other drug" — not mere presence. The statute defines "drug" functionally ("can impair the ability … to operate a vehicle safely"), which on its face reaches THC from any source (medical marijuana, non-patient marijuana, or a consumable hemp product) if impairment is proved. It does not create a separate hemp-driving offence, and it does not exempt a programme patient.
  • Act 662 repeal — what was actually repealed, and a secondary-source conflict to flag: Acts 2024, No. 662, §3 repealed §98(A)(1)(d) and (e). The HB 776 digest for Act 662 describes (d) as the combination-of-alcohol-and-legally-obtainable-non-CDS-drugs element and (e) as the legally-obtainable-drug-in-excess-of-dosage element, with an affirmative-defence deletion. Source: https://billcam.com/bill-texts/hcsAOHeSbC (Act 662 enrolled) — accessed 25 Oct 2026; digest via https://billcam.com/bill-texts/mLB88rQp71 — accessed 25 Oct 2026. CONFLICT / Verify: a secondary DWI guide (LegalClarity, accessed 25 Oct 2026) describes the 2024 amendment as repealing "provisions that made it a DWI to have any detectable amount of a Schedule I controlled substance in your blood". That description does not match the (d)/(e) elements described in the Act 662 digest, and the pre-2024 §98(A)(1)(c) text opened in Run 1 research was "under the influence of any controlled dangerous substance listed in Schedule I–V" — an influence standard, not a detectable-amount standard. Whether a detectable-amount prong existed in a different section (e.g. a prior §98.1/§98.2 penalty provision, or a pre-2020 version) was not resolved — [Verify] before repeating the "detectable amount repealed" claim. The safe, verified statement is only: current §98(A)(1) contains no THC per se or detectable-amount prong; the drug element is impairment.
  • No patient defence in §98. Nothing in §98(A) as opened exempts a §1046 patient, a §1046.1 visiting patient, or a person whose THC came from a lawful hemp product. A medical recommendation is not a defence to an impairment charge on the text opened. (Contrast §9:2798.4(D) below, which is a civil-liability shield, not a criminal defence.)
  • Child endangerment enhancement, §98(B): when the State proves, in addition to the §98(A) elements, that a minor child 12 years of age or younger was a passenger, the execution of the minimum mandatory sentence under §98.1/§98.2 (as appropriate) shall not be suspended (with the §98.3 imprisonment carve-out in (B)(2)(b)). Source: same legis.la.gov §98 page — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Penalty tiers for 1st/2nd/3rd/4th impaired-driving convictions (§§98.1–98.3) were not re-opened in this run — [Verify] before quoting a penalty range; Run 1 did not cover them either. Do not quote a DWI penalty tier from this file.
  • Separate vehicle-consumption offence (not an impairment offence). R.S. 32:300.4.1 (Act 478 of 2022, HB 234, eff. 1 Aug 2022; Run 1 §1.2):

    "A. It shall be unlawful for the operator or any passenger in a motor vehicle, while the motor vehicle is being operated on a public highway or right-of-way, to smoke or vape any form of marijuana as defined by R.S. 40:961, or a substance classified in Schedule I that is marijuana, tetrahydrocannabinol, or chemical derivatives thereof." "C. Whoever violates the provisions of this Section shall be fined one hundred dollars." "D." — secondary enforcement only; non-moving violation, not on the driver's operating record.

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-32/rs-32-300-4-1/ (Run 1) — accessed 25 Oct 2026 (Run 1); digest https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1292538.
  • Notes: (i) This bans smoking/vaping in the vehicle, for operator and passengers, even if no one is impaired — it is not a §98 impairment charge. (ii) It does not on its face ban eating an edible, taking a tincture, or using a topical in a vehicle, nor does it ban mere possession/transport in a vehicle — those are separate questions (possession lawfulness turns on patient/hemp/non-patient status). (iii) A parked vehicle not "being operated on a public highway or right-of-way" is outside (A) on its face — [Verify] case-law application to parked/ignition-off vehicles before advising on it.

12.3.2 Impairment testing — implied consent, chemical tests, and what a test does NOT prove

  • Implied consent, R.S. 32:661(A)(1) (via Justia 2025 text; legis.la.gov re-check recommended):

    "Any person, regardless of age, who operates a motor vehicle upon the public highways of this state shall be deemed to have given consent, subject to the provisions of R.S. 32:662, to a chemical test or tests of his blood, breath, urine, or other bodily substance for the purpose of determining the alcoholic content of his blood and the presence of any drug in his blood if arrested for any offense arising out of acts alleged to have been committed while the person was driving or in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while believed to be under the influence of alcoholic beverages, any drug, combination of drugs, or combination of alcohol and drugs."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-32/rs-32-661/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • The test or tests are administered at the direction of an officer having reasonable grounds to believe the person was driving/in actual physical control while under the influence; the employing agency designates in writing which tests are administered and under what conditions (§661(A)(2)).
  • Refusal / no-refusal cases, R.S. 32:666(A)(1)(a)(i), opened on legis.la.gov:

    "When a law enforcement officer has probable cause to believe that a person has violated R.S. 14:98, 98.6, or any other law or ordinance that prohibits operating a vehicle while intoxicated, that person may not refuse to submit to a chemical test or tests if he has refused to submit to such test or tests on two previous and separate occasions of any previous such violation or in any case wherein a fatality has occurred or a person has sustained serious bodily injury in a crash involving a motor vehicle, aircraft, watercraft, vessel, or other means of conveyance." "The law enforcement officer shall direct that a chemical test or tests be conducted of a person's blood, urine, or other bodily substance, or perform a chemical test of such person's breath, for the purpose of determining the alcoholic content of his blood and the presence of any drug, or combination of drugs, in his blood in such circumstances." "A refusal of any such test or tests shall result in the suspension of driving privileges as provided by the provisions of this Part."

  • Source: https://legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=88505 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • What this does not say: it does not set a THC cutoff for a blood/urine test, it does not state that a positive test alone proves impairment under §98(A)(1)(c), and it does not authorise a roadside saliva/oral-fluid THC test as a §98 element. Whether Louisiana uses Drug Recognition Experts (DREs), standardised field sobriety tests adapted for drugs, or a specific toxicology panel/cutoff for THC in impaired-driving cases was not located in a Louisiana statute, State Police protocol, or LDH rule in this run — [Verify / Unavailable]. Do not describe a Louisiana DRE protocol, oral-fluid device, or THC cutoff as law.
  • Evidence point to state carefully: a blood/urine result showing THC (or its metabolite, which can persist days–weeks after use) is evidence of presence, and the State must still prove impairment under current §98(A)(1)(c). How Louisiana courts weigh a positive test plus officer observation, driving behaviour, and admissions — and whether a metabolite-only result without active THC can support impairment — is case law that was not researched in this run — [Verify]. Do not state that "a positive test = a DWI conviction" or that "a metabolite-only test can never support a conviction".
  • Traffic fatalities — coroner toxicology. R.S. 32:661(A)(2)(b) (Justia text): in all traffic fatalities, the coroner or designee shall perform or cause a toxicology screen for alcohol and any drug/combination, including extracting all necessary bodily-substance samples. Source: same §661 page — accessed 25 Oct 2026. This is a fatality-screening duty, not a per se driving limit.
  • Civil-liability shield that is NOT a criminal defence — R.S. 9:2798.4. Neither the State, a State agency, a political subdivision, nor any person is liable for damages for injury/death/loss of an operator who was operating while under the influence of a controlled dangerous substance described in §98(A)(1)(c) or §40:964, provided the operator is found >25% negligent as a result of that influence and that negligence contributed to the damage (§2798.4(A)–(B)). But §2798.4(D) provides the section "shall not apply if the operator tests positive for any controlled dangerous substance … and the operator is taking that substance pursuant to a valid prescription for the identified substance or a health care provider verifies that he has prescribed or furnished the operator with that particular substance."
  • Source: https://codes.findlaw.com/la/revised-statutes/la-rev-stat-tit-9-sect-2798-4/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026 (FindLaw republication; legis.la.gov re-check recommended).
  • Critical caveat — do not over-read (D): (D) is about civil damages liability for the impaired operator's own injury/death/loss. It does not create a criminal defence to §98, it does not say a §1046 "recommendation" is a "prescription" for (D) purposes (Louisiana medical marijuana is recommended, not prescribed — Run 1 §1.4), and whether a clinician's verification satisfies (D) for a programme patient was not located in case law — [Verify]. State the (D) text, flag the recommendation-vs-prescription gap, and do not advise that a patient is civilly protected.
  • Commercial / safety-sensitive drivers, DOT, and federal testing: Louisiana's §98 applies to "any motor vehicle, aircraft, watercraft, vessel, or other means of conveyance" — it does not set a separate THC limit for commercial drivers. Federal DOT drug-testing rules for safety-sensitive transportation employees are federal law and are outside the given federal baseline; they were not re-researched — [Verify] if the parent wants a DOT paragraph. Do not state a DOT THC cutoff from this file.
  • Hemp-specific driving note: No Louisiana statute sets a driving limit for hemp-derived THC, CBD, delta-8, or any other hemp cannabinoid, and no statute exempts a driver because the THC came from a lawful hemp product. On the §98(A)(3) functional definition ("any substance … that … can impair"), a hemp product that impairs is within the drug-impairment wording on its face. Conversely, a hemp product that does not impair (e.g. a 0-THC CBD product) is not within (c) on its face. Both points are textual readings, not located prosecutions — [Verify].

12.4 Expungement and record clearing for marijuana offences

No automatic expungement. Louisiana expungement is petition-based: the person (or counsel) files a motion to expunge in the court with trial jurisdiction (district, city/parish, mayor's/traffic, juvenile/family, or New Orleans municipal/traffic court, per C.Cr.P. Art. 972.1, secondary summary — [Verify] current Art. 972.1 text). A secondary Jefferson Parish practice guide states flatly: "There is no automatic expungement in Louisiana" (Marino & Ehle, updated 30 July 2026, secondary). Source: https://jeffersontriallawyers.com/practice-areas/criminal-defense/expungements/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. - 2023 automated-process direction — not the same as automatic expungement, and its operational status is Verify. The Collateral Consequences Resource Center 50-state comparison (secondary, accessed 25 Oct 2026) states: "In 2023, the legislature directed development of an automated expungement process, requiring the BCII [Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information] to collect eligible records and provide individuals with a simplified internet filing process, with short timetables established by statute connecting the BCII and court record systems." Source: https://ccresourcecenter.org/state-restoration-profiles/50-state-comparisonjudicial-expungement-sealing-and-set-aside-2-2/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The underlying provision is C.Cr.P. Art. 985.2, which the 2023 Code text notes is "eff. upon appropriation of monies by the Legislature. See Acts 2023, No. 454." Whether Art. 985.2 has been funded and is operational as of 25 Oct 2026 was not located — [Verify / Unavailable]. Do not state that Louisiana now automatically expunges any record. - Effect of expungement (general). Under C.Cr.P. Arts. 972–973 (secondary summary, National Reentry Resource Center): the record is confidential and no longer public, but expungement does not limit the news media's use of the expunged record; it is made available only to persons/entities specified in Art. 973; the person is not required to disclose the arrest or expungement. Source: https://nationalreentryresourcecenter.org/cleanslate/states/louisiana/policies/la-c-2 — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Expunged records may still be accessed by law enforcement and certain licensing agencies and may serve as predicates in the Resource Center's summary — [Verify] Arts. 972–973 text before publishing an "effect" paragraph.

12.4.1 The marijuana-specific fast track — C.Cr.P. Art. 977(D) (90 days) and its fee paragraph's 1 Aug 2026 termination — READ THE SUNSET CAREFULLY

  • Eligibility text, C.Cr.P. Art. 977(D) (Justia 2025 text):

    "D. Notwithstanding any provision of law to the contrary, a person may file a motion to expunge his record of arrest and conviction of a misdemeanor conviction for a first offense possession of marijuana, tetrahydrocannabinol, or chemical derivatives thereof after ninety days from the date of conviction."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/code-of-criminal-procedure/article-977/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • History: added effective 1 Aug 2023 (Acts 2023, No. 342, per the Art. 983 history line; secondary Gilmer & Giglio blog, 18 Dec 2023, confirms the 1 Aug 2023 start). It displaces, for this one category, the ordinary misdemeanour routes in Art. 977(A): (1) conviction set aside + prosecution dismissed under Art. 894(B) (immediate), or (2) >5 years since completion of sentence/deferred adjudication/probation/parole, with no felony conviction during the 5-year period and no pending felony charge (with district-attorney certification). The 90-day route requires neither a set-aside nor 5 years.
  • Fee paragraph, C.Cr.P. Art. 983(M)(1) (Justia 2023 text; LawServer text agrees):

    "M.(1) Notwithstanding Paragraph B of this Article, the total cost to obtain a court order expunging a record of a misdemeanor conviction for a first offense possession of marijuana, tetrahydrocannabinol, or chemical derivatives thereof shall not exceed three hundred dollars. The nonrefundable processing fees for a court order expunging such record shall be as follows: (a) The Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information may charge a processing fee of fifty dollars … (b) The sheriff may charge a processing fee of fifty dollars … (c) The district attorney may charge a processing fee of fifty dollars … (d) The clerk of court may charge a processing fee of one hundred fifty dollars to cover the clerk's costs of the expungement."

  • Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2023/code-of-criminal-procedure/article-983/ ; https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/louisiana/la-codes/louisiana_code_of_criminal_procedure_983 — both accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • General expungement fees for comparison: up to $550 (Art. 983(B)), plus $50 for operating-while-impaired petitions (Art. 984) — secondary, National Reentry Resource Center, same link as above. In forma pauperis is available under Art. 983(L) (Code of Civil Procedure Art. 5181 et seq.) except as provided in Art. 983(F)–(G).
  • The sunset — what actually terminates on 1 Aug 2026, and what is Verify:

    "M.(5) The provisions of this Paragraph shall be null, void, and without effect and shall terminate on August 1, 2026."

  • Source: same Art. 983 pages — accessed 25 Oct 2026. History line: Acts 2023, No. 342, §1 (plus Acts 2024, No. 270, §1 on the LawServer text).
  • Analysis, flagged as analysis + Verify, NOT settled law: On its face, (M)(5) terminates Paragraph (M) — the fee paragraph — not Article 977(D) itself. Article 977(D) as printed in the 2025 Justia text contains no sunset. A secondary firm blog (Gilmer & Giglio, 18 Dec 2023) states the broader proposition: "This special provision will cease to be available to citizens of Louisiana on August 1, 2026. La CCrP Art. 983(M)(5)." Source: https://gilmergiglio.com/blog/expungement-of-marijuana-convictions — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Those two readings conflict in effect: (a) narrow reading — after 1 Aug 2026 the 90-day eligibility in 977(D) survives but the $300 fee cap falls away and the general fee applies; (b) broad secondary reading — the whole 90-day route ends 1 Aug 2026. As of 25 Oct 2026 — i.e. AFTER 1 Aug 2026 — which reading governs, and whether the 2026 Legislature extended (M) or (D), was NOT confirmed on legis.la.gov in this run — [Verify — URGENT for publication]. Do not publish either "the 90-day route is gone" or "the 90-day route survives at the general fee" without opening the current legis.la.gov texts of Arts. 977 and 983 and checking for a 2026 extension Act. This is the single most time-sensitive Verify item in Part 12.
  • If the narrow reading is correct, a first-offense misdemeanour marijuana possessor filing after 1 Aug 2026 would still file after 90 days under 977(D) but pay the general fee (up to $550, subject to in forma pauperis). If the broad reading is correct, that person falls back to Art. 977(A) (set-aside under 894(B), or 5 years). The parent must not pick one without the legis.la.gov check.

12.4.2 General routes for other marijuana records

  • Arrests without conviction — C.Cr.P. Art. 976 (secondary summary, Ikerd Law Firm, updated within 20 days before access): a motion to expunge an arrest record (felony or misdemeanour) that did not result in conviction if: not prosecuted and limitations expired; district attorney declined (including successful pretrial diversion); prosecution disposed by dismissal, motion to quash sustained, or acquittal; or judicial determination of factual innocence. Source: https://www.ikerdlaw.com/expungement-process-louisiana/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. [Verify] Art. 976 text (including the DUI/diversion 5-year carve-out noted in secondary summaries) before quoting.
  • Misdemeanour convictions generally — Art. 977(A)–(C): set-aside/dismissal under Art. 894(B), or >5 years since completion with no felony conviction in the period and no pending felony charge (DA certification required). Excluded from misdemeanour expungement: sex offences as defined in R.S. 15:541 (interim expungement under Art. 985.1 excepted), domestic abuse battery, and stalking (R.S. 14:40.2) — Art. 977(C). Source: same Art. 977 Justia page — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Felony convictions generally — C.Cr.P. Art. 978 (secondary summaries, consistent across Ikerd, National Reentry Resource Center, and the Resource Center comparison): (i) conviction set aside + prosecution dismissed under Art. 893(E) (deferred adjudication — immediate eligibility on successful completion, by motion; not automatic); (ii) entitlement to a first-offender pardon under La. Const. Art. IV, §5(E)(1) (except crimes of violence and sex offences); or (iii) >10 years since completion of sentence/deferred adjudication/probation/parole, with no other criminal convictions during the period and no pending charges (DA certification). Felony expungement only once every 15 years (deferred-adjudication cases excepted); misdemeanour expungement only once every 5 years (DUI 10 years) — Resource Center comparison, same link as above. [Verify] Art. 978 text, including (B) ineligibility and (E) violent-crime exceptions, before quoting a felony route.
  • What is ineligible — distribution/manufacturing. Under Art. 978(B) (secondary summaries): distribution, dispensing, or manufacturing of a controlled dangerous substance is ineligible except: (a) simple possession; (b) possession with intent to distribute where possible imprisonment is <5 years; (c) violations sentenced under Art. 893; or (d) violations eligible for a first-offender pardon. Source: Ikerd summary, same link as above. Practical consequence: a felony marijuana distribution conviction (R.S. 40:966(B)(2): <2.5 lb = 1–10 years; ≥2.5 lb = 1–20 years hard labour — Run 1) is not expungeable on the ordinary 10-year route unless it falls within one of those four exceptions. A simple-possession felony (e.g. a 3rd+ >14 g possession conviction, ≤2 years — Run 1) is in the "simple possession" exception on the secondary summaries' reading — [Verify] Art. 978(B) text.
  • Paraphernalia records — no marijuana-specific fast track located. A marijuana-paraphernalia conviction under §1025(E) is a misdemeanour-level fine-only conviction, but no provision equivalent to Art. 977(D) for paraphernalia was located. It would fall under the general Art. 977 routes (894(B) set-aside, or 5 years) on the structure of the Code — that application was not located in a source — [Verify]. Do not state a 90-day paraphernalia expungement.
  • Hemp records: No hemp-specific expungement provision was located. A consumable-hemp offence under §§93.16/93.17 (2025) would fall under the general misdemeanour/felony routes according to its classification — [Verify] classification and Art. 977/978 application for §§93.16/93.17 specifically. A §93.17 under-21 citation is expressly not on the criminal history record (§93.17(B)(2), §12.2), so there is ordinarily nothing to expunge for that citation — stated as a consequence of the statute's own text.
  • Predicate / washout interaction (possession, not expungement): Separately from expungement, R.S. 40:966(C)(2)(c) provides a person sentenced under (a) (≤14 g) or (b) (>14 g, 1st) with no further marijuana-possession conviction for 2 years from completion of sentence/probation/parole/suspension "shall not have the conviction used as a predicate conviction for enhancement purposes", once per person (Run 1 §1.3.1). That is a predicate-use washout, not an expungement, and it does not clear the record.

12.4.3 Pardons — including the vetoed expedited-pardon bill

  • First-offender pardon (general). La. Const. Art. IV, §5(E)(1) first-offender pardons entitle the holder to immediate felony-expungement eligibility (Art. 978, secondary summaries above), except for crimes of violence and sex offences. A person granted a (non-first-offender) pardon is exempt from expungement processing fees under Art. 983(J); a first-offender pardon holder is not exempt from those fees (Art. 983(J), second sentence, via LawServer text). Source: same Art. 983 page — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • HB 391 (2024) — VETOED, not law (Run 1 anchor confirmed). HB 391 (Boyd) would have added R.S. 15:572.2: a person convicted of first-offense possession of marijuana/THC/derivatives under §966(C)(2)(a) (and, in the reengrossed version, (b)) would be eligible for a Governor's pardon without completion of sentence and without a Board of Pardons recommendation, on payment of all court costs, with a Division of Probation and Parole certificate of full pardon. Source (reengrossed text): https://legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1364658 — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Governor Landry vetoed HB 391 in June 2024 (NORML, 24 June 2024, secondary, same link as §12.1.3). Therefore: there is NO expedited / automatic pardon for first-time marijuana possession in Louisiana law as of 25 Oct 2026. Any secondary article describing HB 391 as enacted (e.g. a May 2024 article headlined "Legislature Approves Bill Allowing Automatic Pardons") describes legislative passage, not enactment — do not cite it as law.
  • No marijuana-specific pardon, clemency, or "clean slate" programme beyond the general pardon + expungement routes above was located in official sources. In particular, no Louisiana analogue to another state's mass pardon for past marijuana possession was located — [Verify] by a Governor / Board of Pardons search if the parent wants an absolute statement.

12.5 Consumption rules

12.5.1 There is no general "private use only" statute — the bans are place- and form-specific

Run 1 §1.3.4 found no general public-consumption statute. That finding stands, with the following place/form bans now pinned down. Do not invent a blanket "you may only consume at home" rule, and do not import another state's public-consumption offence.

Place / form Rule Who it reaches
Vehicle operated on a public highway/right-of-way — smoking/vaping marijuana Banned, $100, secondary enforcement, non-moving, not on driving record — §32:300.4.1 (§12.3.1) Operator AND passengers
Elementary/secondary school property — smoking/vaping marijuana Banned for "any person", punishment via §981.3(A)(1) — §17:240(B)(2)(b), (C)(2)(b) (§12.10) Any person, including patients, visitors, employees, spectators
School property / within 2,000 ft / school bus — violating the Uniform CDS Law (including possession) Enhanced punishment — §981.3(A)(1), as amended by Act 305 of 2026 for marijuana (§12.10) Any person who commits the underlying violation in the zone
Public building, school, public place, enclosed workplace — "smoking" Banned — Smoke-Free Air Act, §1291.11(A) (see §12.5.2) Any person (subject to §1291.11(B) exemptions)
Healthcare facility — terminally ill patient use Permitted (non-smoking/non-vaping forms on the secondary summaries; facility must permit, with documentation + locked-container storage) — new §1046.5, Act 602 of 2026, eff. 1 Aug 2026 (§12.5.3) Terminally ill §1046 patient (or caregiver administering) only; emergency department / emergency services excluded
Private home / private residence / private automobile (not used for child/day care, not public transport of children) Exempt from the Smoke-Free Air Act ban — §1291.11(B)(1) Any person, subject to lease, drug-free-zone (if within 2,000 ft of school property — see §12.10 warning), and criminal possession law
Bar; retail tobacco business; hotel/motel designated smoking room (≤50% of rooms); outdoor area of a place of employment (unless posted no-smoking); limousine under private hire; private/semiprivate assisted-living/long-term-care room where all occupants are smokers who requested it in writing and smoke does not infiltrate prohibited areas Exempt from the Smoke-Free Air Act ban — §1291.11(B)(2)–(7) As stated in each exemption; none of these exemptions authorises marijuana use that is otherwise unlawful (e.g. non-patient possession remains unlawful even in a bar)

12.5.2 The Smoke-Free Air Act — it reaches marijuana smoke by its "combustible plant material" wording, but not vaping on its face

  • Definition, R.S. 40:1291.3(14) (legis.la.gov LawPrint, search text):

    "'Smoking' means inhaling, exhaling, burning, carrying, or possessing any lighted tobacco product, including cigarettes, cigars, pipe tobacco, and any other lighted combustible plant material."

  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=964961 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Consequence: marijuana flower burned in a cigarette/pipe/joint is "any other lighted combustible plant material" and therefore "smoking" under the Act, even though the Act's purpose section (§1291.2) speaks of "tobacco smoke" and its "secondhand smoke" definition (§1291.3(13)) speaks of tobacco. The Act's operative ban (§1291.11(A), below) uses "smoke", which is defined by (14) — so the tobacco-only purpose language does not on its face exclude marijuana smoke. That is a textual reading; no Louisiana case applying §1291.11 to marijuana smoke was located — [Verify].
  • Ban, R.S. 40:1291.11(A) (legis.la.gov LawPrint):

    "A. Except as permitted by Subsection B of this Section, no person shall: (1) Smoke in any public building. (2) Smoke in any school. (3) Smoke in any public place and in any enclosed area within a place of employment. (4) Smoke in any outdoor area proximate to a state office building where smoking is prohibited pursuant to the provisions of R.S. 40:1293.3. (5) As an employer, knowingly permit smoking in any enclosed area within a place of employment."

  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=964962 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • "Public place" (§1291.3(9)) includes educational facilities, healthcare facilities, hotel/motel lobbies, restaurants, retail stores, shopping malls, sports arenas, theatres, and waiting rooms, among others. "School" (§1291.3(12)) means any elementary/secondary school building, campus, buildings on campus, and school buses — narrower than §981.3's "school" (which includes colleges/universities, §12.10).
  • Vaping gap — state Act vs local ordinances: "Smoking" in §1291.3(14) requires a lighted product. A vapour product / THC vape pen is not lighted on its face, so the State Smoke-Free Air Act ban does not on its face reach vaping. Secondary summaries (LegalClarity, Louisiana smoking laws, accessed 25 Oct 2026) state local ordinances in New Orleans and Baton Rouge "go considerably further, covering vaping and eliminating many of the state-level exemptions". Source: https://legalclarity.org/louisiana-smoking-laws-public-and-workplace-restrictions/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Local vaping bans were not verified ordinance-by-ordinance in this run — [Verify] for any specific parish/municipality. Do not state that "vaping marijuana in public is banned statewide" — statewide, the bans that reach vaping are the vehicle ban (§32:300.4.1, which expressly says "smoke or vape"), the school ban (§17:240(B)(2)(b), "smoke or vape"), and the school-zone smoking/vaping paragraph (§981.3(A)(4), as added by Act 305 — see §12.10), not the Smoke-Free Air Act.
  • Non-smoked consumption in public: Eating an edible, taking a tincture/capsule, or applying a topical in a public place is not "smoking" under §1291.3(14) and is not banned by the Smoke-Free Air Act on its face. Whether it is banned elsewhere depends on possession lawfulness (patient vs hemp vs non-patient) and on the place (school property, vehicle, workplace policy, lease). No Louisiana statute banning all public consumption of edibles/tinctures by patients was located — law is silent on that specific point; do not fill it in.
  • Workplaces: §1291.11(A)(5) makes it unlawful for an employer to knowingly permit smoking in an enclosed workplace area. Combined with Run 1 §1.9 (state-employer drug-test protection, §49:1016, which does not protect on-premises/during-hours use or impairment), the workplace picture is: no statute requires a private employer to permit on-premises medical use, and the Smoke-Free Air Act affirmatively bars the employer from permitting smoking in an enclosed workplace. Private-employer accommodation beyond §49:1016 (which covers state employers only) was not located — law silent; do not fill in (see also §12.7 on housing — the same silence applies to employment accommodation generally).

12.5.3 Healthcare facilities — new §1046.5 (Act 602, SB 270, 2026) — Run 1 conflict RESOLVED

Run 1 §1.10 left SB 270's status and effective date as a conflict (engrossed digest: 1 Aug 2026; secondary: "became law without signature / effective 1 June 2026"; no Act number). It is now resolved on the official digest:

  • Act 602 (SB 270), 2026 Regular Session (Jackson-Andrews), effective 1 August 2026. Adds R.S. 40:1046.5. Résumé Digest: "ACT 602 (SB 270) 2026 Regular Session Jackson-Andrews … New law requires healthcare facilities to permit a terminally ill patient to use medical marijuana that has been recommended to the patient pursuant to existing law. New law requires the facility to take certain measures to document the patient's medical marijuana use and ensure proper storage of the medical marijuana. New law does not apply to a patient receiving emergency services or care or to the emergency department of a healthcare facility. New law provides that a healthcare facility is not required to provide a patient with a medical marijuana recommendation or to include medical marijuana in a patient's discharge plan. New law provides that compliance with new law shall not be a condition for obtaining, retaining, or renewing a healthcare facility license. New law authorizes all healthcare facilities to suspend compliance … if a federal regulatory agency, the U.S. Department of Justice, or [CMS] initiates an enforcement action against any healthcare agency or issues a rule or notification … that prohibits compliance with new law. New law provides that a healthcare facility shall not prohibit a terminally ill patient's use of medical marijuana due solely to the fact that marijuana is a Schedule I drug. Effective August 1, 2026. (Adds R.S. 40:1046.5)"
  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1482497 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • What the secondary "1 June 2026" date was: Marijuana Moment (secondary, dated, accessed 25 Oct 2026) reports Governor Landry "allowed the reform to be enacted without his signature on Monday" (the article's Monday, in context June 2026) and that hospitals "will have to create written guidelines allowing covered patients to consume medical cannabis on-site in forms other than smoking or vaping", that "patients and primary caregivers are responsible for acquiring and administering" it, that it "must be stored securely at all times in a locked container provided by the patient", that staff are prohibited from "administering, storing, retrieving, or assisting", and that emergency/outpatient departments are exempted. Source: https://www.marijuanamoment.net/louisiana-will-let-terminally-ill-patients-use-medical-marijuana-in-hospitals-after-governor-allows-bill-to-take-effect-without-his-signature/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Resolution: the June date is the gubernatorial-inaction / enactment date; the effective date is 1 Aug 2026 per the official digest. The Run 1 conflict is therefore resolved in favour of the digest's 1 Aug 2026 effective date. The enrolled text's full §1046.5 (including the "terminally ill" definition, the non-smoking/non-vaping form limitation, and the locked-container/storage/documentation duties) was not opened line-by-line in this run — the enrolled bill is at https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1480182 — [Verify] the enrolled text before quoting §1046.5 verbatim or stating its form limitation as statute text (the form limitation above is secondary-summary only).
  • Scope limits to state plainly: §1046.5 covers terminally ill patients in healthcare facilities — it does not cover schools (§12.10), workplaces, prisons/jails, or the general public, and it does not require a facility to supply marijuana, recommend it, or include it in a discharge plan. A facility may suspend compliance on a federal enforcement action/rule/notification as described. Whether LDH has issued facility guidelines or a rule under §1046.5 as of 25 Oct 2026 was not located — [Verify].

12.5.4 Consumption that the law does not address (silence list for this section)

  • No Louisiana statute was located that: (a) authorises or bans a marijuana "consumption lounge" / on-site consumption at a retailer; (b) bans or permits smoking marijuana on a private balcony/patio as distinct from a private home (lease/HOA rules govern — see §12.7); (c) bans a patient from using a non-smoked form in a public place (see §12.5.2); (d) addresses consumption in a hotel/motel room that is not designated as a smoking room (the Smoke-Free Air Act exemption is only for a designated smoking room, ≤50% of rooms — a non-designated room is within the public-place/enclosed-area analysis, [Verify] hotel-specific application); or (e) addresses consumption by a visiting patient differently from a resident patient (same place/form bans apply on the text opened).

12.6 Visitor and out-of-state patient rules

12.6.1 Run 1 visiting-patient summary — CONFIRMED, with two updates that resolve Run 1 Verify flags

Run 1 §1.4.6 stated: visiting patients under R.S. 40:1046.1 need another jurisdiction's registry card/equivalent + an LDH-approved certification form. That core is confirmed on the current legis.la.gov text opened in this run. Two Run 1 Verify flags are resolved:

  1. PMP vs LMMTS — resolved in favour of LMMTS. The 2022 Justia text used "board" and "prescription monitoring program". The current legis.la.gov text (below) uses "department" (LDH) and "LMMTS" throughout, as amended by Act 693 of 2024, eff. 1 Jan 2025. The pharmacist duties survive, but they are now LMMTS duties, performed by "a pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee" — not PMP duties.
  2. Act/date — confirmed. Acts 2022, No. 438, §1; Acts 2024, No. 693, §1, eff. Jan. 1, 2025 (history line on the legis.la.gov page).

12.6.2 Current statute — R.S. 40:1046.1, opened on legis.la.gov

  • Definition, §1046.1(A)(5):

    "'Visiting qualifying patient' means a patient with a debilitating medical condition who is not a resident of Louisiana or who has been a resident of Louisiana for less than thirty days and who is in actual possession of a valid medical marijuana registry identification card, or its equivalent, which has been issued under the medical marijuana laws of another state, district, territory, commonwealth, or insular possession of the United States."

  • Purchase right, §1046.1(B):

    "A visiting qualifying patient may obtain medical marijuana from a marijuana retail permit holder upon producing evidence of his valid medical marijuana registry identification card, or its equivalent, which has been issued under the medical marijuana laws of another state, district, territory, commonwealth, or insular possession of the United States."

  • Certification form, §1046.1(C)(1):

    "A marijuana retail permit holder shall require each visiting qualifying patient to certify on a form approved by the department that the patient has been diagnosed by an authorized clinician with one or more debilitating medical conditions. The form shall include the full name, address, and phone number of the visiting qualifying patient and shall include a statement to be signed by the patient by which the patient shall attest that the patient will not divert to any person any medical marijuana sold to him by the marijuana retail permit holder."

  • Documents retained, §1046.1(C)(2)(a): the retailer "shall retain a copy of each of the following documents received from a visiting qualifying patient: (i) The patient's valid medical marijuana registry identification card or its equivalent. (ii) The patient's valid driver's license or other government-issued photo identification document. (iii) The original, completed, and signed form provided for in Paragraph (1) of this Subsection." LDH "shall promulgate … a record retention schedule" for those documents (§1046.1(C)(2)(b)).
  • Retention period (LDH rule summary, official LDH Notice of Intent PDF): "A retailer shall retain all documents required by R.S. 40:1046.1(C)(2) for at least three years." Source: https://ldh.la.gov/assets/oph/Center-EH/sanitarian/fooddrug/marijuana/MedicalMarijuanaNoI.Published.5.20.25.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026 (LDH Notice of Intent, published 20 May 2025). [Verify] whether the January 2026 Final Rule retains the 3-year period verbatim.
  • LMMTS review and reporting, §1046.1(D)–(E):

    "D. Prior to dispensing any medical marijuana product to a visiting qualifying patient, a pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee at a marijuana retail location shall review the patient's records in the LMMTS. The pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall resolve any concerns identified in the review of the patient's records by consultation with the patient's physician." "E. Upon sale of any medical marijuana product to a visiting qualifying patient, the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee at a marijuana retail location shall report that transaction to the LMMTS."

  • Mandatory refusal, §1046.1(F): "No marijuana retail permit holder shall sell medical marijuana to a person who holds himself out to be a visiting qualifying patient if the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee at the retail location determines any of the following with respect to that person: (1) The person's medical marijuana registry identification card was revoked, has expired, or is otherwise not valid and current. (2) The person's medical marijuana registry identification card was fraudulently obtained. (3) The person's application or written certifications were falsified in any way. (4) The person knowingly violated any law of this state applicable to medical marijuana."
  • Source for all §1046.1 quotes above: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=1295726 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Other definitions in §1046.1(A): "Debilitating medical condition" has the §1046(A)(2)(a) meaning; "Department" means LDH; "LMMTS" means "the electronic seed-to-sale tracking system approved by the department"; "Medical marijuana" means marijuana for therapeutic use produced pursuant to §1046(H) (i.e. by the two Louisiana licensees — a visiting patient cannot bring in out-of-state product for sale, and a retailer cannot sell out-of-state product to a visitor).

12.6.3 Practical points, limits, and what is NOT reciprocity

  • "In actual possession" matters. The definition requires the visitor to be "in actual possession of" the card/equivalent at the time — a photograph, a lapsed card, a doctor's letter that is not the jurisdiction's card/equivalent, or a Louisiana clinician's recommendation alone does not satisfy (B) on the text opened. Whether a digital card image counts as "actual possession" / "producing evidence" was not located in LDH guidance — [Verify].
  • The 30-day edge. A person who "has been a resident of Louisiana for less than thirty days" and holds another jurisdiction's card qualifies as a visiting patient. On the text's face, on day 30 of Louisiana residency that status ends, and the person needs a Louisiana authorised-clinician recommendation to continue buying. No grace period or transition rule was located — [Verify] LDH guidance on the 30-day count (calendar days, proof of residency start date).
  • No Louisiana card is issued to a visitor. The visitor's home-jurisdiction card is the credential; Louisiana does not issue a temporary Louisiana card on the text opened. The retailer form (secondary example, The Apothecary Shoppe visiting-patient form, accessed 25 Oct 2026) collects name/address/phone/DOB, under-18/disability flags, the attestation (diagnosed by a licensed physician + active valid home card + non-diversion), ICD-10/description of the debilitating condition, treatment requested, and provider/NPI/registry-ID/expiration information, and notes it "contains the basic data elements defined by the Act No. 438". Source (secondary form): https://theapothecaryshoppe.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Visiting-Patient-Form.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026. That form is a retailer's form, not the LDH-approved form itself — [Verify] the current LDH-approved form before reproducing it.
  • Limits that apply to visitors — partially Verify. The 71 g/14-day flower cap in §1046(A)(5)(a) says "to any individual patient" — on its face it includes a visiting patient, and LMMTS reporting (E) is the mechanism that would enforce it. Whether LDH rules state the cap expressly for visitors, and whether a visitor's home-jurisdiction purchase limit or recommendation amount is also honoured, was not located — [Verify].
  • What is NOT reciprocity: (i) Louisiana does not recognise another state's card as a Louisiana recommendation for any purpose other than a §1046.1 retail sale (e.g. it does not confer Louisiana employment protection under §49:1016, which requires a §1046 recommendation — textual reading, [Verify]); (ii) a Louisiana recommendation does not entitle the holder to buy in another state — that depends on the other state's law; (iii) transport across state lines remains unlawful federally and under §1046(C)(2)(c) (no recommended marijuana "sold from, produced from, obtained from, sold to, or transferred to a location outside of this state" — Run 1 §1.1). A visitor who buys in Louisiana and carries it home across a state line is outside Louisiana's protection, even if the home state would have allowed the purchase. Retailers "may not deliver to addresses located outside of the state of Louisiana" (LDH page, https://www.ldh.la.gov/bureau-of-sanitarian-services/medical-marijuana — accessed 25 Oct 2026), and the LDH retailer rule summary adds: "As long as no marijuana product is provided to an out-of-state address, retailer staff may provide marijuana products to a visiting qualifying patient in compliance with … R.S. 40:1046.1" (LDH Notice of Intent PDF, same link as above).
  • Immunity: A "visiting qualifying patient as defined in R.S. 40:1046.1" is expressly within the §966(F)(1) immunity (Run 1 §1.4.7), subject to the same diversion / out-of-scope carve-out. The §966(F) "condition enumerated therein" vs §1046(A)(2)(a)(xxii) catch-all tension flagged in Run 1 applies to visitors too — [Verify] (Run 1 Gap 12, carried forward).
  • Hemp visitors — no visitor rule needed. Consumable hemp is sold to any person 21+ with ID verification (§12.2); there is no residency, registry-card, or visiting-patient procedure for hemp. A non-resident buys hemp on the same terms as a resident. Conversely, a non-resident's home-state medical card does not authorise a hemp purchase by a person under 21 in Louisiana (§93.17 has no medical exception on its face).
  • Out-of-state patients who are NOT visiting qualifying patients: A person with no home-jurisdiction card, or with an expired/revoked/fraudulent card, or who has knowingly violated Louisiana medical-marijuana law, must not be sold to under §1046.1(F). Their only Louisiana route is to become a Louisiana patient via a Louisiana authorised clinician (and, if they have been a Louisiana resident ≥30 days, that is their only route on the text). No "temporary" or "emergency" Louisiana recommendation procedure for visitors was located — law silent; do not fill in.

12.7 Landlord and tenant rules

Headline: Louisiana has no cannabis-specific landlord/tenant statute protecting a tenant's medical use, and no statute banning a landlord from prohibiting smoking. The rules that decide a dispute are (a) the lease, (b) the general Civil Code lease articles, (c) the general eviction procedure, and (d) — for federally assisted housing only — federal law and the public-housing-authority statute. Each is addressed separately; do not blend them.

12.7.1 Private (non-assisted) tenancies — the lease governs, and misuse can dissolve it

  • No tenant protection located. No provision in R.S. 40:1046, Title 3 Part VI, or the Civil Code lease articles (Title IX) was located that: requires a landlord to permit medical-marijuana use or smoking in rented premises; treats medical-marijuana status as a protected class for housing; prohibits a landlord from asking about, testing for, or refusing a tenancy because of marijuana use; or requires a "reasonable accommodation" for a patient's smoking (as distinct from a disability-accommodation analysis under federal/state fair-housing law, which was not researched — [Verify] before advising on disability accommodation for non-smoked forms). Law silent on tenant protection; do not fill in. A patient who needs to use at home should assume a lease smoking ban, if present, is enforceable as a contract term unless a court holds otherwise on disability-accommodation grounds — that holding was not located.
  • Misuse of the thing — La. Civil Code Art. 2686 (Acts 2004, No. 821, eff. 1 Jan 2005):

    "If the lessee uses the thing for a purpose other than that for which it was leased or in a manner that may cause damage to the thing, the lessor may obtain injunctive relief, dissolution of the lease, and any damages he may have sustained."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2023/civil-code/article-2686/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Correction to a secondary citation: a secondary landlord/tenant guide (Generis, accessed 25 Oct 2026) cites "Louisiana Civil Code Article 2716" for eviction for illegal/drug use. That citation is wrong under the current Code: Art. 2716 now provides "A lease granted by a usufructuary terminates upon the termination of the usufruct" (Acts 2004, No. 821). The misuse provision is Art. 2686, quoted above. Source for the Art. 2716 text: https://lcco.law.lsu.edu/?uid=105&ver=enfr (LSU Civil Code) — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Do not cite Art. 2716 for drug-use eviction.
  • Application — stated as application, not as a located holding: (i) Using rented premises to cultivate marijuana (which is unlawful for any non-licensee, Run 1 §1.3.2) is both a use "for a purpose other than that for which it was leased" (a residence is not leased as a cultivation facility) and a use "in a manner that may cause damage" (electrical, moisture, odour, fire risk) — a lessor's Art. 2686 claim is at its strongest there. (ii) Smoking in breach of an express lease no-smoking clause is a breach of the lease's agreed use; whether smoking without an express ban, by a lawful patient, in a way that causes smoke damage/odour complaints, amounts to Art. 2686 misuse is for the court on the circumstances — the 2004 Revision Comments to Art. 2686 state relief "is left to the discretion of the court upon proper weighing of all the circumstances", and the court "may decide to grant none, one, any two, or all three" of injunction, dissolution, and damages. Source: legis.la.gov HB 38 enrolled, Revision Comments, https://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=272863 — accessed 25 Oct 2026. No Louisiana case holding that lawful patient smoking alone, without a lease ban or damage, dissolves a lease was located — [Verify].
  • What Art. 2686 is not: it is not a self-help eviction right. Dissolution is obtained from a court; the eviction procedure (Code of Civil Procedure Arts. 4701 et seq., notice to vacate + rule for possession) still applies. The notice period for a private tenancy depends on the lease term and the ground (non-payment vs other violation) — specific notice periods were not re-verified in this run — [Verify] before quoting a "5-day" or other figure (the 5-day figure in secondary public-housing summaries, §12.7.2, is a public-housing figure, not a general private-lease figure).
  • Lease terms that matter in practice (contract, not statute): no-smoking clauses (including whether they say "tobacco", "smoking", or "marijuana" — a tobacco-only clause's application to marijuana smoke is a contract-interpretation question, [Verify] case law); drug/criminal-activity clauses; cleaning / smoke-damage / odour-remediation charges; guest/visitor clauses (relevant if a caregiver visits to administer); and "illegal activity" clauses (relevant because non-patient possession and home cultivation remain unlawful, while programme-patient possession is lawful under §966(F) — an "illegal activity" clause does not on its face reach lawful programme use, but whether a landlord may treat federally-illegal-but-state-lawful use as "illegal" under a lease clause was not located — [Verify]).
  • Security deposits / damages: No cannabis-specific deposit or cleaning-fee statute was located. Smoke damage, if proved, falls under general damages / deposit-deduction rules — [Verify] parish/municipal deposit rules if the parent wants a deposits paragraph. Do not state a cannabis cleaning fee.
  • Discrimination / screening: No Louisiana statute was located that prohibits a landlord from screening on the basis of a prior marijuana conviction (as distinct from a general criminal-history screening rule), or that requires a landlord to disregard an expunged marijuana record.
