Federal/state fair-housing criminal-history guidance (HUD 2016/2022 guidance, noted in the Loyola manual summary below) addresses admissions policies that exclude people with criminal records generally — its application to a private landlord's marijuana-conviction screen was not verified — [Verify].

12.7.2 Public housing and federally assisted housing — a different, federal regime

  • Louisiana public-housing-authority statute — R.S. 40:506(B) (LawServer republication; legis.la.gov re-check recommended):

    "B. Without limiting the foregoing, a local housing authority may terminate the tenancy of a household or a resident or terminate any other assistance provided by the authority for either: (1) Any unlawful drug-related activity or other criminal behavior on the part of a recipient or head of household or any member of the household, including any child who is a member thereof, or on the part of any guest or invitee of a member of the household, notwithstanding that the head of household or any other member of the household either: (a) Was unaware of the misconduct constituting the ground for termination of tenancy. (b) Did not approve or participate in such misconduct. (c) Was not personally at fault in connection with such misconduct."

  • Source: https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/louisiana/la-laws/louisiana_revised_statutes_40-506 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Notes: (i) This is a public-housing-authority power, not a private-landlord power. (ii) "Unlawful drug-related activity" — programme-patient use that is lawful under Louisiana §966(F) is not "unlawful" under Louisiana law on its face, but federally assisted housing treats marijuana as unlawful federally (see below) — the interaction between §40:506(B)'s "unlawful" and federal illegality was not located in a Louisiana case — [Verify]. (iii) The "notwithstanding unaware / did not approve / not at fault" language mirrors the federal "one-strike" structure upheld in Dept. of Housing and Urban Development v. Rucker (U.S. Supreme Court, 2002) for drug-related criminal activity by a household member or guest — that case is about the federal statute (42 U.S.C. §1437d(l)(6)), not §40:506 itself.
  • Federal rule — admission vs current tenants (the distinction that decides most cases). Under the Quality Housing and Work Responsibility Act framework (secondary ABA explainer, American Bar Association, Affordable Housing Journal, accessed 25 Oct 2026):
  • Applicants: a public housing agency (PHA) or owner of federally assisted housing must establish standards that prohibit admission for a household with a member who is illegally using a controlled substance, or where there is reasonable cause to believe a pattern of illegal use/abuse may interfere with other residents' health, safety, or peaceful enjoyment. HUD has concluded PHAs/owners "are required by [law] to deny admission" to applicants using medical marijuana, because federal law treats that use as illegal. Source: https://www.americanbar.org/groups/affordable_housing/resources/journal/31-2/challenges-guidance-medical-marijuana-patients-federally-assisted-housing/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026; corroborated by CRS Report R42394 (Congress.gov), https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R42394 — accessed 25 Oct 2026: "any individual whom the housing authority reasonably believes is using marijuana could be denied access to, or evicted from, federally assisted housing" and HUD's position is denial for applicants, discretion for current tenants.
  • Current tenants: the lease-termination language is discretionary — a PHA/owner may (is authorised to, not required to) terminate for drug-related criminal activity / illegal use. HUD guidance treats the determination as case-by-case, and "there may be no lease provision for a HUD assisted property that specifically permits the use of marijuana, including medically prescribed marijuana" (HUD memo summary, A.J. Johnson Consulting, secondary). Source: https://www.ajjcs.net/news.php?artid=2093&pr=95 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Practical consequence, stated plainly: a Louisiana medical patient has no federal protection in federally assisted housing by virtue of state-law lawfulness. An applicant using medical marijuana can be denied admission as a matter of federal requirement; a current tenant using it can be evicted as a matter of PHA/owner discretion, subject to the lease, notice, and hearing procedures. A hemp product that is lawful hemp (not marijuana) is not "illegal use of a controlled substance" on its face — but a hemp product that tests over the THC limit and is therefore marijuana would be — [Verify] HUD/PHA treatment of hemp specifically (none was located).
  • Procedure and proof — Louisiana public-housing eviction practice (secondary, Loyola Pro Bono Desk Manual). The Manual's lease-violation section (accessed 25 Oct 2026) collects Fourth Circuit reversals where eviction for alleged drug activity failed for lack of proof: 200 Carondelet v. Bickham (no physical evidence/expert/competent lay testimony), Estates New Orleans v. McCoy (arrest alone insufficient after charges dismissed), Housing Authority of New Orleans v. Sylvester (police report alone insufficient; "nothing in either state or federal jurisprudence that supports … that an arrest … creates a presumption of criminal activity"), Housing Authority of New Orleans v. King (inadmissible police report + counsel argument insufficient), and Guste Homes v. Thomas (off-premises crime without a showing of threat to health/safety/peaceful enjoyment did not warrant eviction). Source: https://probonodeskmanual.loyno.edu/node/384 — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The Manual's procedure section states a PHA must give written notice as required by State and federal law; for drug-related/violent activity or a felony conviction, "a reasonable time not to exceed 30 days" is required federally, and "in Louisiana, this means that eviction proceedings against a public housing tenant for any violation other than nonpayment of rent could be instituted upon a 5-day notice to vacate", with State notice combinable/concurrent with PHA notice. Source: https://probonodeskmanual.loyno.edu/book/export/html/262 — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Both Manual points are secondary practice summaries — [Verify] current PHA admissions/termination policies (e.g. Housing Authority of New Orleans' progressive screening policy, noted in the Manual's criminal-record section) before advising on any specific PHA.
  • Drug-free-zone overlap: Public-housing-authority property is also a §981.3 drug-free-zone location — but only if posted as a drug-free zone (§981.3(A)(3)(b), §12.10). Posting affects the criminal enhancement for a CDS violation on/near that property; it does not itself create a tenancy-termination ground beyond §40:506 / the federal lease terms.
  • Private landlords with no federal assistance: Federal HUD admission/termination rules do not apply. The analysis returns to §12.7.1 (lease + Art. 2686 + eviction procedure). A private landlord who voluntarily adopts a "no drug use" policy is not exercising a HUD power — do not cite HUD rules for a private tenancy.

12.7.3 What Louisiana law does not address for tenants (silence list)

  • No statute on: growing hemp (as distinct from marijuana) in rented premises by an LDAF licensee (a licensee growing in a rented house/yard would still face the lease's use/damage analysis — §12.7.1); storing medical marijuana or hemp products in rented premises (child-resistant packaging / locked storage is an LDH product rule, not a tenancy rule); a landlord's right to enter to inspect for marijuana cultivation (general entry/notice rules govern — [Verify]); or a tenant's right to break a lease because a neighbour's marijuana smoke infiltrates (nuisance / peaceful-enjoyment analysis — [Verify] case law). Do not fill any of these in.

12.8 Gun-ownership conflicts for patients

This section is the sharpest state/federal collision in Part 12. Read the federal and State layers separately; neither cancels the other.

12.8.1 Federal layer — 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) (given baseline applied; ATF guidance post-rescheduling NOT located)

  • Statute (federal, not Louisiana law). 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) makes it unlawful for any person "who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance" to ship, transport, possess, or receive firearms or ammunition. The given federal baseline states state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026. Schedule III is still a "controlled substance" schedule — rescheduling does not remove marijuana from the Controlled Substances Act, and §922(g)(3) on its face reaches "any controlled substance", not only Schedule I/II. The baseline's §280E lifting for Schedule III medical activity does not amend §922(g)(3).
  • ATF Form 4473 and the medical-card warning (secondary, pre-rescheduling guidance — current status Verify). ATF's 2011 Open Letter to Federal Firearms Licensees (secondary summaries, accessed 25 Oct 2026) stated that possession of a State-issued medical-marijuana card gives a dealer "reasonable cause to believe" the buyer is a prohibited person, and Form 4473 asks whether the buyer is an unlawful user of marijuana or another controlled substance; answering falsely is a separate federal offence. Sources (secondary summaries): https://legalclarity.org/louisiana-marijuana-laws-status-penalties-and-medical-use/ ; https://www.veriheal.com/blog/is-it-fair-that-federal-law-prohibits-medical-marijuana-users-from-gun-ownership/ — both accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Louisiana-specific wrinkle: Louisiana issues no resident patient card (Run 1). The ATF "card = reasonable cause" logic therefore does not map neatly onto Louisiana: a Louisiana patient has a clinician recommendation on file with a retailer and an LMMTS record, not a State card to show a dealer. Whether a dealer in Louisiana has "reasonable cause" from a patient's self-disclosure, a retailer record, or any other source, and whether ATF has issued post-Schedule-III guidance addressing Louisiana's no-card model, was not located — [Verify / Unavailable]. Do not state that "Louisiana patients cannot be identified by dealers so the federal ban does not apply" — non-identification is not a legal exception.
  • Hemani — flagged, not relied on. Secondary sources in this run describe United States v. Hemani, No. 24-1234 (decided 18 June 2026), as a narrow as-applied Second Amendment holding that a status-only §922(g)(3) prosecution of a regular marijuana user for in-home possession, with no danger showing, was unconstitutional, while §922(g)(3) itself remains in force. Sources (secondary): https://www.cannamd.com/can-i-own-a-gun-in-florida-if-i-get-my-medical-marijuana-card/ ; https://homesteadhealth.com/medical-cannabis-firearms-federal-law/ — both accessed 25 Oct 2026. This run did NOT re-research the federal baseline and did NOT open the Hemani opinion; the parent's federal research (Run 2, federal Parts) owns the Hemani holding. For Part 12 purposes, the only safe statements are: (i) §922(g)(3) remains on the books after Hemani on the secondary accounts; (ii) whether Hemani protects a Louisiana patient in a dealer-purchase, a concealed-permit, or a possession prosecution is case-specific and Verify — do not advise a patient that Hemani "restores" their gun rights. No post-Hemani ATF guidance for Louisiana patients was located in this run — [Verify].
  • Hemp and guns: Lawful hemp is excluded from the federal definition of marihuana and is not a controlled substance on that basis. A person who uses only lawful hemp products is not an "unlawful user" of marijuana on that basis alone. A person who uses a product that is in fact marijuana (e.g. an over-limit hemp product, or non-patient marijuana) is within the federal analysis. No ATF guidance distinguishing hemp-derived THC (delta-8/delta-9 within State limits) from marijuana for §922(g)(3) purposes was located — [Verify].
  • Non-patient / adult-use: Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I federally (baseline) and remains unlawful under Louisiana law, so a non-patient user is within §922(g)(3) on both layers without any medical-use nuance.

12.8.2 Louisiana State layer — concealed-handgun permits, and felony-conviction firearm bans

  • Concealed-handgun permit — R.S. 40:1379.3. A concealed-handgun permit applicant must, among other qualifications, "Not be an unlawful user of, or addicted to, marijuana, depressants, stimulants, or narcotic drugs" (§1379.3(C)(12) in the Justia 2022/2025 texts; paragraph lettering to be re-checked on legis.la.gov).
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1379-3/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • No medical-patient exception in that paragraph was located. The paragraph does not say "except a §1046 patient" or "except as recommended under §1046". Secondary summaries agree: "The statute does not create a specific exception for medical marijuana patients" (LegalClarity, same link as §12.8.1). Therefore, on the text opened, a Louisiana medical patient who is an "unlawful user of … marijuana" for State-permit purposes is disqualified from a concealed-handgun permit, even though the same use is lawful under §1046 for possession purposes. Whether "unlawful user" in §1379.3 is read to exclude State-lawful medical use — i.e. whether State-lawful use is "unlawful" at all for this paragraph — is a statutory-interpretation question that was not located in a Louisiana case or State Police guidance — [Verify]. Do not state the disqualification as absolutely settled for patients, and do not state a patient exception that is not in the text. State both: the paragraph's wording, the absence of an express patient exception, and the unresolved interpretation.
  • Permit-holder drug-test / suspension: Secondary summaries state a permit holder who tests positive for a controlled dangerous substance faces automatic suspension and potential revocation (LegalClarity, same link). The §1379.3 suspension/revocation paragraphs were not opened in this run — [Verify] before quoting a suspension rule.
  • Permitless carry (2024) — Verify, do not assume. Louisiana enacted permitless concealed carry in 2024 (secondary knowledge; not a Part 12 research point). Permitless carry does not repeal §1379.3's permit qualifications, and it does not repeal §922(g)(3) or §14:95.1. Whether a medical patient may lawfully carry without a permit under the 2024 law, given §1379.3(C)(12) and §922(g)(3), was not researched — [Verify] before advising on permitless carry. Do not state that permitless carry solves the patient-carry problem.
  • Felony-conviction firearm ban — R.S. 14:95.1. It is unlawful for a person convicted of (among other offences) "any violation of the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law which is a felony", or possession of a firearm while in possession of / during sale/distribution of a controlled dangerous substance, to possess a firearm or carry a concealed weapon (§95.1(A)(1)).
  • Source: https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/law.aspx?d=78740 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Penalty (current FindLaw/Justia text): imprisonment at hard labour for not less than 5 nor more than 20 years without benefit of probation, parole, or suspension of sentence, and a fine of not less than $1,000 nor more than $5,000 (§95.1(B)(1)). Source: https://codes.findlaw.com/la/revised-statutes/la-rev-stat-tit-14-sect-95-1/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. (An older 2009 text showed 10–20 years; the 5-year floor is the current text — do not use the older figure.)
  • Duration / restoration — Verify the current paragraph. A secondary LEAAC summary states §95.1 bars possession "for a period of ten years from the date of completion of sentence, probation, parole, or suspension of sentence" for some, but not all, felonies. Source: http://www.leaac.com/faq-resources/concealed-carry-of-weapons-after-a-louisiana-conviction/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The §95.1(C) restoration / 10-year provisions were not opened in this run — [Verify] current §95.1(B)–(C) on legis.la.gov before stating a duration or a restoration route (pardon, expungement, §95.1(C) application). In particular, whether expungement of a felony marijuana conviction (Art. 978, §12.4) restores §95.1 firearm rights, and whether a first-offender pardon does, was not resolved — [Verify].
  • Practical consequence for Part 12: a misdemeanour marijuana possession conviction (≤14 g fine-only, or a §1025(E) paraphernalia fine) is not a §95.1 felony trigger on its face. A felony marijuana conviction (distribution, 3rd+ >14 g possession at ≤2 years, or any other felony CDS violation) is a §95.1 trigger on its face, with the 5–20-year penalty above for a subsequent firearm possession. That distinction is why the felony/misdemeanour line in §§966/1025 matters for guns, not just for jail.
  • Possession vs purchase vs permit — three different questions. (i) Possessing a firearm already owned: federal §922(g)(3) + State §95.1 (if a prior felony) are the operative bans. (ii) Purchasing from a licensed dealer: Form 4473 + NICS + dealer "reasonable cause" are the operative gate, federally. (iii) Obtaining a Louisiana concealed-handgun permit: §1379.3(C)(12) is the operative gate, on State law. A patient could in theory be in different positions on each — do not collapse them into "patients cannot own guns" or "patients can own guns". The accurate summary is: federal law bars purchase/possession by an unlawful user (with Hemani as a narrow, Verify as-applied limit); Louisiana law bars a concealed-handgun permit for an unlawful user of marijuana with no express patient exception (interpretation Verify); and a prior felony CDS conviction bars possession under §95.1 (duration/restoration Verify).

12.9 Pet and veterinary products

12.9.1 What Louisiana law actually says about animals — one definition, and silence everywhere else

  • Pet and feed products ARE consumable hemp products — R.S. 3:1481(3)(b):

    "'Consumable hemp product' shall include commercial feed and pet products."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-3/rs-3-1481/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026 (Justia 2025 text; legis.la.gov re-check recommended — Run 1 flagged a total-THC vs total-delta-9 wording conflict in §1481(5) that is not resolved by this definition paragraph).
  • The full definition (§1481(3)(a)) is: "any product derived from industrial hemp that contains any cannabinoid, including cannabidiol or THC, and is intended for consumption or topical use". A pet product that contains a cannabinoid and is intended for animal consumption/topical use is therefore within Part VI on its face.
  • Consequences that follow from that inclusion (textual, not guidance):
  • A pet hemp product sold at retail in Louisiana must be LDH-registered / label-approved (§1483) and sold by an ATC-permitted retailer (§1484), like any consumable hemp product. An unregistered pet CBD product sold at retail is within §1482(B)(4) ("any product that has not received approval from [LDH]") on its face.
  • A pet hemp product for inhalation or floral hemp material for retail use is banned like any other consumable hemp product (§1482(B)(2)–(3), Run 1 §1.6.3).
  • The 21+ rule (§§1482(A)(2), 93.16, 93.17) applies to "any consumable hemp product" — which, by §1481(3)(b), includes pet products. On its face, therefore, a person under 21 may not purchase or possess a pet hemp product in Louisiana, even though the intended consumer is an animal. Whether LDH/ATC enforce the 21+ rule for pet products, or treat a parent buying a pet product for a family animal differently, was not located in guidance — [Verify]. Do not state a pet-product age exception.
  • Serving/package limits — pet-specific limits NOT located. R.S. 3:1483(B)(6) sets 5 mg/serving, 40 mg/package (non-beverage, non-tincture), beverage, and tincture limits, and provides "(d) Nonedible consumable hemp products shall not be subject to the individual serving and package requirements of this Paragraph" (Run 1 §1.6.2). Whether an edible pet treat is subject to the 5 mg/40 mg limits (as an edible consumable hemp product) or is treated as a "nonedible" / feed product with different limits, and whether LDH's January 2026 hemp rule sets pet/feed-specific limits, was not located — [Verify] in LAC Title 49, Part I, Chapter 5 and the January 2026 final rule before stating a pet-product THC limit. Do not apply the human 5 mg/40 mg limits to pet products as settled law, and do not state that pet products are exempt from them.
  • Commercial feed overlay — Verify. LDAF regulates animal feed generally, and §1481(3)(b) includes "commercial feed" in consumable hemp. Whether a hemp-containing commercial feed needs LDAF feed registration in addition to LDH consumable-hemp registration, and which agency's testing/labelling governs feed, was not located — [Verify] (LDAF feed programme + LDH hemp rule).
  • What Louisiana law does NOT say about animals:
  • No veterinary medical-marijuana law. R.S. 40:1046 authorises recommendations for a patient with a debilitating medical condition by an authorised clinician (physician, nurse practitioner, medical psychologist — §1046(B)). It does not authorise a veterinarian to recommend marijuana for an animal, and it does not authorise an animal as a §1046 patient. A veterinarian who "recommends" marijuana for a dog or cat has no §1046 authority on the text opened, and the animal's owner has no §966(F) immunity for possessing marijuana "for" the animal on the text opened (immunity covers a patient, a §15:1503 caregiver, a domiciliary parent of a minor child, and a visiting qualifying patient — not a pet owner).
  • No Louisiana Board of Veterinary Medicine (LBVM) cannabis/CBD guidance was located in this run. The Board (within LDAF since Act 515 of 2018, eff. 1 Aug 2018 — LBVM "About Us", https://lsbvm.org/about-us/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026) regulates the practice of veterinary medicine (R.S. 37:1513 et seq.; "practice of veterinary medicine" includes prescribing/administering any drug/medicine/biologic/therapeutic substance — R.S. 37:1513, via LawServer summary). Whether the Board has issued a policy on discussing, recommending, or dispensing CBD/hemp products for animals, and whether discussing hemp products exposes a veterinarian to discipline, was not located — [Verify / Unavailable]. Do not state that Louisiana veterinarians "may discuss but not recommend" CBD (that is another State's rule — California's AB 2215 model — and was not located for Louisiana).
  • No FDA-approved veterinary CBD/hemp drug is identified in Louisiana law. The §1483(K) / §1693(B) FDA-approved-product exclusions are about human FDA-approved prescription CBD (e.g. Epidiolex) and §1046 products. No Louisiana provision addresses an FDA-approved animal CBD drug, because none is identified in the sources opened — [Verify] FDA animal-drug status if the parent wants an FDA paragraph. Do not state that pet CBD is "FDA-approved" or "FDA-banned" for animals from Louisiana sources.
  • Animal cruelty / endangerment: Giving an animal a THC product that intoxicates or harms it could implicate general animal-cruelty law (R.S. 14:102 et seq. — not opened in this run — [Verify] before citing a cruelty paragraph). Do not cite a cruelty penalty from this file. The safe statement is only: no cannabis-specific animal-cruelty provision was located; general cruelty law is outside this Part's research.
  • Service animals / assistance animals: No Louisiana provision was located addressing medical-marijuana use by a service-animal handler differently from any other patient, or addressing hemp products for a service animal. Law silent; do not fill in.

12.10 Medical marijuana in schools

Headline: Louisiana law bans smoking/vaping marijuana on elementary/secondary school property for "any person" — with no medical-patient exception on the face of that ban — and, since 1 Aug 2026, imposes up to 1 year + $1,000 for covered marijuana violations in the 2,000-foot school zone. There is NO Louisiana law authorising a school to administer, store, or permit a student's medical marijuana on campus. The details matter because the three school statutes do different things.

12.10.1 The school-property smoking/vaping ban — R.S. 17:240 (elementary/secondary only)

  • Text, R.S. 17:240(B)(2)(b) (Justia 2025 text; St. Tammany Parish School Board republication of the statute agrees):

    "(b) No person shall smoke or vape any form of marijuana as defined by R.S. 40:961 or a substance classified in Schedule I that is marijuana, tetrahydrocannabinol, or chemical derivatives thereof on any school property."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-17/rs-17-240/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026; https://www.stpsb.org/uploaded/CAPS2025/Statutes/170240.htm — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Definitions and scope:
  • "School property" (§17:240(A)(1)) means school grounds, playgrounds, premises, and property, including land, improvements, and school facilities, located on the property of any elementary or secondary school, the Louisiana School for the Deaf, the Louisiana School for the Visually Impaired, and schools in the Special School District; and any school vehicle used for academic/extracurricular programmes and administration at those schools.
  • "Smoking" (§17:240(A)(2)) means possession of a lighted cigar, cigarette, pipe, or any other lighted tobacco or marijuana product, including e-cigs, e-cigarettes, electronic cigarettes, advanced personal vaporisers, vape pens, and vape mods.
  • §17:240(B)(2)(a) separately bans any person from smoking/carrying a lighted smoking object/device on school property (tobacco + devices generally).
  • §17:240(B)(3) bans tobacco use on a school bus/vehicle transporting elementary/secondary students. §17:240(B)(4) provides Subsection B "shall not apply to any school property that is rented, leased, or otherwise made available for use for non-educational purposes" — a narrow carve-out for non-educational rentals, not a general medical exception.
  • §17:240(D): nothing in the Section applies to a home-study programme approved under R.S. 17:236.1.
  • No medical exception on its face. §17:240(B)(2)(b) says "No person" and contains no "except a §1046 patient", "except as recommended", or "except a non-smoked form" proviso. The §17:240(B)(1) tobacco ban's FDA-cessation-product proviso is a tobacco proviso, not a marijuana proviso. Therefore: a §1046 patient — student, employee, parent, visitor, or spectator — who smokes or vapes marijuana on elementary/secondary school property violates §17:240(B)(2)(b) on the text opened, even if the marijuana itself was lawfully obtained through the programme. The LSUE (Louisiana State University at Eunice) campus notice states the same point for the school-zone law: "Students or guests who possess a prescription order to possess marijuana are not exempt from legal recourse if smoking on school property" (LSUE notice, §12.10.2 source). That LSUE sentence uses "prescription order" loosely (Louisiana uses "recommendation", not prescription) — the underlying point, that programme status does not exempt school-property smoking, follows from §17:240's "no person" wording.
  • Penalty — two tracks, do not conflate them:
  • School-authority track: §17:240(C)(2)(a) — the governing authority of each public elementary/secondary school (and, optionally, each nonpublic school) may provide penalties including disciplinary action and/or a fine not to exceed $200, or both; enforcement by local superintendents/designees (§17:240(C)(3)).
  • Criminal track: §17:240(C)(2)(b) — "Any person who violates Subparagraph (B)(2)(b) of this Section shall be subject to punishment pursuant to R.S. 40:981.3(A)(1)." That cross-reference is to the drug-free-zone provision (§12.10.2), not to the $200 school fine. A school-property smoking violation is therefore punishable under the drug-free-zone regime, not merely as a $200 school fine — the $200 figure is the school's own disciplinary/fine authority, not the criminal ceiling.
  • History: Acts 1992, No. 480; amended Acts 2017, No. 351; Acts 2019, No. 411; Acts 2024, No. 352, §1, eff. 28 May 2024 (history line on the St. Tammany republication). The marijuana-smoking paragraph (B)(2)(b) predates Act 305 of 2026; Act 305 changed the punishment via §981.3, not the §17:240 ban itself — [Verify] the Act 352 (2024) vs Act 305 (2026) division of labour on legis.la.gov if the parent wants an amendment history.

12.10.2 The drug-free zone — R.S. 40:981.3, as amended by Act 305 (HB 568) of 2026, eff. 1 Aug 2026 — Run 1 "Verify" RESOLVED in substance, enrolled text still Verify

Run 1 §1.10 reported HB 568 as "reported Act 305, signed, effective 1 Aug 2026" on secondary authority only, with a warning not to copy the "felony for use in your own home" framing without the statute's "underlying violation" qualifier. The substance is now confirmed from the official digest, the LSUE official-university notice, and the Governor's public letter (secondary summaries of the Governor's letter agree):

  • Official digest, HB 568 Engrossed (2026, Firment): "Enhances the penalty for violating the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law with respect to marijuana within 2,000 feet of a school zone. Present law provides that a person who violates certain provisions of the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law (UCDS) within 2,000 feet of a school zone shall be punished by the maximum fine and one and one-half times the longest term of imprisonment provided in the UCDS. Proposed law provides that a person who violates the provisions of the UCDS with respect to marijuana shall be imprisoned with or without hard labor for not more than one year and may be fined up to $1,000. (Amends R.S. 40:981.3(D); Adds R.S. 40:981.3(A)(4) and (E))"
  • Source: http://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1462887 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Pre-Act 305 zone law (FindLaw republication of §981.3, pre-2026 text — use only for the provisions Act 305 did not amend):

    "A.(1) Any person who violates a provision of R.S. 40:966 through 970 of the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law while on any property used for school purposes by any school, within two thousand feet of any such property, or while on a school bus, shall, upon conviction, be punished in accordance with Subsection D of this Section." "B. Lack of knowledge that the prohibited act occurred on or within two thousand feet of school or drug treatment facility property shall not be a defense." "C.(1) 'School' means any public or private elementary, secondary, vocational-technical school, or any public or private college or university in Louisiana. (2) 'School property' means all property used for school purposes, including but not limited to school playgrounds, as well as any building or area owned by the state or by a political subdivision and used or operated as a playground or recreational facility and all parks and recreational areas administered by the office of state parks." "D.(1) Whoever violates a provision of this Section shall be punished by the imposition of the maximum fine and be imprisoned for not more than one and one-half times the longest term of imprisonment authorized by the applicable provisions of R.S. 40:966 through 970."

  • Source: https://codes.findlaw.com/la/revised-statutes/la-rev-stat-tit-40-sect-981-3/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. This FindLaw text predates Act 305 and does NOT contain new (A)(4) or (E) — do not quote it as the current §981.3.
  • What Act 305 changed (from the digest + LSUE notice + Governor's letter summaries — enrolled Act text still Verify):
  • New marijuana-specific penalty (new §981.3(E), per the digest's "Adds … (E)" and LSUE): "Act 305 of the 2026 Regular Session set a new penalty for marijuana possession in a school zone: imprisonment, with or without hard labor, for up to one year, plus a fine of up to $1,000. Before August 1, possessing 14 grams or less carried a fine of up to $100. La. R.S. 40:981.3(E); La. R.S. 40:966(C)(2)(a)(i)" — LSUE notice. Source (official university notice, secondary summary of the statute): https://www.lsue.edu/studentengagement/docs/marijuana-on-campus-crime.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • New smoking/vaping paragraph (new §981.3(A)(4), per the digest's "Adds … (A)(4)"): reaches a person who violates the CDS law "while smoking, vaping, or otherwise abusing" a controlled dangerous substance in the zone locations (school property, within 2,000 feet, school bus). LSUE: "Act 305 added a new paragraph reaching anyone who violates the drug laws 'while smoking, vaping, or otherwise abusing' a controlled dangerous substance in these locations. A THC vape pen counts." Source: same LSUE notice.
  • Zone geography: school property + within 2,000 feet of school property + school bus (§981.3(A)(1)). 2,000 feet is more than one-third of a mile from the property line; on a campus it reaches apartments, dorms, fraternity/sorority houses, parking/tailgating lots, streets, sidewalks, bus stops, and neighbouring homes (LSUE notice; Governor's letter summary via Marijuana Moment, https://www.marijuanamoment.net/louisiana-governor-asks-schools-to-publicize-new-marijuana-penalties-that-will-jail-people-for-smoking-near-campuses/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026, secondary). Lack of knowledge of being within 2,000 feet is not a defence (§981.3(B), pre-Act 305 text, unchanged on the digest's account).
  • Who it reaches: "any person" — students, employees, parents, alumni, spectators, and visitors, not only students (Governor's letter summary, same Marijuana Moment link; LSUE notice: "It reaches any person, so it applies to employees and visitors as well as students"). Colleges/universities are "schools" for §981.3 (§981.3(C)(1) includes "any public or private college or university in Louisiana" and vocational-technical schools) — unlike §17:240, which is elementary/secondary only. A college student smoking in a dorm within the zone, or a spectator vaping at a stadium tailgate within 2,000 feet, is within the zone law on the summaries' reading.
  • Felony characterisation — state it with the qualifier: Because the new penalty allows imprisonment with or without hard labour, and R.S. 14:2(4) defines a felony as a crime for which the offender may be sentenced to imprisonment at hard labour, LSUE characterises the new offence as "felony-level exposure" and notes "A conviction goes on an adult criminal record." Source: same LSUE notice. That characterisation is LSUE's, not a quote from §981.3(E) itself — [Verify] the enrolled Act 305 text and §14:2(4) before publishing "Act 305 creates a felony" as a headline. The safe verified statement is the penalty itself (up to 1 year with/without hard labour + up to $1,000).
  • The "underlying violation" qualifier — Run 1 warning, confirmed as essential: Act 305 does not on the digest's account create a free-standing "smoking near a school is a crime even if the marijuana is lawful" offence. It requires a violation of the Uniform CDS Law (for (A)(1)) or a violation "while smoking, vaping, or otherwise abusing" a CDS (for (A)(4)). Whether a programme patient's lawful possession/use, smoked on school property, is a "violation" for (A)(4) purposes — given §17:240(B)(2)(b) independently bans that smoking for "any person" — is the key unresolved interaction: §17:240's ban supplies a violation, but §966(F) immunity covers programme possession. Do NOT resolve that interaction in this file — [Verify] by opening the enrolled Act 305 text and any LDH/Attorney General guidance. In particular, do not copy the secondary framing "felony for use in your own home within 2,000 feet" without stating: (i) the home must be within 2,000 feet of school property, (ii) there must be an underlying CDS violation (or a §17:240 smoking violation, per the interaction above), and (iii) lawful non-smoked programme use in a private home is not described in the digest/LSUE materials as the target — but the home-within-zone + smoking combination is exactly what the Governor's letter warns about for tailgates/parking lots, and the same geography would reach a home.
  • Other zone locations (unchanged, pre-Act 305 text): drug-treatment-facility property / within 2,000 feet (if marked as a drug-free zone under §1058.10) — §981.3(A)(2); religious-building, public-housing-authority, and child-day-care-centre property / within 2,000 feet — only if posted as a drug-free zone with visible signs stating the zone extends 2,000 feet and violations are severely penalised — §981.3(A)(3). Schools require no posting. The general enhancement formula in old (D)(1) (maximum fine + up to 1.5× longest term) still applies to non-marijuana CDS violations in the zone on the digest's account (Act 305 amended (D) for marijuana; the non-marijuana formula's survival in amended (D) was not opened — [Verify] enrolled text).
  • Act number / Governor action — still secondary for the Act number itself: LSUE and secondary press cite "Act 305" and an August 2026 Governor letter asking schools/LHSAA to publicise the law. The legis.la.gov digest opened is for HB 568 Engrossed, not the enrolled Act, and does not itself state "Act 305" or the Governor's action in the text returned. Act 305 attribution and Governor-action status are therefore [Verify] on the legis.la.gov Bill page for HB 568 (2026) + Secretary of State Act list before publishing "Act 305, signed by Governor Landry" as confirmed. The effective date (1 Aug 2026) is corroborated by LSUE ("LOUISIANA LAW CHANGED ON AUGUST 1, 2026") and by the Governor's letter summaries, and is consistent with the standard 1 Aug effective date for 2026 Regular Session Acts — but the enrolled Act's effective-date clause was not opened — [Verify].

12.10.3 Student discipline — R.S. 17:416, as amended by HB 384 (2025) — secondary summary, Verify current text

  • Secondary summary (BillTrack50, HB 384, 2025 Regular Session, signed/enacted 1 July 2025, effective 1 Aug 2025): HB 384 amended R.S. 17:416(C)(2)(a)–(b) and enacted §17:416(O), relative to discipline of students found in possession of certain substances on school property. Previously, a student in grades 6–12 found guilty of possessing a firearm, a knife ≥2.5 inches, or any illegal narcotic/drug/controlled substance on school property, on a school bus, or at a school-sponsored event, after a hearing, shall be expelled for a minimum of four complete school semesters and referred to the district attorney (superintendent may modify case-by-case in writing). As amended, the minimum is two complete school semesters, and for marijuana specifically: a first occurrence may be recommended for expulsion but is not automatically expelled; a second or subsequent occurrence requires at least two complete semesters + district-attorney referral. Local school boards must collect/report annual expulsion data (first vs subsequent, returns to regular settings).
  • Sources (secondary): https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1882030 — accessed 25 Oct 2026; enrolled HB 384 text (LegiScan PDF, showing the 4→2 semester amendment): https://legiscan.com/LA/text/HB384/id/3254473/Louisiana-2025-HB384-Enrolled.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026; Post South summary (secondary, 4 Sept 2026): https://www.postsouth.com/story/news/local/2026/09/04/louisiana-law-increases-penalties-for-school-drugs/91587622007/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • [Verify] the current legis.la.gov text of §17:416(C)(2) and (O) before quoting a discipline rule, and [Verify] whether "illegal narcotic, drug, or other controlled substance" in §17:416 reaches a student's lawful programme marijuana (on its face, "illegal" excludes programme marijuana possessed within §1046/§966(F), but a school-board policy may prohibit possession on campus regardless of lawfulness — see §12.10.4). Do not state that a first-time programme-patient student "cannot be expelled" — §17:416 as summarised governs illegal possession discipline; campus possession policy is separate.

12.10.4 Administration / possession by a student patient on campus — NO authorising law located

  • General school-medication law — R.S. 17:436.1 (LawServer/Justia text): "medication" includes all prescription and nonprescription drugs; no city/parish school board shall require any employee other than a registered nurse or licensed medical physician to administer medication until: (1) the board has promulgated BESE / Louisiana State Board of Nursing guidelines establishing the procedure, including (a) no medication without an order from a licensed physician/dentist (Louisiana or adjacent State) or other authorised prescriber + a parent/guardian letter of request/authorisation, (b) medication in a container meeting acceptable pharmaceutical standards, (c) letter + container with student name, RX number if any, date, frequency, medication name, dosage, route, prescriber name; (2) at least two employees per school with ≥6 hours' medication-administration training; plus RN/physician assessment and review conditions (§436.1(B)(3)–(4)).
  • Source: https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/louisiana/la-constitution/louisiana_revised_statutes_17-436-1 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Why §436.1 does NOT authorise school administration of medical marijuana: (i) Louisiana medical marijuana is recommended, not prescribed, and is not dispensed in a pharmaceutical container with an RX number in the §436.1 sense — it is dispensed by an LDH-permitted retailer in LDH-rule packaging (§1046, Run 1 §1.7); (ii) §436.1 requires a prescriber's order, which a §1046 recommendation is not on the statute's own terminology; (iii) no §436.1 paragraph, LDH rule, or BESE policy addressing medical marijuana was located. Therefore: no Louisiana law was located that requires or permits a school nurse, teacher, or other employee to administer, store, hold, or supervise a student's medical marijuana on campus. A parent/guardian administering a student's non-smoked dose on campus would still face the campus-possession policy question below, and smoking/vaping on campus is banned (§17:240) regardless of who administers.
  • Possession on campus by a student patient — policy, not statute, decides in practice. §17:240 bans smoking/vaping on school property; it does not on its face ban possession of a non-smoked programme product (tincture, capsule, topical) in a backpack. §17:416 discipline, on the secondary summary, governs illegal possession. School-board policies located in this run (Evangeline Parish JCDAA, Caddo Parish JCDAA — secondary, local policies) prohibit student possession or use of marijuana products in any form on all school-board property/vehicles and at school-sponsored/approved functions, with parental permission expressly not an exemption in the Caddo policy ("Parental permission to possess/use … does not exempt a student from this policy"). Sources (secondary local policies): https://files.gabbart.com/1318/jcdaa-24_.pdf (Evangeline) ; https://files-backend.assets.thrillshare.com/documents/asset/uploaded_file/2615/Cpps/ed03f290-98f0-4170-bf5f-1d2d6d5aa321/JCDAA-Smoking-Use-of-Tobacco-Policy—Revision-Board-Approved-4.21.26.pdf (Caddo, rev. 21 Apr 2026) — both accessed 25 Oct 2026.
  • Therefore, for a student patient, the accurate statement is two-layered: (1) State criminal law: programme possession itself is immunised under §966(F) (subject to the catch-all tension, §12.6.3), but smoking/vaping on school property is banned (§17:240) and a CDS violation in the zone is enhanced (§981.3); (2) School policy: the student's own parish/school-board policy — which must be checked parish by parish — may prohibit possession/use in any form on campus and at school functions, with discipline up to the §17:416 framework, even if the product is lawfully obtained. Do not state a statewide "student patients may possess at school" or "may not possess at school" rule — the State statute does not say either, and local policy fills the gap.
  • Employees: §17:240(B)(1) bans a student or school employee from smoking/chewing/inhaling/absorbing/consuming tobacco on school property beyond the building, and (B)(2)(b) bans any person (including employees) from smoking/vaping marijuana on school property. School-board employee policies located (St. Mary Parish GAMA, rev. Aug 2024, secondary) prohibit employees from using tobacco, smokeless tobacco, or marijuana products of any form on all school-board property/vehicles and at school-sponsored/approved functions, with discipline + tobacco-cessation referral. Source: https://www.stmaryk12.net/departments/human-resources/policies-and-procedures/employee-tobacco-use — accessed 25 Oct 2026. An employee who is a §1046 patient therefore faces the same §17:240 smoking/vaping ban as anyone else, plus board policy for non-smoked forms — and Run 1 §1.9 employment protection (§49:1016) covers State employers' drug-test consequences, not school-board (parish) employers on its face — [Verify] whether a parish school board is a "state employer" for §49:1016 (it is not on the statute's face; do not assume coverage).
  • Colleges/universities — different statutes, same zone: §17:240 does not reach colleges (elementary/secondary + Deaf/Visually Impaired/Special School District only). College smoking/vaping/possession is governed by: (i) §981.3 (college = "school" for the zone law, §12.10.2); (ii) the Smoke-Free Air Act for enclosed public places (§12.5.2); (iii) campus policy / student code (LSUE's notice is an example of a campus publicising the zone law, not a statewide college rule — [Verify] each institution's code). No Louisiana statute authorising a college to administer or permit a student's medical marijuana on campus was located — law silent.
  • Hemp at school: Consumable hemp products are not marijuana, so §§17:240(B)(2)(b) and 981.3 (CDS violations) do not reach a compliant hemp product on their face. But: (i) a person under 21 may not purchase/possess any consumable hemp product (§93.17, §12.2) — so a student under 21 with a hemp gummy violates §93.17 regardless of campus; (ii) an inhalable hemp product or floral hemp at retail is banned statewide (§1482) — possession of a hemp vape by a student is within school vaping-device policies and, if the product is in fact marijuana/THC, within the CDS analysis; (iii) school-board "marijuana products in any form" policies (above) may be applied by a board to hemp-THC products as a policy matter — [Verify] the specific board's definitions. Do not state that "hemp is allowed at school" — the correct statement is that hemp is outside the marijuana school statutes on its face, but inside the under-21 hemp ban and inside local school policy.

12.11 Cross-cutting social rules NOT covered above (brief, to prevent gaps being read as silence)

  • Child custody / child-welfare — no marijuana-specific Louisiana rule located. No Louisiana statute was located that makes programme-patient status alone a ground for loss of custody, a finding of neglect/abuse, or a Child in Need of Care adjudication. The Children's Code definitions (Art. 1003, via Justia 2021 text) define "neglect" as failure to supply necessary food/clothing/shelter/care/treatment/counselling resulting in substantial threat/impairment to the child's health/safety, and "substance abuse" as use "to the extent that it renders the person dangerous to himself or others or renders the person gravely disabled" — i.e. the inquiry is harm/impairment-based, not status-based, on the definitions' face. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2021/children-s-code/article-1003/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Secondary family-law summaries agree a single incident / card alone does not automatically defeat custody, while a pattern endangering the child can affect it — but no Louisiana custody case holding on programme-patient status was located — [Verify] before advising on custody. Do not state a custody protection or a custody penalty from this file.
  • Organ transplantation, adoption/foster-care licensing, professional licensing (other than guns/driving): No Louisiana cannabis-specific provision was located for transplant eligibility, foster/adoptive-parent eligibility on the basis of programme-patient status, or professional-licence discipline for lawful programme use (as distinct from impairment on duty / CDS convictions). Law silent on each; do not fill in. (State-employer drug-test protection, §49:1016, is Run 1 §1.9 and is not repeated here except as noted in §§12.5/12.10.)
  • Public benefits (SNAP/TANF/housing): Federally, SNAP medical-expense deductions exclude medical-marijuana expenses (CRS R42394, §12.7.2 source) and federally assisted housing treats marijuana as illegal ( §12.7.2). No Louisiana-specific SNAP/TANF drug-testing or benefit rule for programme patients was located in this run — [Verify] if the parent wants a benefits paragraph. Do not state a Louisiana benefits ban from federal law alone.

RESEARCH NOTES — Combined, Runs 1 and 2 (Parts 0–12)

Scope of this section: This is the combined research-notes section required at the end of Run 2. It does not replace the gaps lists at the end of each part group in the body above (Run 1 Parts 0–1, Parts 2–3, Parts 4–6; Run 2 Parts 7–8, Parts 9–10, Parts 11 and 12). Those per-part lists remain the detailed record. This section reconciles them, records what Run 2 resolved, what it preserved as a conflict, and what remains unavailable. Every item below is dated to the research window, 25 October 2026, unless a source itself is dated otherwise.

1. Cross-run consistency — what was checked and what stands

The following Run 1 anchors were re-read before Run 2 and were not contradicted on re-quote in Run 2, except where §2 or §3 below says otherwise:

  • Medical only; no adult-use law enacted. Adult-use items (HB 373 of 2026 pilot; HB 627 of 2025 predecessor) remain PROPOSED only.
  • LDH is lead regulator: production/labs under Acts 491/492 of 2022 (1 Aug 2022); retailers from the Board of Pharmacy to LDH under Act 693 of 2024 (1 Jan 2025).
  • Two medical cultivation licences only, transferred 1 July 2024 under Act 150 of 2024 to Good Day Farm Louisiana LLC and Advanced Biomedics LLC dba Ilera Holistic Healthcare; programme sunset 1 July 2030.
  • 10 base marijuana-pharmacy permits; 19 satellites listed on the LDH page opened 25 Oct 2026 (29 locations in total); 30-location maximum; satellites at 3,500 / 7,000 active patients per region.
  • Fees: cultivation $100,000/year + 7% of gross sales; retail $22,500/year per permit holder; LDAF hemp licences $500 each/year; LDH consumable-hemp processor $175–$1,375/year by sales tier; LDH product registration $50 per product; ATC retail/special-event statutory cap $175/year, wholesaler cap $500/year.
  • No patient card or registry for residents; clinician-discretion qualification; flower limit 71 g / 14 days; no home grow; non-patient possession ≤14 g fine-only ≤$100 (Act 247 of 2021).
  • Consumable hemp under Act 752 of 2024 (1 Jan 2025): 5 mg total THC per serving, 40 mg per package (non-beverage/tincture); beverages 5 mg in ≥12 oz; age 21+; LDH registration + ATC permits.
  • Medical marijuana exempt from state AND local sales tax (R.S. 47:305.2(B)(11)); consumable hemp excise 3%.
  • Louisiana runs its own USDA-approved state hemp plan (USDA AMS list updated 17 Feb 2026), not USDA direct licensing.
  • Given federal baseline (Schedule III medical from 28 Apr 2026; 280E lifted for Schedule III medical only; PL 119-37 / PL 119-103 hemp dates 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026; 0.4 mg/container cap after 11 Dec 2026) was not contradicted by any Louisiana source opened in either run.

2. Conflicts and gaps RESOLVED in Run 2 (with the resolution)

  • HB 165 Act number — RESOLVED. Run 1 left the Act number open; Run 2 confirms HB 165 is Act 682 of 2024, effective 1 Aug 2024 (R.S. 40:1025(E): $100 / $500 / $2,500 fine-only for possession of personal-use marijuana paraphernalia only).
  • SB 270 effective date — RESOLVED in substance. Run 1 flagged a 1 June vs 1 Aug 2026 conflict; Run 2 confirms Act 602 (SB 270) of 2026, effective 1 Aug 2026, adding R.S. 40:1046.5 for terminally ill patients in healthcare facilities. The "terminally ill" definition and any non-smoking/non-vaping form limit remain secondary-only — see §3.
  • HB 568 / Act 305 school-zone scope — RESOLVED in substance. Act 305 (HB 568) of 2026, effective 1 Aug 2026, amends the drug-free zone (R.S. 40:981.3). Enrolled text line-by-line remains [VERIFY].
  • Visiting-patient tracking — RESOLVED. Run 1 left PMP vs LMMTS [VERIFY]; Run 2 confirms current R.S. 40:1046.1 requires LMMTS review/reporting by pharmacist/designee, with 3-year document retention in the LDH Notice of Intent text. Visiting patients still need another jurisdiction's card/equivalent + LDH-approved form; there is no outward reciprocity and no out-of-state delivery.
  • Licensed-lab list question — RESOLVED as a list question. Use the LDH list dated by access date 25 Oct 2026: LDAF lab (Baton Rouge), Ceres Scientific LLC (Baton Rouge), Acre Analytical LLC (West Monroe). Whether Ceres is a rename/successor/replacement for the earlier Orion Laboratories listing at the same Baton Rouge address, and the date the list changed, were NOT established — see §3.
  • LDAF background-check cadence — CLARIFIED. Current R.S. 3:1465(D)(1) is initial check + every 3 years thereafter (Act 498 change), not annual renewal. The 60-day multiple-licence rule is separate.
  • Hemp harvest window — CLARIFIED. Use 30 days after sample collection (unless LDAF authorises otherwise in writing); the 15-day figure in older material is superseded.
  • Stale secondary claims REJECTED (do not re-add): universities still shown as licensees (CannBus); an 8 mg/serving Act 752 cap (LegalClarity); the 1991 bill "failed to pass" (StateRegsToday — Act 874 exists); first sales in Feb 2022 (StateRegsToday — first sales were 6 Aug 2019); 10 federally recognised Louisiana tribes (directory claim — 4 federal + 11 state-recognised); "no out-of-state cards accepted" (pre-2022 pages — R.S. 40:1046.1 stands); ~23 pharmacies / ongoing Board licensing (IndicaOnline — LDH 10 + 19 = 29 stands); a public-media advertising ban as current law (traces to un-enacted 2021 HB 699); a $100,000 marijuana-pharmacy surety bond as current law (former Board regime, secondary/historic only); "no tracking/recall system" (LMMTS + recall-plan requirement exist); SB 495 (2024) $250 grower fee and 2023 HB 605 $250 retail cap as law (both proposed only, final status [VERIFY]).
  • "Contract carrier" label — HISTORIC. Current R.S. 3:1465 and the LDAF page use Handler, not contract carrier. An LAC §1303 definition still saying "contract carrier" (March 2026 compilation, search-index text) does not revive it.

3. Conflicts and gaps PRESERVED — do not publish either side as settled

Highest priority (check before relying on the affected rule)

  1. Expungement fast-track sunset — URGENT. C.Cr.P. Art. 983(M)(5) terminates the fee paragraph on 1 Aug 2026, but Art. 977(D) (90-day first-offense misdemeanour marijuana possession eligibility) has no sunset in the 2025 text, while a secondary firm blog reads the whole route as ended. As of 25 Oct 2026 it is unconfirmed on legis.la.gov whether the 90-day route survives (at the general fee) or ended, and whether the 2026 Legislature extended it. Do not publish either version without that check.
  2. LDH January 2026 final rule (Louisiana Register 52:59) — NOI vs final. The Register excerpt opened ran only through LAC 51:XXIX §505. Later medical chapters (especially Chapter 25 retailer operations) are cited in Run 2 to the May 2025 Notice of Intent text with a "[Verify — NOI-to-final survival]" flag. The final rule was confirmed to reenact/amend Part XXIX and enact Subpart 2 (Marijuana Retailers), but line-by-line final text for Chapters 7, 9, 21, 23, 25 was not opened. Do not present NOI-cited retailer provisions (security components, transport vehicle/crew/GPS, solvent/heavy-metal/mycotoxin/microbial numeric limits, facility requirements, lab independence, revocation procedure/hearing rights, delivery-agent/vehicle rules, recall-execution section, sample/giveaway/discount/advertising rules, safe/vault standard, manufacturer rendering method, lab security, retailer personnel records) as confirmed final-rule text without that check.
  3. Louisiana §280E decoupling — CONFLICT, not resolved. Secondary directories list Louisiana as decoupling, citing no statute. A Louisiana tax specialist analysis (AndreTaxCo, cited in Run 1 Part 2) states Louisiana conforms (individual = federal AGI starting point; corporate = federal taxable income) and that "there is no provision that states Section 280E does not apply." No Louisiana §280E decoupling statute was located, and no Louisiana Department of Revenue guidance on the post-28 Apr 2026 Schedule III change was located. Follow the mechanism-based analysis in Part 2; do not publish Louisiana as "decoupled" on directory authority.
  4. Current legis.la.gov verbatim text — RE-CHECK REQUIRED. Several passages in both runs were read via Justia republications of the Louisiana Laws or search-indexed legis.la.gov text because the legis.la.gov law page could not be opened in full in the window. Re-open current legis.la.gov text before quoting as current official text, in particular: R.S. 40:961, 40:964, 40:966(C)(2)(f), 40:1046 (including Acts 513/514 of 2025 subjects and the visiting-patient form-approver post-Act 693), 40:1046.1, 40:1046.2, 40:1046.3, 40:1046.4, 40:1047 (including any Act 150 conforming amendment), 3:1467 (fee cap), 3:1468 (total delta-9 THC vs "Total THC" wording; §1468(B)), 3:1469, 3:1471, 3:1472, 3:1481 (total-THC wording), 3:1483 (including §1483(F) and (G) 60-day clock), 3:1484 (post-Act 752 text, paragraph lettering, renewal cycle, transfer/relocation, §1484(B)(5) alcohol-premises grandfather, §1484(F) tax-suspension mechanism, §1484(H)), 3:1485 (permit-holder qualifications), and R.S. 40:981.3 / 40:966(F) interaction for patients at schools.
  5. LDH 60-day product-registration clock — UNRESOLVED. LDH page (clock resets on each documentation request) vs R.S. 3:1483(G)(1) (initial review in 60 business days; sale from day 61 if LDH fails to notify) vs an older 15-day excerpt. Do not advise day-61 sale on either text alone.
  6. Board of Pharmacy Schedule I clinician authorisation — STALE OR LIVE? The Board's Authorized Clinicians page is still live and still describes a Schedule I authorisation step, while LDH's page says the State Board of Medical Examiners no longer tracks/monitors authorised clinicians for recommendation oversight. Confirm with LDH/Board before advising a clinician that Board authorisation is still required.
  7. Medical retail transfer tension — INFERENCE ONLY. R.S. 40:1046(G)(1)(d) allows transfer of a membership interest in the permit-holding entity without department approval, while LAC 51:XXIX §2303(B) says permits are not transferable to other locations or owners. Run 2's reconciliation (new-packet-on-surrender/reissue vs no approval for a mere membership-interest transfer) is inference, not LDH guidance — verify with LDH. The same applies to §1047 university-contractor language vs post-Act 150 direct licensees, and to satellite fee practice (per holder vs per location).
  8. Mississippi reciprocity — DIRECT CONFLICT, neither side adopted. Secondary tables disagree with each other on whether Mississippi recognises out-of-state patients. Arkansas visiting-card terms and Texas Compassionate Use / residents-only rules are likewise secondary-only [VERIFY] in Run 2 Part 10.
  9. Hemp THC wording tension. R.S. 3:1468 ("total delta-9 THC") vs LDAF page ("Total THC") vs R.S. 3:1481 consumable-hemp wording — verify current §§1468/1481 on legis.la.gov before advising on THCA / total-THC measurement.
  10. USDA hemp-plan dates — UNRESOLVED. LSU 23 Dec 2019 vs USDA announcement 27 Dec 2019 for plan approval, and LSU 27 Dec 2019 vs LDAF "early February 2020" for applications opening. Reconciliation hypothesis (approval vs announcement/application-open) is not proven. Any AMS re-submission requirement for the post-11 Dec 2026 federal definition is also unconfirmed.
